In the reason in a seed all things are together and in the same place, none fighting another, none at odds or in the way. Then something comes to be in bulk, one part here, another there, and one may even hinder another, and one use another up. So too from one intellect, and the reason that comes from it, this universe rose up and stood apart. Of necessity some things became friendly and gentle, others hostile and warlike; some, willingly or unwillingly, harmed one another, and in perishing some brought about the becoming of others. And yet, doing and suffering such things, they set up one harmony among them, each sounding its own note, while reason makes the harmony over them, and one ordering for the whole.
!flag the divine Realm imposes the one harmonious act | In the Greek the things themselves, harming and destroying one another, "set up one harmony" (μίαν ... ἁρμονίαν ἐνεστήσατο), while reason makes the harmony over them; "the divine Realm" is MacKenna's.
!flag sometimes of choice and sometimes incidentally | The Greek says "some willingly, some unwillingly" (τὰ μὲν ἑκόντα, τὰ δὲ καὶ ἄκοντα).

@p
@greek ἔστι γὰρ τὸ πᾶν τόδε
For this universe is not, like the world there, intellect and reason, but shares in intellect and reason. That is why it needed harmony: intellect and necessity came together in it, and necessity drags towards the worse and carries towards unreason, since it is itself without reason; but intellect rules over necessity all the same. For the intelligible is reason only, and nothing else that came to be could be reason only. If something else came to be, it had to be less than that, and not reason; nor again could it be matter, for matter is without order. So it is a mixture. What it ends in is matter and reason; where it begins is soul, set over the mixture. We must not think that soul suffers hardship: it manages this universe with great ease, by a kind of presence.
!flag the meeting ground of Necessity and divine Reason | The Greek says "intellect and necessity came together" (συνελθόντος νοῦ καὶ ἀνάγκης), the pair of the Timaeus; MacKenna has "divine Reason" for intellect.
!flag Its two extremes are Matter and the Divine Reason | The Greek says the mixture "ends in" (λήγει) matter and reason and "begins from" soul (ὅθεν δὲ ἄρχεται ψυχή). "Divine" is MacKenna's: the reason here is the one that has come down into the world, not the intelligible.
!note Timaeus 47e-48a: this world was born mixed, from necessity and intellect, intellect ruling necessity by persuading it to lead most things to the best.

@ch III.2.3 | The whole, not the parts: the world speaks
Nor should anyone blame this world as not beautiful, or blame its cause: it came by necessity from a better nature, and even if reasoning had made it, the maker would not be ashamed of a whole all-beautiful and self-sufficient. To blame the whole for its parts is like looking at a hair and not the man, or bringing on Thersites. Listen to the world: a god made me, complete, holding gods, peoples of daemons, good souls and men happy by virtue; the heavens too are full of soul. Everything reaches for the good as it can; we must not demand the same of unequal things.

@p
No one could reasonably blame this world either, as not beautiful, or not the best of the things that have a body; nor again blame the cause of its being. First, because it exists of necessity and did not come to be from reasoning: a better nature begat it, by nature, like itself. Second, even if reasoning had made it, it would not be ashamed of what it made. For it made a whole that is altogether beautiful, sufficient to itself, and dear to itself and to its parts, both the more sovereign and the lesser, as fitting to it. So whoever blames the whole from its parts would be out of place in his charge. The parts must be looked at in relation to the whole itself, whether they agree and fit with it; and when one looks at the whole, one must not look at some small parts. That is not blaming the world, but taking one of its things by itself. It is as if, ignoring the whole man, a marvellous sight, one were to look at a hair of the whole animal, or at a toe of the parts that walk on the ground; or, by Zeus, were to pass over the other animals and take the meanest; or, leaving out a whole race, the human, were to bring Thersites into the middle.
!flag serving at once its own purpose and that of all its parts | The Greek says the whole is "dear (φίλον) to itself and to its parts", the friendship of chapter 2; "purpose" is MacKenna's.
!note Thersites is the ugliest man who came to Troy, who rails at Agamemnon and is beaten by Odysseus (Iliad II.212-277). The part is made for the whole, not the whole for the part: Laws X 903b-d.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ οὖν τὸ γενόμενον
Since what has come to be is the whole world, if you look at it you might hear it say: "A god made me, and from there I came to be complete, made from all living things, sufficient to myself and self-sufficient, needing nothing, since all things are in me: plants and animals and the nature of all things born, and many gods, and peoples of daemons, and good souls, and men happy by virtue. For it is not that the earth is adorned with all plants and animals of every kind, and the power of soul has come as far as the sea, while the whole air and ether and the whole heaven have no share in soul. Up there are all the good souls, giving life to the stars and to the well-ordered, everlasting revolution of the heaven, which, in imitation of intellect, is carried round in a circle about the same centre, wisely, for ever; for it seeks nothing outside.
!flag nations of Spirit-Beings and lofty souls | The Greek has "peoples of daemons (δαιμόνων δῆμοι) and good souls (ψυχαὶ ἀγαθαί)": daemons, not spirits, and souls that are good, not lofty.
!note The world as a living thing that holds all living things, self-sufficient and needing nothing, is the Timaeus' (30c-31b, 33c-34b), as is the circling of the heaven about the same centre in imitation of intellect (34a, 40a-b).

@p
@greek πάντα δὲ τὰ ἐν ἐμοὶ
"All the things in me reach for the good, and each attains it according to its own power. For the whole heaven hangs from it, and all my soul, and the gods in my parts, and all the animals and plants, and whatever in me seems to be without soul. Some things seem to share only in being, others in living, others more in perceiving, others already have reason, others all life." We must not demand equal things of things that are not equal. Seeing does not belong to the fingers, but to the eyes; to a finger belongs something else: to be a finger, I think, and to have what is its own.

@ch III.2.4 | Fire, beasts and men: destruction, wrong and justice
Fire quenched by water is no wonder: what was made by another perishes by another, and another fire takes its place. In the bodiless heaven each thing stays; here the whole lives for ever, souls change bodies, and bodies live on in their kinds, a moving life breathed out from the still one. Animals must prey on one another, since they are not everlasting; men wrong one another reaching for the good and failing, and are punished, for nothing escapes the law of the All. Order is not for the sake of disorder: there is disorder because order is brought in from outside. Free beings turn sometimes to the worse; the first small turn grows, and justice follows. Only the good are happy.

@p
If fire is quenched by water, and something else destroyed by fire, do not wonder. Something else brought it into being, and, since it was not brought into being by itself, it was destroyed by another. It came into being through the destruction of another, and its own destruction, if that is so, would bring nothing terrible to it; and in place of the fire destroyed there is another fire. In the bodiless heaven each thing stays as it is. But in this heaven the whole lives for ever, and so do all its honoured and sovereign parts, while the souls, changing bodies, come to be now in one form, now in another; and, when it can, a soul stands outside becoming and is with the soul of the All. Bodies live by their form, and as wholes, each of them, since animals will come from them and be nourished from them: for life here is moving, but there unmoved. Motion had to come from rest, and from the life that stays in itself another life had to come out of it, a life breathing and not at rest, the breath of the life that is still.
!flag individual or partial things exist by virtue of Universals | The Greek says "bodies live by their form (κατ’ εἶδος), and as wholes each" (καθ’ ὅλα ἕκαστα): bodies live on in their kinds and as whole masses, though single ones perish. "Universals" are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ζῴων δὲ εἰς ἄλληλα
Animals' attacks on one another, and their destruction, are necessary, for they did not come to be everlasting. They came to be because reason took hold of all matter, and had all things in itself, since they are there in the heaven above; for where would they have come from, if they were not there? Men's wrongs to one another might have as their cause a reaching for the good; failing through their inability to attain it, they turn on one another. But when they do wrong they pay the penalty, made worse in their souls by the activities of vice, and set in a worse place; for nothing set in the law of the All ever escapes it.
!flag since things here are derived | The Greek says "for they did not come to be everlasting" (οὐ γὰρ ἀίδια ἐγένετο): animals must die, and so may be eaten; "derived" is MacKenna's.
!note Laws X 904a-905b: the soul that grows worse goes to a worse place, and "you will never be neglected by this justice of the gods, not if you make yourself small and sink into the depths of the earth".

@p
@greek ἔστι δὲ οὐ διὰ τὴν ἀταξίαν
Order is not for the sake of disorder, nor law for the sake of lawlessness, as someone thinks, so that those better things might come to be, and might show, because of the worse. Order is there because of order, which is brought in from outside. There is disorder because there is order, and because of law and reason; and lawlessness and folly because there is reason. It is not that the better made the worse, but that the things that needed to receive the better could not receive them, through their own nature, or by chance and the hindrance of others. For what has its order brought in from outside may fail to attain it, either through itself and from itself, or through another and from another; and it suffers much from others too, even when those who act do not intend it, and are aiming at something else. Living things that have a self-determined motion of their own may lean now towards the better, now towards the worse.
!note "As someone thinks": so Chrysippus, who argued that goods could not exist without evils, as justice without injustice (Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights VII.1).

@p
@greek τὴν δὲ πρὸς τὰ χείρω τροπὴν
It is perhaps not worth asking where the turn towards the worse comes from. A small turn at the start, going on in that direction, always makes the error wider and greater; and there is the body with it, and, of necessity, desire. The first step, the sudden one, overlooked and not taken back at once, has even made a choice of what one fell into. Justice follows, at any rate. It is not unjust that one who has become of such a kind should suffer what follows from his state; nor should we demand that happiness belong to those who have not done what is worthy of happiness. Only the good are happy; that is why the gods too are happy.
!flag ends by establishing a set habit where there was at first only a fall | The Greek says the first slip, overlooked, "made a choice (αἵρεσιν) of what one fell into": the fall becomes a choice, not a habit.

@ch III.2.5 | Poverty, disease and vice in the whole
If souls can be happy here, those who are not must blame their own weakness in the contest where virtue's prizes are set out. Poverty and disease are nothing to the good and useful to the bad, and they too serve the whole: reason uses what perishes for new births, and vice becomes a pattern of justice and wakes the mind. Evil is not there for this; but it is the mark of the greatest power to use evils well. Evil is a lack of good, necessary here because the good is in something other than itself.

@p
If, then, souls can be happy in this universe, and some are not happy, we must not blame the place but their own weakness, which could not compete well where the prizes of virtue are set out. And what is terrible if those who have not become divine do not have a divine life? Poverty and disease are nothing to the good, and of use to the bad; and those who have bodies must fall ill. Nor are these things wholly useless for the ordering and completing of the whole. When some things perish, the reason of the All uses what has perished for the becoming of others (for nothing anywhere escapes being held by it); so too, when the body is harmed, and the soul that suffers such things is weakened, what is taken over by disease and vice is put under another chain and another order. Some of these things, like poverty and disease, have been of use to those who suffered them; and vice has done something useful for the whole, becoming a pattern of justice, an example of it, and furnishing many useful things from itself. For it has made men watchful, and wakes up intellect and understanding in those who stand against the ways of wickedness; and it makes them learn what a good thing virtue is, by setting beside it the evils the wicked have. Evils did not come to be for these reasons; but, as has been said, since they have come to be, reason uses them too for what is needed. This is the mark of the greatest power: to be able to use even evils well, and to be able to use things that have become formless for other forms.
!flag Men are not born divine | The Greek asks "what is terrible if those who have not become divine do not have a divine life?" (μὴ θείους δὲ γενομένους): becoming divine is something done, as in I.2, not a matter of birth.
!flag it acts as a lesson in right doing | The Greek says vice became "a pattern of justice" (παράδειγμα δίκης): in the punishment it brings, an example of justice done, not a lesson in right doing.
!flag to make it the material of unknown forms | The Greek says "for other forms" (εἰς ἑτέρας μορφάς), not unknown ones.
!note The prizes of virtue: Republic X 613b-614a, where the just, like good runners, carry off the prizes in the end.

@p
@greek ὅλως δὲ τὸ κακὸν
In general, we must set down evil as a lack of good; and there must be a lack of good here, because the good is in something else. That other thing, in which the good is, being other than the good, makes the lack; for it was not good. That is why evils cannot be destroyed: because some things are less than others in relation to the nature of the good, and because things are other than the good, though they took the cause of their existence from there, and became such by being far away.
!note Theaetetus 176a: "evils can never pass away, for there must always be something opposed to the good"; they have their seat not among the gods but in mortal nature and this place.

@ch III.2.6 | The good poor, the bad in power
But what of the undeserved lot, the good in evils and the bad in the opposite? True, nothing is evil to the good, nor good to the bad; but the fitting and the deserved would be the work of the best providence, and it seems unfitting that the bad should be masters and rulers of cities and the decent their slaves, that the wicked should win wars and abuse their prisoners. A maker must look to the whole, but order the parts rightly too, above all those with life and reason; providence must reach everything. So it must be shown how each of these things is well.

@p
Then there is the undeserved: when the good have evils, and the bad the opposite. To say that nothing is evil to the good, nor again good to the bad, is rightly said. But why does what is against nature fall to the one, and what is according to nature to the wicked? How is it a fine thing to distribute in this way? Yet if what is according to nature adds nothing to being happy, and what is against nature takes nothing away from the evil in the bad, what difference does it make whether it is this way or that? No more than if one man is beautiful in body and another ugly. But the fitting, the proportionate and the deserved would have been there in that other way, and now are not; and that would have belonged to the best providence. And indeed, that the bad should be masters and rulers of cities, and the decent slaves, was not fitting, even if these things bring no addition to the getting of good and evil. And yet a wicked ruler could do the most lawless things; and the bad win in wars, and do every shameful thing to the prisoners they take.
!flag why should what essentially offends our nature fall to the good | The Greek says simply "what is against nature" (τὰ παρὰ φύσιν), and "what is according to nature" for its opposite: the Stoics' names for sickness, poverty and the like, and for health and wealth. MacKenna makes them what "offends our nature" and what it "demands".
!note The Stoics called health, wealth and their like "according to nature" and their opposites "against nature", but held both indifferent to happiness, which lies in virtue alone (Diogenes Laertius VII.102-107).

@p
@greek πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ἀπορεῖν ποιεῖ
All these things leave one at a loss how they come about if there is providence. For even if whoever is going to make anything must look to the whole, it is right to set the parts too in their due places, above all when they have soul and life and reason; and providence must reach to all things, and its work must be just this, to neglect nothing. If, then, we say that this universe hangs from intellect, and that its power has come to all things, we must try to show how each of these things is well.
!flag we cannot be absolved from the attempt to show in what way the detail of this sphere is just | The Greek says "how each of these things is well" (ὅπῃ ἕκαστα τούτων καλῶς ἔχει), not that it is just.
!note Laws X 902e-903a: the gods, like a good craftsman or physician, take care of the small as well as the great.

@ch III.2.7 | The mixed world; the souls' own works; does providence reach the earth?
In a mixture we must not demand what the unmixed has, but praise what it could take from reason: a man of flesh and bone is not the man in intellect. The harm that bad souls do stays with them, and the blame is the chooser's: souls were to have motions of their own, and were the world's before the world was. But the good poor, the bad rich and ruling? Providence reaches the earth, as plants and animals show; to say it reaches but does not rule is like saying that a man's head is nature's work and the rest is chance's.

@p
First, then, we must grasp that those who look for the good in what is mixed must not demand in every way as much good as the unmixed has, nor look for the first things in the second. Since the world has a body too, we must allow that something comes into the All from this as well, and praise what the mixture could receive from reason, if it lacks nothing of this. If someone were looking for the most beautiful of men perceived by the senses, he would surely not think it right that this one be the same as the man in intellect. He would be content with the maker if, though the man is in flesh and sinews and bones, the maker had taken hold of him with reason, so as to make these beautiful too, and to let reason come up over matter. Setting this down, we must go on from here to what we are looking for: for perhaps in these things we would find the wonder of providence, and of the power from which this universe came to be.
!flag must begin from this principle of gradation | The Greek says only "setting this down" (ταῦτα τοίνυν ὑποθέμενον), that the mixed must not be judged by the unmixed; "gradation" is MacKenna's.
!note "The man in intellect" is the form of man, which Plotinus places in intellect (VI.7.4-6); the man of the senses is its image in flesh.

@p
@greek ὅσα μὲν οὖν ἔργα ψυχῶν
As for the works of souls that stay in the souls that do the worse things, such as all the harm bad souls have done to others, and bad souls to one another: unless one blames what provides for their being bad at all, it is not fitting to demand an account of providence or to call it to answer, when we give the blame to the soul that chose. For it has been said that souls too had to have motions of their own, and that they are not souls only, but already living things; and it is no wonder that, being what they are, they have a life that follows from it. They did not come because there was a world: before the world they had it in them to be the world's, to care for it, to bring it into being, to manage it and to make it, in whatever way they do: whether they stay above and give something of themselves, or come down, or some do one and some the other. We are not asking about this now, but only saying that, whichever way it is, providence is not to be blamed for these things.
!flag it is not abstract Spirit | The Greek says souls are "not souls only, but already living things" (οὐ ψυχαὶ μόνον, ἀλλὰ ζῷα ἤδη): souls joined to bodies. "Abstract Spirit" is MacKenna's.
!flag to presuppose it | The Greek says "to bring it into being" (ὑφιστάναι), to make it subsist.
!note Republic X 617e: "The blame is the chooser's; god is blameless" (αἰτία ἑλομένου· θεὸς ἀναίτιος), the words read out to the souls about to choose their lives. Plotinus' "giving the blame to the soul that chose" (αἰτίαν ἑλομένῃ διδόντας) takes them up.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ὅταν πρὸς τοὺς ὑπεναντίους
But what when one looks at the evils set against the opposite people: the good poor, and the wicked rich, and the worse having more of what men, being men, need to have, and ruling, with the peoples and the cities in their hands? Is it because providence does not reach as far as the earth? But that the other things come to be by reason is a witness that it does reach as far as the earth: for animals and plants share in reason and soul and life. Then it reaches, but does not rule? But since the All is one living thing, this would be as if someone said that a man's head and face come to be by nature and reason ruling, but gave the rest to other causes, chances or necessities, and said it had turned out poor because of this, or through the weakness of nature. It is neither holy nor pious to grant that these things are not well, and to find fault with the work.
!flag And even granting that those less noble members are not in themselves admirable | The Greek says it is neither holy nor pious "to grant that these things are not well (ἐνδόντας τὸ μὴ καλῶς ταῦτα ἔχειν) and to find fault with the work": the granting is the impiety. MacKenna has Plotinus grant it.

@ch III.2.8 | Men between gods and beasts; the lazy and the armed
In every animal the upper parts are finest; men are in the middle and below, with the heaven and its gods above, and the earth like a single star. Men wonder at wrongdoing because they take man for the best thing in the All; but he lies between gods and beasts. The beast-like drag the middle ones about; the better are beaten in so far as they are worse and unprepared. As well-trained but uneducated boys rob soft ones, the lazy pay for their laziness, the wolves for being wolves. In war the law saves the brave, not those who pray, as harvests come to those who farm. Bad men rule through the cowardice of the ruled, and that is just.

@p
It remains, then, to look for how these things are well, and how they share in order; or at least how they are not badly. In every animal the upper parts, the face and the head, are more beautiful, and the middle and lower parts are not their equal. Men are in the middle and below; above are the heaven and the gods in it. The greatest part of the world is gods and the whole heaven round about, and the earth is like a centre, and like one of the stars. People wonder at the wrong among men because they think man the honoured thing in the All, as though there were nothing wiser. But he lies in the middle between gods and beasts, and leans towards both: some become like the one, some like the other, and most are in between. Those who have been made bad, so that they come near to irrational animals and beasts, drag the middle ones about and force them. These are better than those who force them, but they are mastered by the worse in so far as they are worse themselves: they are not good, and have not prepared themselves not to suffer it.
!flag they have not trained themselves in self-defence | The Greek says they "are not good, and have not prepared themselves not to suffer" (οὐκ εἰσὶν ἀγαθοὶ οὐδὲ παρεσκεύασαν αὑτοὺς μὴ παθεῖν): what they lack is goodness, not training in self-defence.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν παῖδες ἀσκήσαντες
Suppose boys who have trained their bodies, but whose souls, for lack of education, are worse than their bodies, were to win at wrestling against those trained neither in body nor in soul, and snatch their food and take their soft clothes: what would the thing be but a joke? Or how would it not be right for the lawgiver, too, to allow the others to suffer this, as the penalty for their idleness and luxury? Training grounds had been set out for them, and through idleness and soft and slack living they let themselves become fattened lambs, the prey of wolves. For those who do this, the first penalty is to be wolves and ill-starred men; and then what such men must suffer is laid up for them too. For it does not stop here, with dying when they have become bad; but on what went before there always follows what is according to reason and nature, worse things for the worse, and better for the better.
!flag in the disaster to their human quality | The Greek says their first penalty is to be "wolves and ill-starred men" (λύκοις εἶναι καὶ κακοδαίμοσιν ἀνθρώποις): men with an evil daemon, unhappy, whose wickedness is itself their misfortune.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ οὐ παλαίστρα τὰ τοιαῦτα
But such things are not a wrestling school, for there it is play. When the boys have grown bigger, both kinds still foolish, both must now gird themselves and have weapons, and the sight is finer than at wrestling practice. But now some are unarmed, and those who have armed themselves win. Then it was not for a god to fight for the unwarlike himself: the law says that men are saved from wars by being brave, not by praying. Nor do they bring home harvests by praying, but by taking care of the earth; nor are they healthy if they do not take care of their health. Nor must we be angry if the bad get more harvest, or if it goes better for them altogether, when they are the ones who farm.
!flag This at once brings us outside the gymnasium with its fun for boys | The Greek says "such things are not a wrestling school, for there it is play" (ἀλλ’ οὐ παλαίστρα τὰ τοιαῦτα: παιδιὰ γὰρ ἐκεῖ): life is not the wrestling school, but war.
!flag Not even a God would have the right to deal a blow for the unwarlike | The Greek says "it was not for a god to fight for the unwarlike himself" (οὐ θεὸν ἔδει ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀπολέμων αὐτὸν μάχεσθαι): what is fitting, not what is a god's right.

@p
@greek ἔπειτα γελοῖον τὰ μὲν ἄλλα
Then it is ridiculous for men to do all the other things in life by their own judgement, even if they do not do them in the way dear to the gods, and to be saved by the gods alone, without even doing the things through which the gods command them to be saved. And so death is better for them than to go on living in a way that the laws in the All do not want them to live. If the opposite happened, and peace were kept amid every folly and vice, the affairs of providence would be in a careless state, letting the worse rule in this way. The bad rule through the cowardice of those they rule: for this is just, and the other is not.
!flag Yet death would be better for us | The Greek says death is better "for them" (αὐτοῖς), those who will not do what the gods command; MacKenna takes it to us all.
!flag the triumph of weaklings would not be just | The Greek says only "this is just, and that is not" (τοῦτο γὰρ δίκαιον, καὶ οὐκ ἐκεῖνο): it is just that the cowardly be ruled, and the other way would not be; "the triumph of weaklings" is MacKenna's reading of "the other".
!note Men between gods and beasts: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a27-29 (who cannot live in a city is a beast or a god), and Plato's man that may grow divine or bestial (Timaeus 90a-d, 91d-92c). That safety in war comes to the brave and not to those who pray is a commonplace of Greek proverb and oratory (Xenophon, Cyropaedia I.6.5-6).

@ch III.2.9 | Providence keeps us ourselves; man in the middle; the beasts
Providence must not make us nothing: if it were all, it would be of nothing. It comes to man to keep him man, living by its law: a good life for the good, now and after, the opposite for the bad. The bad may not pray to be saved by others, nor that gods or good men rule them for them. Man, a middle creature who chose his rank, is not let perish but always drawn upward; he keeps his reason and shares in wisdom, intellect, craft and justice, a beautiful work as far as he can be. Nor should anyone blame the lesser animals: they bite, but they have their uses, and why wonder that wild beasts defend themselves?

@p
For providence must not be such that we are nothing. If providence were all things, and there were only providence, it would not exist either: for of what would it still be the providence? There would be only the divine. That exists now too; but it has come to something else, not to do away with the other, but, coming upon something, upon a man, say, there was providence over him keeping him a man: that is, living by the law of providence, which means doing what its law says. And it says that for those who have become good there will be a good life, now and laid up for afterwards too, and for the bad the opposite.
!flag It would not be just, because Providence cannot be a something reducing us to nothingness | The Greek begins "For providence must not be such that we are nothing" (οὐ γὰρ δὴ οὕτως τὴν πρόνοιαν εἶναι δεῖ, ὥστε μηδὲν ἡμᾶς εἶναι); "It would not be just" is MacKenna's link to the last line of chapter 8.
!flag is to annihilate the Universe | The Greek says that providence, if it were all, "would not exist either: for of what would it still be?" (οὐδ’ ἂν εἴη: τίνος γὰρ ἂν ἔτι εἴη;): providence itself would vanish, having nothing to provide for.

@p
@greek κακοὺς δὲ γενομένους ἀξιοῦν
For those who have become bad to ask that others be their saviours, when they have thrown themselves away, is not a lawful prayer. So the gods are not to rule them in each detail, leaving their own life to do it; nor are the good men, who live another life, better than human rule, to be their rulers. For the bad themselves never took care that good men should become rulers of the others, so that they themselves might be cared for; they envy anyone who grows good of himself. And yet there would have been more good men, if they had made such men their leaders.
!flag their prayers should bring others to sacrifice themselves for their sakes | The Greek says it is not a lawful prayer for the bad "to ask that others be their saviours, having thrown themselves away" (ἑαυτοὺς προεμένους): it is the bad who have given themselves up, and nothing is said of others sacrificing themselves.
!flag nor do they take any steps to improve themselves | The Greek says they never took care that good rulers should come to be "so that they themselves might be cared for" (ὅπως αὐτοὶ εἶεν ἐπιμελούμενοι); nothing is said of improving themselves.
!note Republic I 347b-d: the good will not rule for money or honour, and must be made to by the penalty of being ruled by worse men; Republic VI 488a-489c: the sailors who will not have the true pilot.

@p
@greek γενόμενον τοίνυν ζῷον οὐκ ἄριστον
Man, then, has come to be a living thing that is not the best, but holds a middle rank, and has chosen it. Yet in the place where he lies he is not let perish by providence, but is always brought back up towards what is above by all kinds of means, which the divine uses to make virtue the stronger. The human race has not lost its being rational: it shares, if not to the highest degree, in wisdom and intellect and craft and justice, the justice at least of each towards one another (and those they wrong, they think they wrong justly, since they deserve it). So man is a beautiful work, as beautiful as he can be, and, woven into the All, he has a lot better than all the other animals on earth.
!flag to increase the dominance of moral value | The Greek says "making virtue the stronger" (ἐπικρατεστέραν ἀρετὴν ποιοῦν).
!flag wisdom, intelligence, executive power and right doing | The Greek has "wisdom, intellect, craft (τέχνης) and justice (δικαιοσύνης)": craft, not executive power, and justice, not right doing.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὅσα ἐλάττω
Nor does anyone who has intellect blame the other animals that are less than he, which bring adornment to the earth. It would be ridiculous if one blamed them because they bite men, as if men ought to live asleep. These too must exist. Some of their benefits are plain, and many that were not obvious time has found out, so that none of them is there in vain, even for men. It is ridiculous, too, to blame many of them for being wild, when there are wild men too. And if they do not trust men, but, not trusting them, defend themselves, what is there to wonder at?
!note The Stoics defended providence by the uses of animals (Cicero, On the nature of the gods II.154-162); Chrysippus said that bugs are useful for waking us, and mice for making us careful not to leave things about (Plutarch, On Stoic self-contradictions 1044d).

@ch III.2.10 | Unwilling, yet their own doing
If men are bad unwillingly, how can wrongdoers be blamed? And if necessity, from the heavens or a first principle, makes them bad, is reason not unjust? Wrong is unwilling as all error is, but the wrongdoers do it themselves. The necessity is not from outside; the heavens do not take away what is up to us, or men could not set themselves against the gods. Given a first principle, the rest follows, but men too are principles, moved by their own nature towards the beautiful, a principle that is its own master.

@p
But if men are bad unwillingly, and are such not willingly, one could neither blame those who do wrong, nor blame those who suffer, as if they suffered through their own fault. And if it is necessary that they become bad in this way, whether by the revolution of the heavens or by the first principle giving what follows from it, then it is so by nature. And if reason itself is what makes them, how is this not unjust? But they are unwilling in the sense that error is unwilling. This does not do away with the doers themselves acting from themselves; it is because they themselves act that they themselves err. Or they would not have erred at all, if they were not themselves the doers.
!flag Men are no doubt involuntary sinners in the sense that they do not actually desire to sin | The Greek says they are unwilling "because error is unwilling" (ὅτι ἁμαρτία ἀκούσιον), Socrates' saying that no one errs willingly; nothing is said of desire.
!note "No one errs willingly": Protagoras 345d-e, Gorgias 509e, Laws V 731c and IX 860d.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ τῆς ἀνάγκης
The necessity is not from outside, but lies in its holding altogether. And the revolution of the heavens is not such that nothing is up to us. For if everything came from outside, it would be just as those who made it wanted; so men would not set themselves against them, nor would there be impious men, if the gods made everything. As it is, this comes from men themselves. When a principle is given, what comes next is carried through, all the other principles there are being taken along into the sequence too; and men too are principles. At any rate, they are moved towards beautiful things by their own nature, and this principle is its own master.
!flag exists only in the sense of a universal relationship | The Greek says the necessity is "not from outside, but in that it holds altogether" (ἀλλ’ ὅτι πάντως): the deed, once done by the doer, is done of necessity; nothing is said of a relationship.
!flag Now Men are Principles, or, at least, they are moved | The Greek says "men too are principles" (ἀρχαὶ δὲ καὶ ἄνθρωποι), without hedging; "at any rate" (γοῦν) gives the proof, that they are moved by their own nature.
!note "What is up to us" (τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν) and the heavens' part in our doings are argued in III.1.5-10 and II.3.

@ch III.2.11 | Reason wills the variety: the painting and the play
Is everything so by natural necessity, as good as it can be? Rather reason rules and makes all, and wills even the so-called evils, not wishing all to be good, as a craftsman does not make the whole animal eyes. So reason made gods, daemons, men and animals, not from envy but out of the variety of intellect. We blame it as the untrained blame a painter's colours, or a play for having slaves and rustics among its heroes.

@p
Is each thing, then, so by natural necessities and sequences, and well, as far as it can be? Or not so: reason makes all these things, ruling, and wills them so, and itself makes the so-called evils according to reason, not wishing all things to be good; as a craftsman would not make all the parts of an animal eyes. So reason did not make all things gods, but some gods, some daemons, a second nature, then men and animals after them: not from envy, but by a reason that has an intellectual variety. We are like those unskilled in painting who blame the painter because the colours are not beautiful everywhere, when he has given each place what fits it; or like someone who finds fault with a play because not all in it are heroes, but there is a servant too, and a rustic who speaks coarsely. But it is not beautiful if one takes out the worse characters; it is made complete by them too.
!flag it cannot desire all to be good | The Greek says reason does "not wish (οὐ βουλόμενος) all things to be good": it is reason's choice, not something it cannot do.
!flag celestial spirits, the intermediate order | The Greek says "daemons, a second nature" (δαίμονας, δευτέραν φύσιν).
!note "Not from envy": Timaeus 29e, the maker was good, and in the good no envy ever arises about anything. The eyes: Republic IV 420c-d, where a statue's eyes, the finest part, are not to be painted purple, but each part given its own colour, to make the whole beautiful.

@ch III.2.12 | Souls are parts of reason, set where they deserve
If reason, fitting itself into matter, made things as it is, unlike in its parts, nothing could be more beautiful than its work, and a reason made of things all alike would be no reason. But if it brought souls in from outside and forced them against their nature, how is that right? Rather the souls are like parts of it, and it sets them where they deserve to be.

@p
If, then, reason itself, fitting itself into matter, made these things, being what it is, unlike in its parts, and being so from what is before it, then what has come to be, having come to be in this way, could not have anything else more beautiful than itself. Reason would not have come from things all like and close to one another; and this way is not to be blamed, since it is all things, each one differently. But if it brought in other things from outside itself, souls, say, and forced them against their own nature, fitting many of them into its work towards the worse, how is that right? We must say that the souls too are like parts of it, and that it does not make them worse to fit them in, but places them where it is fitting for them, according to what they deserve.
!flag retaining, that is, the hostility to partition | The Greek says reason is "unlike in its parts" (ἀνόμοιος τοῖς μέρεσιν), made of different reasons; MacKenna makes it averse to being divided, the opposite of the point.
!note "Souls, say": the Greek text here reads οἷνον φυχάς, a misprint for οἷον ψυχάς.

@ch III.2.13 | Past lives, Adrasteia, and the art in small things
Reason looks not only at the present but at past and future periods: the bad master becomes a slave, the rich who misused wealth poor, the unjust killer is killed, unjustly by the killer but justly for him; one who killed his mother is born a woman and killed by her son. This order is Adrasteia, Justice and a wonderful wisdom. The same art shows in the smallest things, animals, fruits, leaves, flowers, always made anew. Nothing changes at random: the divine makes as its nature is, and its nature brings out the beautiful and the just.

@p
For we must not throw out that account either which says that reason does not look each time to the present, but to the periods before and again to what is to come, so as to set from there what each deserves. It changes those who were masters before into slaves, if they were bad masters, and because this is good for them; it makes poor those who used wealth badly, and because it is no harm to the good to be poor; it has those who killed unjustly be killed, unjustly on the part of the one who does it, but justly for the one who suffers it; and it brings the one who is to suffer together with one fit to do to him what he had to suffer. For no one is a slave by accident, nor a captive by chance, nor outraged in body at random: he once did the things he now suffers. One who killed his mother will be killed by a son, having become a woman; and one who raped a woman will be a woman, to be raped.
!flag Those that have money will be made poor | The Greek says reason makes them poor "if they used wealth badly" (εἰ κακῶς ἐχρήσαντο πλούτῳ), not all who have money.
!flag a man that wrongs a woman will become a woman, to be wronged | The Greek says "raped" (βιασάμενος ... ἵνα βιασθῇ): violence, not a wrong in general.
!note Laws IX 872d-873a: the old story told by priests, that one who has killed his mother must be born again a woman, and be killed by her own children.

@p
@greek ὅθεν καὶ θεία φήμη
That is where the divine saying of Adrasteia comes from: for this ordering is truly Adrasteia, and truly Justice, and a wonderful wisdom. From what we see in the All we must judge that the order of the whole is always something of this kind: it reaches to everything, even the very smallest. The art is wonderful not only in divine things but also in those one might have supposed providence would despise as small: such as the varied wonder-working in any animal at all, and the fair form that reaches as far as the plants, in fruits and even in leaves, and their easy blossoming, slender and varied; and that it was not made once and then stopped, but is always being made, as the things above move in the same way, though not alike.
!note Adrasteia, "she whom none escapes", is the goddess of inescapable justice. Phaedrus 248c gives "the law of Adrasteia" for the souls' fall and return; Republic V 451a, "I bow to Adrasteia", is said before words that may be punished.

@p
@greek μετατίθεται τοίνυν τὰ μετατιθέμενα
So the things that change change not at random, nor take other shapes at random, but as is beautiful, and as it would befit divine powers to make. For all that is divine makes as its nature is; and its nature is according to its substance; and its substance is what brings out together, in its activities, the beautiful and the just. For if these are not there, where would they be?
!flag produce as one thing the desirable and the just | The Greek says "the beautiful (τὸ καλόν) and the just": the beautiful, not the desirable.

@ch III.2.14 | Each kind sufficient; the part is not the whole
The order is according to intellect without reasoning, such that the best reasoner would wonder that reasoning could find nothing better, as in the works of each nature. No kind can be blamed for not being like the eternal things, or for lacking horns: reason had to reach everything, and the lesser must be in the greater and the parts unequal. Above, each is all; below, each is not all, and a man as a part is not the whole, nor can he be asked to reach the peak of virtue. Yet the whole does not grudge the part that grows finer, and a man may shine like the stars on a great statue.

@p
So the order is according to intellect in such a way that it is without reasoning, and yet in such a way that, if someone could use reasoning in the best way, he would wonder that reasoning would not have found how to make it otherwise. This is known in the natures of single things too, as they come to be, always in a more intellectual way than by an ordering of reasoning. In each of the kinds that are always coming to be, then, one cannot blame the reason that makes them, unless one thinks each ought to have come to be like the things that have not come to be but are eternal, always the same, among the intelligibles and among the things of sense; asking for a greater addition of good, and not holding the form given to each sufficient: blaming this animal, say, because it has no horns. Such a man does not see that reason could not but reach to everything, but that the lesser had to be in the greater, and the parts in the whole, and that they could not be equal: or they would not be parts.
!flag displays the Divine Intelligence to a degree in which no arranging by reason could express it | The Greek says the natures of single things come to be "in a more intellectual way than by the ordering of reasoning" (νοερώτερον ἢ κατὰ λογισμοῦ διάταξιν); "the Divine Intelligence" is MacKenna's.
!flag In that case, things of the Intellectual realm and things of the realm of sense must remain one unbroken identity for ever | The Greek speaks of the eternal things "among the intelligibles and among the things of sense" (ἔν τε νοητοῖς ἔν τε αἰσθητοῖς), the intelligible world and the everlasting heavens, which are always the same; it does not say the two realms would be one.

@p
@greek τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἄνω πᾶν πάντα
For above, everything is all things; but below, each thing is not all things. And a man, each one, in so far as he is a part, is not the whole. But if somewhere in some parts there is also something else, which is not a part, by this the part is that whole too. So the single man, as such, is not to be required to be perfect, to the height of virtue: for then he would no longer be a part. Nor, again, does the whole grudge the part that has been adorned to greater worth; for, adorned with greater worth, it makes the whole more beautiful. It becomes such by being made like the whole, and, as it were, allowed to be such and set in order so, that in the place of man too something might shine out in him, as the stars do in the divine heaven; and that what is perceived from here might be as of a great and beautiful statue, whether living or made by the art of Hephaestus, with stars glittering on its face, and others on its breast, and wherever the position of the stars set there would allow.
!flag with stars radiant not only in the ears and on the brow | The Greek says "on the face" (κατὰ τὸ πρόσωπον) and on the breast; the ears are MacKenna's.
!flag wrought in the furnaces of craftsmanship | The Greek says "made by the art of Hephaestus" (τέχνῃ Ἡφαίστου), the smith god.
!note Hephaestus' golden maidservants, made by his art, move, speak and think like the living (Iliad XVIII.417-420). "Above, everything is all things": V.8.4, where in the intelligible world each thing has all in itself and sees all in another.

@ch III.2.15 | The war of all things, a play on a stage
Taken one by one, things are well; but their weaving together brings a harder question: beasts eat one another, men attack one another, there is war without truce, and reason is said to have made it so. The old answer, that matter is to blame, no longer serves, since reason is the principle of all. The eating is a change of living things, which could not last anyway, like the murdered actor who comes back in another mask; and it is better than no life at all. Men's wars are like a war dance: their concerns are play, death is nothing terrible, possessions were never theirs. Murders and sacked cities are scenes on a stage; it is the outer shadow of a man that weeps. Only the serious is to be taken seriously; the rest of man is a toy, and tears are no proof of evil.

@p
So it is with each thing looked at by itself. But the weaving together of these things, born and always being born, would bring a halt and a difficulty: over the eating of one another among the other animals, and the attacks of men on one another; and that there is always war, which never takes a pause or a truce; and above all if reason has made it so, and it is said to be well so. For that account no longer helps those who say this: that things are well, as far as they can be, and that matter is the cause of their being so, of their being less well; and that evils cannot be destroyed. For if things had to be so, and it is well so, then matter did not come in and get the mastery, but was brought in so that things might be so; or rather, it too is so through the cause of reason. Reason, then, is the principle, and all things are reason, and what comes to be according to it, and is ordered together at its coming to be, is altogether so.
!flag The Divine Reason is the beginning and the end | The Greek says "reason, then, is the principle, and all things are reason" (ἀρχὴ οὖν λόγος καὶ πάντα λόγος); "divine" and "the end" are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek τίς οὖν ἡ τοῦ πολέμου
What, then, is the necessity of the undeclared war among animals and among men? Their eating of one another is necessary, being changes of animals which could not stay as they are for ever, even if no one killed them. And if, at the time when they had to go, they had to go in such a way as to be of use to others, why grudge it? What if, once eaten, they grew again as others? It is as if on the stage an actor who has been murdered changes his costume and comes on again in another mask: he has not truly died. If, then, dying is a change of body, as of costume there, or for some a complete putting off of body, as there the complete exit from the stage of one who will never come back to compete again, what would be terrible in such a change of animals into one another, which is much better than if they had never come to be at all? For then there would be a desert of life, and no power for the life that is in something else; but as it is, a great life in the All makes all things and varies them in its living, and cannot bear not to be always making beautiful and shapely living toys.
!flag the necessity of this bandit war | The Greek says "the undeclared war" (τοῦ πολέμου τοῦ ἀκηρύκτου), a war without heralds, which no truce ends; nothing is said of bandits.
!note "An undeclared war" (πόλεμος ἀκήρυκτος) of all against all is what the Cretan in Plato's Laws says nature has set between every city and every other (Laws I 626a).

@p
@greek ἀνθρώπων δὲ ἐπ’ ἀλλήλους ὅπλα
Men, mortal as they are, turning their weapons on one another, and fighting in a seemly order, as they do in play in the war dances, show that all human concerns are games, and tell us that deaths are nothing terrible, and that to die in wars and battles is to be a little ahead of what comes in old age, going away sooner and coming back. And if they are robbed of their goods while they live, they might come to know that these were not theirs before either, and that for the robbers themselves the possession is a joke, since others will rob them of it; for even for those who are not robbed, possession turns out worse than being robbed.
!note The war dances (πυρρίχαι) were dances in armour, imitating the moves of battle (Laws VII 815a).

@p
@greek ὥσπερ δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν θεάτρων
As on the stages of the theatres, so we must watch murders and all deaths, and the taking and sacking of cities: all are changes of scene and of costume, and acted laments and wails. For here too, in each thing in life, it is not the soul within but the shadow of the man outside that wails and laments and does everything, on a stage that is the whole earth, where men have set up stages in many places. Such are the works of a man who knows only how to live the lower and outer life, and does not know that in his tears and his serious things he is playing. Only the serious man should be serious, in serious works; the other man is a toy. Toys too are taken seriously by those who do not know how to be serious, and who are toys themselves. But if a serious man plays along with them and suffers such things, let him know that he has fallen into a children's game, having put off the mask he wore. And if Socrates too plays, he plays in the outer Socrates. We must bear this in mind as well: we must not take weeping and lamenting as proofs that things are evil, since children too weep and wail over things that are not evil.
!flag the other kind of man is himself a futility | The Greek says "the other man is a toy" (ὁ δ’ ἄλλος ἄνθρωπος παίγνιον), Plato's plaything of the gods; "futility" loses the image that the rest of the chapter plays on.
!flag comes to look on life with their eyes | The Greek says that a serious man who plays along and suffers such things "has fallen into a children's game, having put off the mask he wore" (τὸ περὶ αὑτὸν ἀποθέμενος πρόσωπον); "to look on life with their eyes" is MacKenna's.
!note Laws VII 803c-804b: man has been made a plaything of god, and that is the best thing about him, so we should live playing the finest games; and Laws I 644d-645b, the living puppets of the gods.

@ch III.2.16 | Reason, a life that shapes, one made of contraries
But then where are wickedness, wrong and sin, if all is well done? How is anything against nature, or impious? It would be like a poet writing an actor's part that abuses the poet. So: this reason is not pure intellect nor pure soul, but a shining out from both, a life with a reason in it. Every life is an activity that gives form, artful, like a dancer's. Coming from one intellect and one life, reason is neither one life nor one intellect, and does not give itself whole; setting part against part, it made war, and is one whole, if not one thing, like a play full of fights, or rather a harmony of opposed notes. A reason must be many and different, and the greatest difference is contrariety; so it makes contraries, and is complete by making itself contrary.

@p
But if this is well said, how will there still be wickedness? Where is wrong, and where is sin? How, when all things come to be well, can those who act do wrong or sin? And how can they be miserable, if they do not sin or do wrong? How shall we say that some things that come to be are according to nature and others against nature, if all that is done is according to nature? And how could there be any impiety towards the divine, when what makes and what is made are such? It would be as if a poet were to write an actor in a play abusing and running down the poet of the play.

@p
@greek πάλιν οὖν σαφέστερον λέγωμεν
Let us say again, more clearly, what the reason is, and how it is fitting that it is such. This reason, then (let us dare to say it: perhaps we may even hit the mark), is not unmixed intellect, nor intellect itself, nor even of the kind of pure soul, but it hangs from soul, and is as it were a shining out from both: intellect and soul, soul disposed according to intellect, begot this reason, a life that holds a reason quietly in it. Every life is an activity, even the poor one: an activity, not as fire acts, but its activity, even if there is no perception, is a motion that is not random. At any rate, whatever things it is present to, and that share in it in any way at all, at once have a reason in them, that is, they are given form; since the activity that goes with life can give form, and moves in such a way as to give form. So its activity is artful, as the dancer moving would be: for the dancer himself is like such an artful life, and the art moves him, and moves him so, since life itself is somehow of this kind. Let this be said for the sake of what we must think every life, of whatever kind, to be.
!flag Life, then, aims at pattern as does the pantomimic dancer with his set movements | The Greek says "its activity is artful (τεχνική), as the dancer moving would be": the dancer's art moves him, not a pattern set before him; and nothing is said of mime or of symbolising life.

@p
@greek ἥκων τοίνυν οὗτος ὁ λόγος
This reason, then, coming from one intellect and one life, each of them full, is neither one life nor one intellect, nor full everywhere, nor does it give itself whole and entire to those it gives to. Setting the parts against one another, and making them in need, it brought about the making and the becoming of war and battle; and so it is one whole, if not one thing. For becoming hostile to itself in its parts, it is in this way one and friendly, as the plot of a play is one, though it holds many fights in it. The play brings its conflicts, once fought out, as it were into one harmony, making as it were one tale of all the fighters; but there the fight of the things standing apart comes from one reason. So one would rather liken it to the harmony that comes from conflicting notes, and ask why there are conflicting things in the reasons.
!flag (By an imperfect communication) it sets up a conflict of part against part | The words in brackets are MacKenna's: the Greek says reason "set the parts against one another and made them in need" (ἀντιθεὶς δὲ ἀλλήλοις τὰ μέρη καὶ ποιήσας ἐνδεᾶ).

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν καὶ ἐνταῦθα ὀξὺ καὶ βαρὺ
If, then, here too reasons make high and low, and, being reasons of harmony, come together into one, into harmony itself, another and greater reason, while they are lesser and parts; and if we see contraries in the All too, white and black, hot and cold, winged and wingless, footed and footless, rational and irrational, but all parts of one living thing, the whole of things, and the All agrees with itself while its parts fight in many places, but the All is according to reason: then this one reason too must be one made of contrary reasons, such contrariety carrying its very structure, and as it were its being. For if it were not many, it would not be whole, nor would it be reason; but being reason it differs from itself, and the greatest difference is contrariety. So if it makes something other at all, and makes it other most of all, and not less, then, making it other to the highest degree, it will make contraries too, of necessity, and will be complete, not if it makes itself only into different things, but if into contrary things too.
!note Heraclitus: "what is opposed agrees, and from things that differ comes the finest harmony" (fr. B8), and "a harmony turning back on itself, as of the bow and the lyre" (fr. B51). That contrariety is the greatest difference is Aristotle's (Metaphysics X.4, 1055a3-5).

@ch III.2.17 | The good and the bad as actors in reason's play
The more reason is spread out, the more contrary its works: the world of sense is less one than its reason, more many, its parts more eager for life and for union, and lovers destroy what they love. So the good and the bad are like a dancer's contrary steps in one art. The bad are still bad, though not of themselves; and reason makes us not pardon them. As a poet gives parts to actors who already are what they are, so each soul goes to the place that fits it, and speaks impious or holy words. In this truer play the soul is the actor, taking its fortunes from the poet as costumes, and brings its own good or bad playing, and is honoured or dismissed for it. These actors play on a bigger stage and choose their places; they are fitted to the reason of the All as strings to their notes, the lesser voice too adding to the harmony, as the faint notes of a panpipe do; and the bad soul is like the executioner in a well-run city.

@p
Being such that it makes everything, it will make the things it makes much more contrary, the more they stand apart. The world of sense is less one than its reason; so it is more many, and its contrariety greater, and each thing's longing for life greater, and its love of coming into one greater. But lovers often destroy what they love, hurrying towards their own good, when it is perishable; and the longing of the part for the whole drags to itself what it can.
!flag the partial thing (a human being, for example) | The bracket is MacKenna's: the Greek speaks of the longing of any part for the whole (ἡ ἔφεσις τοῦ μέρους πρὸς τὸ ὅλον).

@p
@greek οὕτως οὖν καὶ οἱ ἀγαθοὶ
So, then, there are good and bad, as the contrary movements of a dancer come from the same art; and we shall say that one part of him is good and another bad, and that it is well so. But then are the bad no longer bad? No: their being bad is not done away with, only their being such of themselves. But perhaps there is pardon for the bad? Unless reason makes what is pardoned and what is not: and reason makes us not pardon such things.
!flag and the Reason-Principle does not excuse them | The Greek says reason "makes us not pardon such things" (ποιεῖ δὲ ὁ λόγος μηδὲ συγγνώμονας ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις εἶναι): what reason makes is our refusal to pardon.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τὸ μὲν μέρος αὐτοῦ ἀγαθὸς ἀνήρ
But if one part of it is a good man, and another a wicked one, and the wicked are the more parts, it is as in plays: the poet assigns some parts, but uses others who already are what they are. For he does not himself make the first actor, or the second or third, but giving each the words that fit him, he has already given each the place where he must be set. So too there is a place for each, one fitting the good, another the bad. Each of the two, then, according to nature and according to reason, goes to each place, the fitting one, holding the place he chose. Then he speaks and does, the one impious words and deeds, the other the contrary: for the actors were such even before the play, and give themselves to the play.

@p
@greek ἐν μὲν οὖν τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις δράμασιν
In human plays the poet gave the words, but the actors each have from themselves and of themselves their playing well or badly; for they have a work of their own, beyond the poet's lines. In the truer poem, which men with a poet's nature imitate in part, the soul is the actor, and what it plays it takes from the poet. As the actors here get their masks, their clothes, their saffron robes and their rags, so the soul itself takes its fortunes, not at random, for these too are according to reason. Fitting these to itself, it comes into tune, and orders itself to the play and to the whole reason. Then it as it were speaks out its deeds, and the other things a soul might do in its own way, as one sings a song. An actor, with his voice and his bearing, by his own beauty or ugliness, either added grace to the poem, as it would seem, or, adding the badness of his voice, did not make the play other than it was, but showed himself unseemly; and the poet of the play sent him away in disgrace, as he deserved, doing the work of a good judge, and brought the other on to greater honours and, if he had them, to finer plays, and the first to worse ones, if he had any. So the soul comes into this poem of the All and makes itself a part of the play, bringing from itself its good or bad playing; it is set in its place on its entrance, and takes all the rest apart from itself and its own deeds; and it has penalties and honours in turn.
!flag accepting from the author its entire role | The Greek says the soul takes "all the rest apart from itself and its own deeds" (τὰ ἄλλα πάντα χωρὶς ἑαυτῆς καὶ τῶν ἔργων αὑτῆς): the poet gives everything except the soul and what it does; MacKenna makes the whole role given and laid over its character.
!flag robes of state or rags | The Greek has "saffron robes" (τοὺς κροκωτούς), the yellow gowns of women's and Dionysus' parts on the stage, and rags.

@p
@greek πρόσεστι δέ τι τοῖς ὑποκριταῖς
These actors have something more, since they play in a place bigger than the measure of a stage, and the poet of the All has made them masters, and there is a greater power of going to many kinds of places. They fix their own honours and dishonours, by taking a hand themselves in their honours and dishonours, each place being fitted to their characters, so that it agrees with the reason of the All, each being fitted justly to the parts that will receive him, as each string is set in its own fitting place according to the reason of its sounding, according to what its power is for that. For in the whole there is the fitting and the beautiful, if each is set where he should be, sounding evil sounds in the darkness and in Tartarus: for there it is beautiful to sound so. And this whole is beautiful not if each is a stone, but if each, bringing in his own sound, contributes to one harmony, sounding a life himself, though a lesser one, and worse, and less complete. So in a panpipe too there is not one sound, but even a lesser and faint one contributes to the harmony of the whole pipe, since the harmony is divided into unequal parts; all the notes are unequal, but the complete one is one, made from them all.
!flag All is just and good in the Universe | The Greek says that in the whole there is "the fitting and the beautiful" (τὸ πρέπον καὶ τὸ καλόν); "just" is MacKenna's.
!note Tartarus, the deepest pit under the earth, where the incurable are thrown: Phaedo 112a-114b, Gorgias 525c-e.

@p
@greek καὶ δὴ καὶ ὁ λόγος ὁ πᾶς εἷς
And so the whole reason is one, but divided into unequal parts. That is why there are different places in the All, better and worse, and souls not equal fit themselves so to places not equal. And so it comes about here too that the places are unlike, and the souls not the same, but unequal and with unlike ways, as with the unlikenesses of a panpipe or some other instrument; they are in places different from one another, and in each place they sound their own notes, in tune both with the places and with the whole. What is badly with them will lie in the beautiful as regards the All, and what is against nature will be according to nature for the All, and will be no less a lesser sound. But the soul that sounds so has not made the whole worse, as the executioner, wicked as he is, has not made the well-governed city worse, if we must use another image too. For there is need of him too in a city ("and there is often need of such a man"), and he too is set well.
!flag and the corresponding moral type is often serviceable | The Greek, in words set off as a saying, says "there is often need of such a man too" (δεῖ δὲ καὶ ἀνθρώπου τοιούτου πολλάκις): of the man himself, not of a moral type.

@ch III.2.18 | Do the actors add their own lines? The question left open
Souls are worse and better, some for other causes, some unequal as it were from the start, unequal parts of reason; and soul does not always act with the same parts. Perhaps we should not bring in actors who say other than the poet's lines, as if the play were incomplete and the poet had left gaps; for even what follows on bad deeds is reason's, as better children come of adultery and rape, and better cities rise after sacked ones. But if bringing in souls who do good and evil is absurd, why not make the actors' deeds parts of reason, as of a play? Then why make evil, and what are souls, if all are parts of reason? The question goes on in III.3.

@p
Souls are worse and better, some for other causes, and some as it were not all equal from the beginning: for, in proportion to the reason, they too are unequal parts, since they have stood apart. We must also bear in mind the second and the third things, and that soul does not always act with the same parts. But we must say it again in this way too: for the argument longs for much clarity.
!flag its expression may take any one of three main forms | The Greek says only that we must bear in mind "the second and the third" (τὰ δεύτερα καὶ τὰ τρίτα), and that soul does not always act with the same parts; the "three main forms" are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek μὴ γὰρ οὐδὲν δεῖ ἐπεισάγειν
Perhaps there is no need at all to bring in actors of the kind who will say something other than the poet's words, as though the play were incomplete in itself and they were filling in what is lacking, and the poet had left empty places in between; as though the actors were to be not actors but part of the poet, and he foreknew what they would say, so as to be able to join on the rest and what follows. For in the All too, what follows, and what comes after bad deeds, are reasons and according to reason: as from adultery and the carrying off of a captive come children better by nature, and men too, it may be; and other cities better than those sacked by wicked men.
!flag We may perhaps think of actors having the right to add something to the poet's words | The Greek doubts whether there is any need "to bring in actors who will say something other than the poet's words" (μὴ γὰρ οὐδὲν δεῖ ἐπεισάγειν τοιούτους ὑποκριτάς): the thought is put in question, not granted as a right.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν ἄτοπος ἡ εἰσαγωγὴ
If, then, it is absurd to bring in souls, some of which will do the wicked things and others the good (for we shall rob reason of the good things too, if we take the wicked away from it), what prevents us from making the actors' deeds parts too, of the reason in the All as of the play there, and both the good playing and its contrary from here, so that it comes to each of the actors from reason itself, so much the more as this play is the more complete, and all things come from reason? But then, to make evil: for what? And the souls, even the more divine, would no longer be anything in the All, but all would be parts of reason. And either all the reasons are souls, or why are some souls and others only reasons, when the All belongs to a soul?
!flag when the All is itself a Soul | The Greek says "the All belonging to a soul" (τοῦ παντὸς ψυχῆς τινος ὄντος): the All is a soul's, not itself a soul.
!note The questions are taken up in III.3, the second part of the treatise; Porphyry divided Plotinus' one long writing On providence into two, the forty-seventh and forty-eighth in the order of writing (Life 6).

@treatise III.3 | On providence, second part
The second part of the writing On providence takes up the question left open at the end of III.2: if one reason holds all things, the bad with the good, how are we to blame? The whole reason is made of parts, as the soul it comes from has parts, and the parts are at odds with one another as horses fight within one kind, yet all are drawn back into one order, as the troops of a great general whose plan leaves nothing outside it. Our choices are counted in that order, not added to it. Men are blamed, as plants and beasts are not, because they have another principle, a free one, which not all of them use; if they are worse than they might be, the fault is theirs, or their former lives', and still the giver deserves more wonder than blame. Providence reaches from top to bottom, not equally but in proportion, as in one living body; above is providence alone, below it destiny. The good man acts according to providence, not by it; the bad man neither by it nor according to it, and his evil is mended by what follows. Seers foretell the bad as well as the good because the world is one living thing whose parts answer to one another in proportion, and they read it as letters. Without the worse there would be nothing for providence to provide for: all things come from one root, like the branches, leaves and fruit of one tree, and act on one another like brothers.

@ch III.3.1 | One reason, at war with itself, one order
What, then, of the bad and the good? The reason of the whole holds both as its parts: it does not beget them, but is with them. The reasons are the activity of a whole soul, its parts of its parts, so the works too differ. They agree as a whole made of contraries, all drawn back into one order because they come from one, as horses that bite and fight are still one kind. Go up through the kinds to being, and to what gives being; then come down again and see the one spread out into an animal of many parts, each doing its own work, and good and bad lives following from natures and works.

@p
What, then, do we think about these things? This: the whole reason holds within it the bad things as well as the good, and these too are parts of it. For the whole reason does not beget them; it is the whole together with them. The reasons are the activity of a whole soul, and their parts the activity of its parts; and since the soul is one but has different parts, so in proportion do the reasons, and so do their works, which are the last things they beget. The souls agree with one another, and so do their works; they agree in such a way that one thing comes from them, even if it comes from contraries. For all things that set out from some one thing come together into one by the necessity of nature, so that, even if they grow out different and become contrary, they are still drawn together into one order, because they come from one. It is as with each kind of animal: horses are one kind, even though they fight, and bite one another, and contend for the first place, and rage with jealousy; and the other kinds are one in the same way; and so we must think of men too.
!flag does not engender them but encompasses them | The Greek says the whole reason does not beget them "but is the whole with them" (ἀλλ’ ὁ πᾶς ἐστι μετὰ τούτων): it is a whole of which they are parts, not a container round them; "this Universal Idea" is MacKenna's.
!flag its parts (i.e. events good and evil) are expressions of these Soul-parts | The Greek says the reasons are the activity of a whole soul, "and their parts of its parts" (τῶν δὲ μερῶν τὰ μέρη); the gloss "events good and evil" is MacKenna's.
!flag show malice and angry envy | The Greek says the horses "contend for victory" (φιλονεικῶσι) and "rage with jealousy" (ζήλῳ θυμῶνται): rivalry, not malice.

@p
@greek συναπτέον τοίνυν αὖ πάλιν
Then we must join all these species together again into one kind, the kind of living things; then the things that are not living, by their species, then into one, the non-living; then both together, if you like, into being; then into what gives being. And having tied all to this, come down again, dividing, and see the one scattering itself, because it reaches to all things and yet holds them together in one order: so that, though divided, it is one animal of many parts, each of the things in it doing what it does by its own nature, while still being in the whole. So fire burns, a horse does a horse's work, men each do their own work as they are by nature, and different men different works. And following their natures come their works, and the good or bad of their lives.
!note "What gives being" (τὸ παρέχον τὸ εἶναι) is above being, as the One gives intellect its being in V.1.7 and VI.9.2; the ladder of kinds up to being recalls Plato's division and collection in the Sophist (253d) and Philebus (16c-17a).

@ch III.3.2 | Providence as a general
Chance meetings are not masters of the good life: they follow in agreement with what went before, woven into the sequence. The leader weaves all together, as a general leads and his ranks breathe with him. The All was ordered by a general's providence, which foresaw actions, sufferings, food, drink, weapons and engines, and how they would combine, so that the outcome could be well placed. A human general cannot command what the enemy will do; but if the great leader is the one under whom all things are, what could be out of order?

@p
Chance meetings are not masters of the good: they too follow, in agreement with what goes before them, and go on, woven into the sequence. The leading principle weaves all things together, while the things on either side are brought together according to nature, as in a campaign, where the general leads and those ranked under him breathe together with him. The All has been ordered by a general's providence, which sees the actions and the sufferings, and what must be at hand, food and drink and every weapon and engine, and all that has been foreseen of how these will combine, so that what results from them may have room to be placed well; and everything has come from the general in a well-contrived way, even though what the enemy were going to do was outside him, and he could not command their army too. But if the great leader were the one under whom all things are, what could be out of order, what could not be fitted in?
!flag The Leading-Principle holds all the threads while the minor agents, the individuals, serve according to their own capacities | The Greek says the leading principle "weaves all together" (συμπλέκει) while "the things on either side" (τῶν ἐφ̓ ἑκάτερα) come together by nature; "the minor agents, the individuals" and "their own capacities" are MacKenna's.
!flag so as to make it probable that the final event may be success | The Greek says "so that what results from them may have room to be placed well" (ἔχῃ χώραν τοῦ τεθῆναι εὖ): the plan leaves a place for every outcome; it does not make success probable.
!note Aristotle compares the good of the world to the good of an army, which is both in its order and in its general, and more in the general (Metaphysics XII.10, 1075a13-15). "The great leader" (ὁ μέγας ἡγεμών) is Zeus driving his winged chariot at the head of the army of gods and daemons in the Phaedrus (246e).

@ch III.3.3 | Counted in, not added; why men are not gods
Even if I am master of my choice, the choice is counted in the order of the whole: you are not an episode added to it. Where does such a one come from? Do we blame the maker, or the thing made, or no one, as with plants and beasts? To complain that men are not better is like complaining that they are not gods; if the better was in their power, they are to blame; if it had to come from outside, it is absurd to ask for more than was given. Things are unequal not by a decision but by nature: reason follows soul, soul intellect, and intellect is all things, and what is many has first, second and third. What comes to be falls far short and yet is a marvel; its maker is above all blame, and if it gave more than they could take, the blame falls on them and providence is the greater.

@p
For even if I am master of choosing these things or those, still the choice is ranked into the order, because your part is not an episode added to the All: you have been counted in, such as you are.
!flag Your personality does not come from outside into the universal scheme | The Greek says your part is not "an episode" (ἐπεισόδιον) in the All, an added scene, "but you have been counted in, such as you are" (ἠρίθμησαι ὁ τοιόσδε).
!note An "episodic" plot is the worst kind, whose episodes follow one another without likelihood or necessity (Aristotle, Poetics 9, 1451b33-35); nature, says Aristotle, "is not episodic, like a bad tragedy" (Metaphysics XIV.3, 1090b19-20). The figure of the play goes on from III.2.15-18.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ πόθεν ὁ τοιόσδε
But where does one of this kind come from? There are two things the argument asks.
