One is whether we must refer the cause of the quality of each man's character to the one who made him, if there is one, or to what has come to be itself; or whether no one is to be blamed at all, as no one is in the coming to be of plants, because they do not perceive, or of the other animals, because they are not as men are. For that is the same as asking why men are not what gods are. Why is it that here we reasonably blame neither the things themselves nor the one who made them, but in the case of men we blame them because they are not better than they are? If it is because a man could have been more beautiful, then, if he could have added something towards the better from himself, he is the cause of his own state, he who did not do it. But if it was not from himself, and something had to be added from outside, from the one who begot him, then the man who asks for more than was given is absurd, as he would be if he asked it in the case of the other animals and of plants. For we must not ask whether one thing is less than another, but whether it is sufficient as itself; it was not right that all things should be equal. Did he, then, measure things out by a decision that all should not be equal? Not at all: it was by nature that things had to come to be so.
!flag Reason acquits plant and animal and, their maker | The Greek asks why "we reasonably blame" (εὐλόγως αἰτιώμεθα) neither the things nor their maker; MacKenna makes reason itself the judge.
!flag universal equality there cannot be | The Greek says "it was not right that all things should be equal" (οὐ γὰρ πάντα ἴσα ἔδει): a thing of what ought to be, not only of what can be.

@p
@greek ἀκόλουθος γὰρ οὗτος ὁ λόγος
For this reason follows on another soul, and this soul follows on intellect; and intellect is not one of these things, but all things. And all things are many; and being many, and not the same, some were going to be first, some second, and some next in order, in rank too. So the animals that come to be are not souls only, but lessenings of souls, as if they were already fading as they go forward. For the reason of the animal, even if it has a soul, is another soul, not the one from which the reason comes; and this whole reason becomes less as it hurries towards matter, and what comes to be from it is more lacking.
!flag the Reason-Principle of this Universe follows upon a phase of the Soul | The Greek says this reason "follows on another soul" (ἀκόλουθος ... ψυχῇ ἄλλῃ), a soul other than the reason itself, not "a phase" of one.
!note Each level follows on the one before it: reason on soul, soul on intellect, and intellect is all things, being the intelligible world itself (V.9.6, V.1.4). The "fading" (ἐξίτηλος) of what goes forward is a word of colours that fade and lines of descent that die out.

@p
@greek σκόπει δὴ ὅσον ἀφέστηκε
Look how far what has come to be stands away, and yet it is a marvel. So if what has come to be is of this kind, it does not follow that what is before it is of this kind too. For that is better than everything that has come to be, and outside blame; and we should rather wonder at it, that it gave something after itself, and that its traces are such. And if it gave more than they have been able to take, we must welcome it all the more: so that the blame seems to go to those who have come to be, and the part of providence to be the greater.
!flag In sum nothing can secure to a thing of process the quality of the prior order | The Greek says the reverse inference fails: "if what has come to be is of this kind, it does not follow that what is before it is of this kind too" (οὐ τοίνυν, εἰ τοιοῦτον τὸ γενόμενον, καὶ τὸ πρὸ αὐτοῦ τοιοῦτον). It defends the cause from the faults of the effect.
!flag the debt is the heavier | The Greek says "we must welcome it all the more" (ἔτι μᾶλλον ἀποδεκτέον): gratitude, not a debt.

@ch III.3.4 | Another principle, a free one
If man were only a made thing, acting and suffering always the same way, he would no more be blamed than the beasts; but only the bad man is blamed, and rightly, because he has another principle, a free one, not outside providence, for the higher shines on the lower, and providence from above and the reason joined to it make one web. Not all men use all they have; why is the free principle idle in some? Whether by a muddy constitution or the rule of desires, the cause is in the substrate; but the substrate of that principle is reason itself, not matter. A former life may have dimmed the reason; reason holds the reason of its matter, and the soul that turns into an ox does so justly. Why was the worse made at all? Not all things are first; a small tilt is enough to leave the straight way; and what is less was less from the beginning.

@p
If man were simple (I mean simple in that he were only what he has been made, and acted and suffered always in the same way), there would be no cause for censure, any more than with the other animals. But as it is, among them man alone is blamed, the bad man, and perhaps reasonably. For he is not only what he has been made: he has another principle, a free one. It is not outside providence, or outside the reason of the whole; for the higher things are not cut off from these. The better shine upon the worse, and this is the perfect providence. Of reason, one kind makes, and another joins the better to the things that have come to be: those are providence from above, and the other is the providence that comes from the one above, the second reason joined to the first; and from both comes the whole web, the whole of providence.
!flag subject to reproach and punishment than the mere animals | The Greek says only that "there would be no cause for censure" (ἀπῆν ἂν αἰτία ἡ κατὰ τὴν ἐπιτίμησιν); "punishment" is MacKenna's.
!flag cannot be dependent upon the World of Sense | The Greek says "those are not cut off from these" (οὐ γὰρ ἀπήρτηται ἐκεῖνα τούτων): the higher things are not detached from the lower, which is why the free principle is within providence. MacKenna turns it into a question of which depends on which.

@p
@greek ἀρχὴν μὲν οὖν ἔχουσιν ἄλλην
So men have another principle; but not all of them use all they have. Some use the one, some the other, or the others, the worse ones. Those are present too, even when they are not active towards them, though they are not idle in themselves: each does its own work. "But why," someone might say, "are they not active towards these men, though present?" Perhaps they are not present. And yet we say they are present everywhere, and nothing is empty of them. Perhaps not present to these men, in whom it is not active towards them. Why then is it not active towards all, if they too are parts of them? I mean this kind of principle. In the other animals this principle is not theirs at all, and in men not in all. Then is it not the only one in all of them? But why not the only one? In some it is the only one, and their life is by it, and the rest only so far as is necessary.
!flag So this Principle is not the only effective force in all men | The Greek asks two questions, "then is it not the only one in all?" and "but why not the only one?", and answers that "in some it is the only one" (ἐφ̓ ὧν δὲ μόνη); MacKenna's "There is no reason why it should not be" answers a question the Greek does not put.

@p
@greek εἴτε γὰρ ἡ σύστασις
For whether the constitution is such as to throw one, as it were, into muddy water, or the desires prevail, we must still say that the cause is in the substrate. But, first, it will seem then to be no longer in the reason, but rather in matter, and matter, not reason, will prevail; and, second, the substrate as it has been moulded. Or rather, the substrate of this principle is reason, and what has come to be from reason and is according to reason; so it will not be matter that prevails, nor the moulding.
!flag drive him down the troubled paths | The Greek says "as if to throw him into muddy water" (οἷον εἰς θολερὸν ἐμβάλλειν): a body whose mixture clouds the soul, like silt stirred up in water.

@p
@greek καὶ τὸ τοιόνδε εἶναι
And one might refer his being of this kind to his former life, as if the reason had become dim, from his former doings, compared with the reason before it, as when a soul has become weaker; but later it will shine out again. And let the reason be said to have in itself the reason of its matter too, which it will work for itself, either making the matter of its own quality or finding it in agreement with it. For the reason of an ox is not found in any matter but that of an ox. That is why he says that the soul passes into the other animals too, as if the soul had become other and the reason had been altered, so that the soul of an ox comes to be which was before a man; so that the worse comes about with justice.
!flag the Soul which later will shine out again is for the present at a feebler power | The Greek says the reason has become dim, "as when a soul has become weaker" (οἷον ψυχῆς ἀσθενεστέρας γενομένης), and will "shine out" (ἐκλάμψει) later; it is a comparison, not a statement about the soul now.
!note "He says": Plato, whose souls pass into beasts by the life they chose (Phaedrus 249b, Republic X 620a-d, Timaeus 42b-c, 91d-92c). III.4.2 gives the list.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἀρχῆς διὰ τί
But why did the worse come to be from the beginning, and how did it go wrong? It has often been said that not all things are first, but that the second and third have a nature less than those before them, and a small tilt is enough to leave what is straight. And the weaving of one thing with another is like a blending, in which another thing comes to be from both. The worse did not lessen something that was; what is less came to be less from the beginning, and is what it became, less by its own nature; and if it suffers what follows, it suffers what it deserves. And we must carry our reasoning back to former lives too, since what follows hangs from them as well.
!flag how does the higher fall to it | The Greek asks "how did it go wrong" (πῶς ἐσφάλη), of the worse itself; nothing is said of the higher falling to it.
!flag it is not that the greater and prior suffers any diminution of its own nature | The Greek says "it did not lessen something that was" (οὐκ ὄντος ἠλάττωσεν): the less was not made less from something greater, but was less from the start; "the greater and prior" is MacKenna's.

@ch III.3.5 | Providence, destiny, and what we do
@older 4
Providence comes down from beginning to end, not equal by number but in proportion, as in one animal whose parts each have their own work, and whose sounds and sufferings make one voice and one life. It is one; destiny begins from the worse, and above is providence alone. Reason comes divided unequally; what is done in agreement with it is dear to the gods. Our deeds are woven in, but not made by providence, which takes up any good that follows and mends what went wrong, as reason heals a wound. Evils follow of necessity, from causes in us. The same thing does different things to different men, as Helen's beauty did to Paris and to Idomeneus. The good man's act is according to providence, not by it, as a patient follows his doctor.

@p
Providence, then, comes down from the beginning to the end, from above, not equal as if by number, but different in different places in proportion, as in one animal hung from its beginning to its end, each part having its own: the better part the better of the activity, the part towards the bottom by then the lower, acting itself and suffering what is its own, both towards itself and in its place in the order with another. So, struck in such a way, the parts that make sounds speak out in such a way, while others suffer in silence and move in ways that follow; and from all the sounds, and all the sufferings and activities, comes as it were one voice of the animal, and one life, and one way of living. For the members too are different and have different activities: the feet do one thing, the eyes another, thinking another, and intellect another.
!flag the personal voice, life and history of the living form | The Greek says "one voice of the animal, as it were, and one life and way of living" (μία τοῦ ζῴου οἷον φωνὴ καὶ ζωὴ καὶ βίος); the stress is on "one", and "personal" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἓν δὲ ἐκ πάντων καὶ πρόνοια μία
But one thing comes from them all, and providence is one: destiny begins from the worse, and what is above is providence only. For in the intelligible world all is reason and beyond reason, for there is intellect and pure soul. What comes from there is by now providence: as much as comes from there, as much as is in pure soul, and as much as goes from there into the animals. But reason comes divided, not in equal parts, and so it does not make equal things, as in each animal too. From here on, the things that are done follow, and keep company with providence, if one does what is dear to the gods; for the reason of providence was dear to god.
!flag Divine Mind and unmingled Soul | The Greek says "intellect and pure soul" (νοῦς γὰρ καὶ ψυχὴ καθαρά); "Divine Mind" is MacKenna's.
!flag the Reason-Principle of providence is god-serving | The Greek says it is "dear to god" (θεοφιλής), loved by god, not serving god.
!note Destiny (εἱμαρμένη) is the Stoic chain of causes (III.1); here it is placed under providence, beginning from the worse, as in the Middle Platonists' "providence above destiny" (pseudo-Plutarch, On fate 9, 572f-573a). "Dear to the gods": the self-controlled man is dear to god, since like is dear to like (Laws IV 716c-d).

@p
@greek συνείρεται μὲν οὖν
Such works are strung on together with them, then, but they are not made by providence. Things come about from men, or from anything at all, living or lifeless; and if anything good follows on what has come about, it is taken up again by providence, so that virtue rules everywhere, and what has gone wrong is changed and set right. It is as in one body, given health by the providence of the animal: if a cut is made, or any wound at all, the reason that governs it joins and draws together again, heals and sets right the part that suffered.
!flag In the total, then, the right rules | The Greek says "virtue rules everywhere" (πανταχοῦ ἀρετὴν κρατεῖν), and what went wrong is changed and set right.

@p
@greek ὥστε τὰ κακὰ ἑπόμενα εἶναι
So evils are things that follow, but of necessity. They come from us, from causes we are not forced into by providence: we join them, of ourselves, to the works of providence and to those that come from it, but we are not able to string on what follows according to its will, only according to the will of those who acted, or of something else in the All, which itself did not act according to providence or caused some suffering in us.
!flag consults the desire of the agent alone | The Greek says what follows is strung on "according to the will of those who acted" (κατὰ τὴν τῶν πραξάντων), the same word as providence's will; "alone" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ τὸ αὐτὸ ποιεῖ πᾶν
For the same thing, coming upon everyone, does not do the same thing to all, but the same thing does one thing to one and another to another. So Helen's beauty worked one thing on Paris, and Idomeneus did not suffer the same. A licentious man meeting a licentious one, a handsome one meeting a handsome one, bring about one thing; the self-controlled handsome man brings about another with a self-controlled man like him, and the same man another with a licentious one; and the licentious man another with him.
!flag two handsome people of loose character and two living honourably | The Greek says "a licentious man meeting a licentious, a handsome a handsome" (ἀκόλαστος ἀκολάστῳ, καλὸς καλῷ), and then "the self-controlled handsome man" (ὁ δὲ σώφρων καλός) with one like him: the virtue named is self-control.
!note On the walls of Troy Helen points out Idomeneus to Priam: Menelaus often had him as a guest in their house (Iliad III.230-233). He saw her beauty and was not carried away by it, as Paris was.

@p
@greek καὶ παρὰ μὲν τοῦ ἀκολάστου
And the deed done by the licentious man is done neither by providence nor according to providence. The work done by the self-controlled man is not done by providence, since it is done by him, but it is according to providence; for it agrees with the reason. So too, when one does something healthy of himself, he does it according to the doctor's reason; for this is what the doctor too gave from his art, for the healthy and for the sick. But what one does that is not healthy, he does himself, and he has worked against the providence of the doctor.

@ch III.3.6 | How seers foretell evils: the world as one animal
@older 4
Seers foretell the worse too, looking at the circuit of the All, because contraries are woven together, as form and matter in a composite animal: whoever sees the form sees what is formed. The All is an animal, so whoever sees what happens in it sees what it is made of and the providence over it, all mixed. Only a god could tell providence apart from what the substrate gives; the seer says only that a thing is, not why, reading nature's letters, which show order. All things answer to one another in proportion, as eye to eye and virtue to justice, and so one can foretell; they act on one another as the parts of one animal, not as maker and made.

@p
How is it, then, that seers foretell the worse things too, and that those who look at the circuit of the All foretell these things as well as other kinds of divination? It is plain: because all contraries are woven together, as form and matter are. In an animal, which is composite, whoever looks at the form and the reason sees also what has been formed. For he does not look at the intelligible animal and the composite animal in the same way; in the composite he sees the reason of the animal shaping the worse things. Since the All is an animal, whoever looks at what comes to be in it sees at once what it is made of and the providence over it; and that providence extends to all things, even to what comes to be.
!flag Clearly the reason is that all contraries coalesce | The Greek says all contraries are "woven together" (συμπεπλέχθαι), the weaving of III.3.2 and III.3.4; they do not coalesce, but stay contraries in one web.
!flag Take, for example, Shape and (its contrary) Matter | The Greek has "form and matter" (τὴν μορφὴν καὶ τὴν ὕλην) as an example of things woven together; "its contrary" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek τὰ δέ ἐστι καὶ ζῷα
These are animals, and their actions and dispositions, mastered by reason and mixed with necessity. So he sees them mixed, and always being mixed; and he cannot himself tell apart providence and what is according to providence, on one side, and on the other what the substrate gives of itself to what comes to be. Nor is this the work of a man, even a wise and godlike one; a god might have this privilege, one might say.

@p
@greek καὶ γὰρ οὐ τοῦ μάντεως
For it is not the seer's task to say why, but only that; and his art is a reading of nature's letters, letters that show order and never turn aside to what is without order; or rather, the circuit bears witness, and brings to light, even before it shows itself in them, what each one is and how much. For these things here move together with those there, and those with these, and together they work for the coming together and the everlastingness of the world; and by proportion they signal the rest to the one who has watched; since the other kinds of divination too work by what is proportional.
!flag the scriptures of Nature | The Greek has "a reading of natural letters" (ἀνάγνωσις φυσικῶν γραμμάτων): reading, not scripture.
!flag Here conspires with There and There with Here | The Greek says "these things move together with those, and those with these" (συμφέρεται γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα ἐκείνοις κἀκεῖνα τούτοις): the signs and the things signified, here below and in the heaven; the intelligible "There" is not meant.
!note The stars are "like letters always being written in the heaven" (II.3.7), which the trained can read without the stars causing what they show; that is the argument of II.3, Whether the stars are causes.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ ἔδει ἀπηρτῆσθαι
For it was not right that all things should be cut off from one another; they had to be made like one another somehow. And this may be what is meant by the saying that proportion holds all things together. Proportion is such that the worse stands to the worse as the better to the better: as eye to eye and foot to foot, the one to the other, and, if you like, as virtue to justice, so vice to injustice. If, then, there is proportion in the All, it is possible to foretell. And if those things act on these, they act in the way that the parts in every animal act on one another: not as one begets another, for they are begotten together, but as each is made by nature, so it suffers what suits its own nature; and because this is such, that other is such: for so too the reason is one.
!flag Universal interdependence, there could not be, but universal resemblance there must | The Greek says the opposite of the first half: "it was not right that all things should be cut off from one another" (οὐ γὰρ ἔδει ἀπηρτῆσθαι ἀλλήλων τὰ πάντα), but they must be made like one another somehow.
!flag Correspondences maintain the Universe | The Greek says "proportion holds all things together" (συνέχει τὰ πάντα ἀναλογία), the proportion of the Timaeus.
!flag virtue with right action and vice with unrighteousness | The Greek has "as virtue to justice, so vice to injustice" (ὡς ἀρετὴ πρὸς δικαιοσύνην καὶ κακία πρὸς ἀδικίαν): justice, the virtue, not "right action".
!note The saying: Timaeus 31c-32a, where proportion (ἀναλογία) is the most beautiful of bonds, which makes one thing of itself and the things it binds; the world's body is held together by it.

@ch III.3.7 | Without the worse no providence: one root, many branches
@older 4
If there is better, there is worse; we should not blame the worse in the better, but welcome the better for giving of itself to the worse. Those who would take away the worse take away providence, which is named for what is below. All things are together in one principle, from which they go out while it stays, as from one root that stays in itself, flowering into a many in which each bears an image of it: branches, tips, leaves and fruit, some staying, some always coming to be. What acts on what comes from far off, but from the same start, like brothers.

@p
And because there are better things, there are worse ones too. For how could there be anything worse in what has many forms, unless there were something better, or anything better unless there were something worse? So we must not blame the worse in the better, but welcome the better, because it gave of itself to the worse. And, in general, those who think fit to do away with the worse in the All do away with providence itself. For what would it be providence for? Not for itself, nor for the better; for even when we name the providence above, we speak of it in relation to what is below.
!flag We cannot complain about the lower in the higher | The Greek says "we must not blame the worse in the better" (οὐκ αἰτιατέον τὸ χεῖρον ἐν τῷ βελτίονι), the worse that is in the better whole; MacKenna's "complain" softens a charge of blame.

@p
@greek τὸ μὲν γὰρ εἰς ἓν πάντα
For the principle that holds all things in one is the one in which all are together, and all is a whole. From it the single things go out, while it stays within, as from one root standing still in itself. They flowered out into a many, divided, each bearing an image of it; and here one thing came to be in another, and some were near the root, while others went forward into the distance and split, as far as branches and tips, fruit and leaves. Some stayed always; others, the fruit and the leaves, always came to be; and the things that came to be always had in them the reasons of what was above them, as if they wanted to be small trees; and if they begot before they perished, they begot only what was near them.
!flag each single outgrowth bearing its trace of the common source | The Greek says each bears "an image" (εἴδωλον) of it, the word for the image of a pattern, not a trace.

@p
@greek τὰ δὲ διάκενα
The empty spaces between, as it were, of the branches were filled again from the root, the branches themselves having grown another way; and from them the tips of the branches were affected too, so that one would think the affection came only from what was next to them. But at the origin one part was affected and another acted, and the origin itself hung from something too. For the things that act on one another came from far off, and are other; but from the beginning they are from the same, as if brothers were to do something to one another, made like one another because they set out from the same parents.
!flag operation is to be traced only from point to next point | The Greek says that one "would think" (ὡς ... οἴεσθαι) the affection came only from the neighbour: an appearance, which the next sentence corrects.

@treatise III.4 | On the daemon allotted to us
Plato says that each of us has a daemon allotted to him, who leads him in life and to judgment after death, and that we choose our daemon. Plotinus explains it by the soul's many powers. Soul makes nature and growth down to plants, and below them body, the last of things. The soul is everything, and in each of us the power that leads in life is what we become: those who kept the man are men again; those who lived by perception, beasts; those who lived by growth alone, plants. The daemon is the power just above the one that leads us, standing over us idle; if we follow it, it rules and another stands above it, up to the highest. The choice of lives in the myth is the soul's character, which outside chances do not overturn. The good man lives by intellect, and his daemon is a god. After death the daemon leads the soul to judgment; souls go to the stars that suit them, or beyond; and when the soul returns it is set in a seat of fortune, as in a ship carried round by the circuit, and what comes to it, and how it answers, is destiny.

@ch III.4.1 | From soul to body, the last of things
Higher things make what comes after them while they stay; soul makes while moving: perception, nature, down to plants. The growth-power is in us too, but does not rule; in plants it rules alone. What it makes is no longer alive: like everything made before, it is made unformed and takes form by turning back to its maker; but this is utter indefiniteness, which, completed, becomes body, the receptacle of what made it.

@p
Some, while they stay, have things that come into existence from them. But soul, it was said, makes while moving: both perception, which exists as a reality of its own, and nature, down to the plants. For the soul has nature in us too, but nature does not rule in us, being a part; when it comes to be in plants, it rules there, as if it had come to be alone. Does it, then, make nothing? Or it makes something altogether other than itself; for after it there is no longer life, but what it makes is lifeless.
!flag in our view, the Soul generates by its motion | The Greek says soul "was said" (ἐλέγετο) to make while moving: a reference to what has been shown before, not a view put forward here.
!flag but is not the dominant since it is not the whole man | The Greek says nature "does not rule, being a part" (οὐ κρατεῖ δὲ μέρος οὖσα); "the whole man", and the Intellectual Principle in MacKenna's brackets, are his.
!note "It was said": V.2.1, written earlier, where intellect makes soul while it stays, but soul makes its image, perception and nature in plants, while it moves. Plotinus' word for what comes into existence from a higher thing is hypostasis (ὑπόστασις), "what stands under", the word later used for his three: the One, intellect and soul.

@p
@greek τί οὖν; ἤ, ὥσπερ πᾶν
What then? Just as everything made before this was made unformed, and was given its form by turning back to what made it, as if being reared by it, so here too what is made must no longer be a form of soul (for it no longer lives) but utter indefiniteness. For even if there was indefiniteness in the earlier things, it was within form: they were not indefinite altogether, but only in relation to their completion; but this is indefinite altogether. Completed, it becomes body, taking the shape suited to its power, a receptacle for what made and reared it; and this alone, in body, is the last of the things above in the last of the things below.
!flag Let it be raised to its highest degree and it becomes body | The Greek says "being completed (τελειούμενον) it becomes body": brought to its end, given a shape. Nothing is "raised"; the indefinite is made definite.
!note What is made turns back to its source and is formed by it: so intellect from the One (V.2.1, V.1.7). Matter as "receptacle" (ὑποδοχή) is the Timaeus' (49a, 51a).

@ch III.4.2 | We become what we lived by
All soul cares for what has no soul, and goes round all the heaven in different forms at different times: the part of it that rules makes what suits it, and the rest is idle. In man the worse parts are with the better, and he lives partly by perception and much like a plant; he is ranked by the better, but the soul, when it leaves, becomes what was strongest in it. So we must flee upward to intellect and god. Those who kept the man are men again; those who lived by perception, beasts, wild or gluttonous; the dull, plants; the music-lovers singing birds, unreasoning kings eagles, sky-gazers without wisdom high-flying birds; those with civic virtue men again, or bees.

@p
And "all soul cares for what has no soul" is said above all of this soul; the others in other ways. "It goes round all the heaven, at different times in different forms": either in the form of perception, or of reason, or in the form of growth itself. For the part of it that rules makes what suits itself, and the others are idle; for they are outside.
!flag forms varying with the variety of place | The Greek, quoting the Phaedrus, says "at different times" (ἄλλοτε) in different forms: the soul changes over time, from life to life, not from place to place.
!note Phaedrus 246b: "all soul cares for all that has no soul, and goes round all the heaven, coming to be at different times in different forms."

@p
@greek ἐν δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ οὐ κρατεῖ τὰ χείρω
In man the worse parts do not rule, but they are with him; nor does the better always rule; for these too have a place of their own. So we are also perceivers, for we have organs of perception; and much of us is like plants, for we have a body that grows and begets. So all the parts work together, but the whole form, man, is ranked by the better. But the soul, when it goes out, becomes what was strongest in it. That is why we must flee upward, so as not to sink into the perceiving part, following the images of sense, nor into the growing part, following the urge to beget and the greed for food, but rise into the thinking part, and into intellect, and into god.
!flag the lower element also has a footing | The Greek says the worse parts "have a place of their own" (χώραν τινὰ ἔχοντα); MacKenna's sentence makes them a footing for the better, where the Greek says only that neither rules always.
!note The flight upward is the Theaetetus' (176a-b), the flight from here that is becoming like god; Plotinus takes it up in I.2.1.

@p
@greek ὅσοι μὲν οὖν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐτήρησαν
So those who kept the man in them are men again; those who lived by perception alone, animals. If perception went with spirit, they are wild beasts, and the difference among these makes the difference among such beasts; those who lived with desire and the pleasure of the desiring part are the licentious and gluttonous animals. If they did not live even by perception with these, but with a dullness of perception, they become plants too: for only this, or this above all, was active in them, the growing part, and they were practising to become trees. Those who loved music but were otherwise pure become singing creatures; kings who ruled without reason, eagles, if no other vice was present; those who studied the things on high without wisdom, always lifted towards the heaven, birds that fly high. Whoever kept civic virtue is a man; whoever had less of civic virtue is a civic animal, a bee or the like.
!flag futile and flighty visionaries ever soaring skyward | The Greek says "students of the things on high without wisdom" (μετεωρολόγους δὲ ἄνευ φρονήσεως), those who study the heavens, as in the Timaeus; "futile" and "visionaries" are MacKenna's.
!flag observance of civic and secular virtue | The Greek has only "civic virtue" (τὴν πολιτικὴν ἀρετήν); "secular" is MacKenna's.
!note The lives of beasts follow Plato: gluttons become asses, the unjust wolves and hawks, those with popular and civic virtue "some civic and gentle kind, bees or wasps or ants, or men again" (Phaedo 81e-82b); Orpheus chose a swan's life, Agamemnon an eagle's (Republic X 620a-b); and harmless men "who studied the things on high but thought that sight gave the surest proofs" became birds (Timaeus 91d-e). Aristotle calls the bee a "civic" animal (History of animals I.1, 488a7-10; Politics I.2, 1253a7-9).

@ch III.4.3 | Which is the daemon?
The daemon is the power just above the one that leads us here: if we live by perception, reason; if by reason, what is above it, standing over us idle and letting the lower work. So we choose our daemon by our life. It leads us while we live; when we die, it hands its activity to another. If the bad man is weighed down, he pays; if one can follow the daemon above, he lives by it, and then by the next, up to the top. For the soul is many and all things, and each of us is an intelligible world, bound below by our last part, which gives an activity downward while what is above is not lessened.

@p
Which, then, is the daemon? The one that is here too. And which the god? The one here. For what has been active leads each of us, since here too it is what leads. Is this, then, the daemon "that was allotted to him while he lived"? No: it is the one before it; for that stands over us idle, while the one after it acts. If what acts in us is the part by which we are perceivers, the daemon is the reasoning part; if we live by the reasoning part, the daemon is what is above it, standing over us idle, letting the one at work do its work. So it is rightly said that "we shall choose" him; for we choose the one that stands above us by the life we live.
!flag What, then, is the spirit | The Greek has δαίμων, "daemon", Plato's word in the passages Plotinus is reading (Phaedo 107d, Republic X 617e, 620d-e, Timaeus 90a); MacKenna's "spirit" is not the word, and it hides that the daemon here is a power of our own soul.
!flag the dominant is the spirit which takes possession of the human being at birth | The Greek says the daemon "that was allotted to him while he lived" (ὅσπερ ζῶντα εἰλήχει), the Phaedo's words; nothing is said of taking possession at birth.
!note "The daemon of each, who was allotted to him while he lived, tries to lead him to a certain place" after death (Phaedo 107d); "no daemon shall be allotted to you, but you shall choose your daemon" (Republic X 617e). III.4 reads these passages together.

@p
@greek διὰ τί οὖν αὐτὸς ἄγει
Why, then, does he lead? It is not possible to lead someone who has lived out his life; he leads before, while the man lives. When the man has stopped living, the daemon hands over his activity to another, since the man has died to the life he lived by his activity. That other wants to lead, and if it prevails, it lives itself, and it too has another daemon. But if it is weighed down by the strength of the worse character, he has his punishment. In this way the bad man, since what was active in his life sank by its weight towards the worse, goes to a beast's life, by likeness to it. But if he can follow the daemon above him, he comes to be above, living by him, having put in charge the better part of himself, towards which he is led; and after that one, another, up to the top.
!flag the spirit of the previous life pays the penalty | The Greek says only "he has his punishment" (ἔχει ἐκεῖνος τὴν δίκην): the man whose worse character weighs him down. It is not the daemon that is punished.

@p
@greek ἔστι γὰρ καὶ πολλὰ ἡ ψυχὴ
For the soul is many things, and all things, both the things above and the things below again, down to every life; and each of us is an intelligible world, joined to this world by what is below, and to the intelligible by what is above. With all the rest of the intelligible in us we stay above, but by its last edge we are bound to what is below, giving to what is below, as it were, an outflow from it, or rather an activity, while that is not lessened.
!flag by what is the highest, to the Divine Intellect | The Greek says we are joined "by what is above to the intelligible" (τοῖς δὲ ἄνω τῷ νοητῷ), the intelligible world, not "the Divine Intellect".
!note Each of us an intelligible world: the soul has in it all that is, the things above as well as below, and part of it never came down (IV.8.8). "Outflow" (ἀπόρροια) is corrected to "activity" because nothing is lost from the source.

@ch III.4.4 | The world's soul never came down
Is our last part always in body? No: if we turn, it turns with us. The soul of the All never inclined with its last part; it neither came nor came down, and the world's body is attached to it and lit up by it, without troubling it. The world has no sight, as the Timaeus says, nor other senses, nor the awareness we have of ourselves: where all is in its natural state there is rest, and no pleasure. Its growth and perception are present without being present.

@p
Is this part, then, always in body? No: if we turn, it turns with us too. What, then, of the soul of the All? Will its part stand away from body too, when it turns? No: it did not even incline with its last part. For it neither came nor came down; while it stays, the body of the world is attached to it, and is lit up by it, as it were, without troubling it or giving it cares, since the world lies in safety.
!flag simply lying unmoved before it | The Greek says the world "lies in safety" (ἐν ἀσφαλεῖ τοῦ κόσμου κειμένου), which is why it gives its soul no cares.
!note The soul of the All does not come down, while ours do (IV.8.2, IV.3.4). Inclining (νεῦσις) is the word Plotinus uses, against the Gnostics, for the soul's descent (II.9.4, I.1.12).

@p
@greek τί οὖν; οὐκ αἰσθάνεταί
What then? Does it perceive with no perception? "It has no sight," he says, since it has no eyes; nor ears, plainly, nor nostrils, nor tongue. What then? Has it a self-awareness of what is within it, as we have? No: where all things are in like state according to nature, there is rest; nor is there pleasure. So the growing power is present without being present, and so is the perceiving power. But about the world we shall speak elsewhere; for now, as much has been said as the question touched on.
!flag Sensibility is present as the quality of growth is, unrecognised | The Greek says "the growing part is present not being present, and the perceiving part likewise" (πάρεστιν ... οὐ παρὸν): present without being there, not present unrecognised.
!note Timaeus 33c: the world's body "had no need of eyes, since nothing visible was left outside it, nor of hearing". The world's perception is taken up in IV.4.24-26.

@ch III.4.5 | The choice of lives
If the soul chooses its daemon and life there, how are we masters of anything here? The choice in the myth hints at the soul's choice and character, everywhere. But then the body is to blame for nothing, and no one becomes good or bad here; or both are so in potency and become so in act. A good soul with a bad body can still bring its body to its own ways, as outside chances do not overturn the whole choice; the lots, the patterns of lives and the chances leave the sovereignty with the souls. The Timaeus' daemon is ours as souls, not ours as men; it fulfils what one chose, and does not let one go far into the worse.

@p
But if the soul chooses its daemon and its life there, how are we still masters of anything? The choice that is said to be there hints at the soul's deliberate choice and disposition, as a whole and everywhere. But if the soul's choice is master, and the part it has ready to hand from its former lives prevails, then the body is no longer the cause of any evil for it. For if the soul's character comes before the body, and has what it chose, and "does not change its daemon", as he says, then neither the good man nor the bad comes to be here. Is each of them, then, so in potency, and comes to be so in act? What then if one good in character were to get a bad body, and another the opposite? Each soul can bring its body, more or less, to what belongs to it, since the other chances from outside do not overturn the whole choice either.
!flag merely an allegorical statement of the Soul's tendency and temperament | The Greek says the choice "hints in riddles" (αἰνίττεται) at the soul's "deliberate choice" (προαίρεσις) and disposition: Plato's myth is read for a truth, and the truth is a choice, which "tendency and temperament" lose.

@p
@greek ὅταν δὲ λέγηται
When it is said that first come the lots, then the patterns of lives, then the chances, and that they choose their lives from what is there according to their characters, he gives the sovereignty rather to the souls, who arrange what was given to suit their own characters.
!flag the sample lives are exhibited with the casual circumstances attending them and that the choice is made upon vision | The Greek has "the patterns of lives" (τὰ τῶν βίων παραδείγματα), the Republic's words, and says they choose "from what is there" (ἐκ τῶν παρόντων) according to their characters; "sample" and "made upon vision" are MacKenna's.
!note Republic X 617d-620d: the souls draw lots for the order of choosing; the patterns of lives are laid before them, "of every kind", with wealth, poverty, health and disease mixed in; each chooses for the most part "by the habit of his former life" (620a).

@p
@greek ὅτι γὰρ ὁ δαίμων οὗτος
For that this daemon is not wholly outside us, but is outside in the sense that he is not bound to us and is not the one acting; that he is ours as said of the soul, and not ours in so far as we are men of this kind, having the life that is under him: the Timaeus bears witness to this. If it is taken in this way, it will have no conflict; it would have some discord if the daemon were taken otherwise. And the words "fulfiller of what one chose" agree with it too. For, sitting above, he does not let one go much further down into the worse; only what is under him is active, neither what is above him nor what is equal to him; for it cannot become other than what it is.
!flag Man cannot cease to be characteristically Man | The Greek says "it cannot become other than what it is" (οὐ γὰρ δύναται ἄλλο γενέσθαι ἢ ᾗ ἔστιν): the part that acts cannot be above itself; man is not named.
!note Timaeus 90a: god has given each of us, as a daemon, the most sovereign kind of soul in us, which dwells at the top of the body and lifts us towards our kin in heaven. Republic X 620d-e: Lachesis sends with each the daemon he chose, "as guardian of his life and fulfiller of what he chose".

@ch III.4.6 | The good man's daemon, the stars, and the ship
The good man acts by the better; intellect is active in him, so he is a daemon, or lives by one, and his daemon is a god. Why not from the start? Because of the confusion of birth. The daemon leads the soul to judgment and then stays with it in its punishment; souls in beasts have a daemon too, a bad or simple one; souls above go to the sun or a planet or the fixed sphere, as they lived by reason, for our soul has a world in it like the world-soul's, and each goes to the star that suits it. Those beyond pass the daemonic nature and destiny. When the soul comes back, it embarks with its daemon on the All as on a ship, the spindle sets it in a seat of fortune, and what comes to it, and how it answers, is destiny.

@p
Who, then, is the good man? The one who acts by the better part. Or would he not be good, when he has his daemon working with him? For in him intellect is active. So either he is a daemon himself, or he lives by a daemon, and his daemon is a god. Is he then above intellect, if his daemon is what is above intellect? Why, then, was he not so from the beginning? Because of the confusion that comes from birth. And yet even before reasoning there is the movement within, reaching for what is its own. Does he then succeed in everything? Not in everything, since the soul is so disposed that, being such a soul among such things, it has such a life and such a choice.
!flag It does not suffice to perfect virtue to have only this Spirit | The Greek asks whether he would not be good "when he has his daemon working with him" (συνεργοῦντα ἑαυτῷ τὸν δαίμονα ἔχων), and answers that intellect is active in him; "perfect virtue", "only", and "equivalent in all men" are MacKenna's.
!flag An instinct which the Sage finally rectifies in every respect | The Greek asks "does he then succeed in everything?" (πάντως οὖν κατορθοῖ): of the good man's acts, not of an instinct rectified.

@p
@greek ὁ μέντοι δαίμων οὗτος
This daemon we speak of, having led the soul to Hades, is said not to remain the same, unless the soul chooses the same things again. But how before that? To lead to the judgment is for the soul to come, after it leaves birth, into the same figure it had before birth. Then, as from another beginning, he is present to the souls being punished, for the time between, until their later birth. Or rather, that is not life for them, but penalty. What of the souls that go into the bodies of beasts: is theirs less than a daemon? It is a daemon, but a bad one, or a simple one.
!note Phaedo 107d-108c, 113d: the daemon leads the dead to the place of judgment, and another guide brings them back after long periods of time. "A simple one" (εὐήθης): good-natured and simple-minded at once.

@p
@greek ταῖς δὲ ἄνω
And the souls above? Of those above, some are in the sensible world, some outside it. Those in the sensible world are in the sun or in another of the planets, others in the fixed sphere, each according as it was active by reason here. For we must think that there is a world in our soul too, not only an intelligible one, but a disposition of the same form as the soul of the world. Since that soul is distributed into the fixed sphere and the planets by different powers, the powers in us too are of the same form as these powers, and there is an activity from each; and, set free, the souls go there, to the star in harmony with the character and power that was active in them and lived, and they will have such a god, and daemon: either this very power or the one above it. But this must be looked at better.
!flag this star or the next highest power will stand to them as God or more exactly as. tutelary spirit | The Greek says they will have "such a god, and daemon" (τοιούτῳ θεῷ καὶ δαίμονί γε), "either this very one or the one above this power": the god or daemon is a power of the soul, not the star itself.
!note Timaeus 41d-42b: the maker sows each soul in a star, and whoever lives well returns to the dwelling of his star. Our soul, like the world's, is ordered as the fixed sphere and the planets (Timaeus 36b-d, 43a).

@p
@greek τὰς δὴ ἔξω γενομένας
Those that have come to be outside have passed beyond the daemonic nature and all the destiny of birth, and, in short, what is in this visible world, as long as they are there; and the part of the soul's being that loves birth has been carried up with them. If one were to say that this is the soul that comes to be divided about bodies, multiplying itself and dividing itself along with bodies, he would speak rightly. But it is divided not by magnitude: for the same is whole in all, and again one; and from one animal many are always born, this soul dividing in this way, as from plants too; for this too is divided about bodies. Sometimes it gives while it stays in the same thing, as the soul in plants does; sometimes, going away, it gave before it went away, as in plants that have been pulled up, or in animals that have died, when many are born from one by rotting. And such a power, being the same, works with it here from the All as well.
!flag its unity can always be reconstructed | The Greek says "the same is whole in all, and again one" (τὸ γὰρ αὐτὸ ἐν πᾶσιν ὅλον καὶ πάλιν ἕν): it is never broken, so nothing has to be reconstructed.
!note "Divided about bodies": Timaeus 35a, where the soul is mixed from the being that is undivided and the being "that comes to be divided about bodies"; Plotinus reads the passage in IV.2.

@p
@greek πάλιν δὲ ἐὰν ἴῃ
If the soul comes here again, it has the same daemon or another, according to the life it will lead. It embarks with this daemon on this All first, as on a skiff; then the nature called the spindle's takes it over and sets it, as in a ship, in some seat of fortune. As the circuit carries round, like a wind, the one who sits on the ship, or moves about on it, many and varied sights come to him, and changes and accidents, as on the ship itself: either from the tossing of the ship, or from himself, moved by an impulse of his own, which he might have from being on the ship in his own way. For not everyone in the same circumstances moves, or wills, or acts alike. So different things come to different people, either from the same events or from different ones, or the same things to others, even if the events differ. For such is destiny.
!flag this (personal answer to incident) it is that constitutes destiny | The Greek says "for such is destiny" (τοιοῦτον γὰρ ἡ εἱμαρμένη): destiny is the whole, ship, wind and passenger together, not the personal answer alone.
!note The spindle of Necessity, on which all the circles of the heaven turn, and the three Fates who turn it, are Plato's (Republic X 616c-617d); the souls, having chosen, are led under its turning (620e).

@treatise III.5 | On love
Plotinus asks whether love is a god, a daemon or a passion of the soul, and reads Plato's Symposium and Phaedrus for the answer. The passion is the soul's longing for a beauty it knows from before: some love the beauty here as an image of the beauty there and remember it, some are content with the beauty here, and some fall from it into the ugly. Love the god is the eye that the heavenly Aphrodite, the soul that stays above with intellect, begot in looking at intellect; the soul of the world begot another love, a daemon, and every soul has its own. Daemons are between gods and men, born from the soul of the All, and share in an intelligible matter. Then the myth of Eros' birth from Resource and Poverty at Aphrodite's birthday feast is read piece by piece: Zeus is intellect, Aphrodite his soul, Resource the reason-principle that flows from intellect into soul, drunk with nectar and asleep in the garden of Zeus, and Poverty the soul's indefinite longing, its matter. Love, their child, is always in need and always resourceful: a daemon, never filled.

@ch III.5.1 | Love the passion
Is love a god, a daemon or a passion? The passion is the soul's longing for beauty, which it knows and is akin to from before: nature makes by looking to the beautiful. Those who love bodies love them as images; those who recollect love them as images of the beauty there, those who do not take them for the truth. Some love beauty alone, some want also to beget, and so to be immortal; those who beget against nature have slipped from the road. Both the lover of beauty and the lover of women are self-controlled, but the first is better; and the longing for good often falls into evil.

@p
On love: is it a god, or a daemon, or a passion of the soul? Or is one love a god or a daemon, and another a passion too? And what is each of them like? It is worth looking into this, going through the thoughts of other people, and those that have arisen in philosophy about these things, and above all what the divine Plato holds, who wrote much about love in many places in his works. He says not only that it is a passion that comes to be in souls, but also calls it a daemon, and he tells of its birth, how and from what parents it was born.
!flag a Celestial Spirit, a state of mind | The Greek has δαίμων, "daemon", Plato's word for Eros in the Symposium (202d-e), and πάθος, a "passion" of the soul; MacKenna's "Celestial Spirit" is not the word, and he keeps changing it ("Spirit-being", "Celestial", "Supernal") through the treatise.
!flag from a point of view entirely his own | The Greek says Plato "wrote much about love in many places in his works" (πολλὰ πολλαχῇ τῶν ἑαυτοῦ): τῶν ἑαυτοῦ is "of his own writings", not a point of view of his own.
!note Plato on love: Diotima's speech in the Symposium (201d-212a), where Eros is a great daemon between gods and men (202d-e) and his birth is told (203b-e); and the Phaedrus, where love is a madness from the gods and Eros a god (242d-e, 249d-256e).

@p
@greek περὶ μὲν οὖν τοῦ πάθους
As for the passion that we blame on love: that it comes to be in souls that long to be joined with something beautiful, and that this longing is, in some, that of the self-controlled, who are at home with beauty itself, while in others it wants to end in some shameful act, no one, I suppose, is unaware. But where each of the two has its origin, it is fitting to examine from here on, with philosophy.
!flag that of the good whose devotion is for beauty itself | The Greek says the one longing is "of the self-controlled" (παρὰ σωφρόνων), made at home with beauty itself; MacKenna's "the good" loses the virtue, to which the chapter comes back: for the self-controlled, the attachment to beauty here is without fault.

@p
@greek ἀρχην δὲ εἴ τις θεῖτο
If one were to lay down as the origin the longing for beauty itself that is in souls beforehand, their recognition of it, their kinship with it, and an unreasoning awareness that it is their own, he would hit, I think, on the true cause. For the ugly is opposed both to nature and to god. Nature makes by looking to the beautiful, and it looks to the defined, which is in the column of the good; the undefined is ugly, and of the other column. And nature has its origin from there, from the good, and plainly from the beautiful too. Whatever one delights in and is akin to, one is drawn to its images too.
!flag a tendency of the Soul towards pure beauty | The Greek speaks of the longing for beauty itself that is in souls "beforehand" (πρότερον), before any beautiful body is seen, together with a "recognition" (ἐπίγνωσις) of it: love begins from what the soul already knows. MacKenna's "tendency" loses the "beforehand".
!flag the consistent total of the good | The Greek συστοιχία is a "column" of the Pythagorean table of opposites, in which the limited stands with the good and the unlimited with the bad; "the consistent total" and "the system of evil" hide the reference.
!note The two columns: the Pythagoreans set out ten pairs of opposites, limit and unlimited, odd and even, one and many, and so on to good and bad, in two columns (Aristotle, Metaphysics I.5, 986a22-26). The defined (ὡρισμένον) stands with limit, and so with the good; the undefined (ἀόριστον) with the unlimited.

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις ταύτην τὴν αἰτίαν ἀνέλοι
If one takes away this cause, he will not be able to say how the passion arises, or for what causes, not even in the case of the loves that aim at intercourse. For these too want to beget in beauty; it would be absurd for nature, which wants to make beautiful things, to want to beget in the ugly. But those who are moved to beget here are content to have the beauty here, which is present in images and bodies, since the archetype is not present to them, the archetype that is the cause of their loving even this beauty. For those who have come from this beauty to the recollection of that one, this one is loved as an image; but those who have not recollected, not knowing what is happening to them, take it for the true one. For the self-controlled, the attachment to the beauty here is without fault; but the fall into intercourse is a fault.
!note To "beget in beauty" (τίκτειν ἐν καλῷ) is Diotima's account of what love does (Symposium 206b-e). The sight of beauty here reminds the soul of the beauty it saw before birth, and those who are not newly initiated "do not know what is happening to them" (Phaedrus 249d-250b).

@p
@greek καὶ ὅτῳ μὲν καθαρὸς
Whoever has a pure love of the beautiful loves beauty alone, whether he has recollected or not. But whoever has another desire mixed in too, the desire to be immortal, as far as a mortal can, seeks the beautiful in what is always being born and everlasting; and, going according to nature, he sows and begets in beauty: sowing for always, and in beauty, because of his kinship with the beautiful. For the everlasting is akin to the beautiful; the everlasting nature is the first thing of this kind, and all that comes from it is such. So what does not want to beget is more self-sufficient in beauty; what longs to make something wants to make a beautiful thing out of need, and is not self-sufficient, and it thinks it will make such a thing if it begets in beauty. But those who want to beget lawlessly and against nature made their start from the road according to nature, and were carried aside from it; they lie where they fell, as if they had slipped on a road, knowing neither the love that was leading them, nor the longing to beget, nor the use of the image of beauty, nor what beauty itself is.
!note "Love is of immortality too": mortal nature shares in immortality by begetting (Symposium 206e-208b). Love against nature: in the Phaedrus the one who is not newly initiated, seeing beauty, "gives himself over to pleasure and tries to mount and beget like a beast, and pursues pleasure against nature" (250e-251a); compare Laws VIII 836c, 841d.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ οὖν οἵ τε σωμάτων
Those who love beautiful bodies, not for intercourse, love them because they are beautiful; those who have the love called mixed, the love of women, love so that there may also be the "always". As long as they do not slip towards other things, both are self-controlled, but the first are better. But some revere the beauty here and are content with it; others, all who have recollected, revere that beauty too, and do not dishonour this one either, as a product of that one and its plaything. These, then, are about the beautiful without the ugly; others fall into the ugly because of the beautiful, for the longing for good often has its fall into evil. These, then, are the passions of the soul.
!flag a last outgrowth, an attenuation of the higher | The Greek calls the beauty here "a product" (ἀποτέλεσμα) and "a plaything" (παίγνιον) of the beauty there; "attenuation" is MacKenna's, and the plaything is lost.
!note The plaything: Plato's man is "a plaything of god" (Laws VII 803c), and Plotinus calls the world's wars and changes a play (III.2.15). The "always" is the immortality of the kind, which the lover of women seeks by begetting (Symposium 207d-208b).

@ch III.5.2 | The heavenly Aphrodite and her love
Plato calls Eros a god, Aphrodite's, overseer of beautiful boys, and in the Symposium says he was born at Aphrodite's birthday feast from Poverty and Resource. So who is Aphrodite? There are two: the heavenly, motherless daughter of Ouranos, and the daughter of Zeus and Dione, who has to do with marriages. The heavenly one, from Kronos, who is intellect, is the most divine soul, which stays above, pure, a god and not a daemon. Looking to intellect she loved it and begot Eros, who looks there with her: the eye of the lover, which sees the beauty before it lets the lover see.

@p
As for the love that is held to be a god, not only by other people but by the theologians, and by Plato in many places, who speaks of Eros as Aphrodite's and says that his work is to be the overseer of beautiful boys and to move souls towards the beauty there, or to strengthen the impulse towards it that is there already: about this above all we must philosophize. And we must take in too all that is said in the Symposium, where he says that Eros was not born of Aphrodite, but at Aphrodite's birthday feast, from Poverty and Resource. The account seems to demand that we say something about Aphrodite too, since Eros is said to have been born either from her or with her. First, then, who is Aphrodite? Then, how is Eros from her, or with her, or in what way is he both from her and with her at once?
!flag Theologians (Orphic teachers) | The Greek has only "theologians" (θεολόγοι), those who tell of the gods, Hesiod as well as the Orphic poets; MacKenna's bracket narrows them.
!flag minister of beautiful children | The Greek ἔφορον καλῶν παίδων is "overseer of beautiful boys", Plato's words for Eros in the Phaedrus (265c): the boys are the young who are loved, not children who are born.
!flag Poros, Possession, the father | Πόρος is a "way through", a "means", "resource": the son of Metis, Cunning (Symposium 203b), the opposite of the helplessness (ἀπορία) of his partner Poverty; "Possession" makes him a having rather than a finding of ways.
!note Eros as Aphrodite's son: Phaedrus 242d; as overseer of beautiful boys: Phaedrus 265c. His birth at the feast for Aphrodite's birth, from Poros, Metis' son, and Penia: Symposium 203b-c.

@p
@greek λέγομεν δὴ τὴν Ἀφροδίτην εἶναι διττήν
We say, then, that Aphrodite is twofold: the heavenly one, who we say is Ouranos', and the one born of Zeus and Dione, who has to do with the marriages here. The heavenly one is motherless and beyond marriages, since there are no marriages in heaven either. The one called heavenly, from Kronos, who is intellect, must be the most divine soul, coming straight from him, pure from pure, staying above, so that she neither wanted nor was able to come to the things here, since she was not of a nature to go down among the things below, being a separate reality and a being that has no share in matter (which is why they hinted at her by this, that she is motherless). One would rightly call her a god, not a daemon, since she is unmixed and stays pure by herself. For what is born straight from intellect is pure too, since it is strong by itself through its nearness, and since its desire and its settled place are towards what begot it, which is able to hold it above. So a soul that hangs from intellect could not fall away, much less than the sun could lose the light that shines round it, which comes from it and is bound to it.
!flag justly called not Celestial Spirit but God | The Greek has δαίμονα, "a daemon": the heavenly Aphrodite is a god and not a daemon, because she is unmixed. MacKenna's "Celestial Spirit" hides that the distinction is Plato's, between gods and daemons (Symposium 202d-203a).
!note Pausanias' speech in the Symposium (180d-181c) has the two Aphrodites, the elder and motherless daughter of Ouranos, called heavenly, and the younger daughter of Zeus and Dione, called common, each with her Eros. In Hesiod (Theogony 188-200) Aphrodite rises from the foam round the parts of Ouranos that Kronos cut off; Dione is her mother in Homer (Iliad V.370-371). Kronos is intellect for Plotinus (V.1.4, V.1.7), after the Cratylus (396b), where his name means the pure and unmixed of intellect.

@p
@greek ἐφεπομένη δὲ τῷ Κρόνῳ
Following Kronos, or, if you like, Kronos' father Ouranos, she was active towards him and became his own, and in love with him she begot Eros, and with him she looks towards him; and her activity made a reality and a being. And both look there, the mother and the beautiful Eros she bore, a reality always ranked towards another beautiful thing, and having its being in this: between, as it were, the one who longs and the one longed for. He is the eye of the one who longs, giving the lover through himself the power to see the beloved, but running ahead himself, and, before he gives the other the power to see through the organ, filling himself with the sight. He sees first, though not in like manner, in that he fixes the sight in the lover, but himself reaps the vision of the beauty as it runs past him.
!flag not even in the same order | The Greek says love sees first, "though not in the same way" (οὐ μὴν ὁμοίως ὁρῶν): it fixes the sight in the lover and itself reaps the vision. Nothing is said of an order, nor that desire sees "only through the efficacy of Love".
!flag beauty playing immediately above it | The Greek says the beauty "runs past" it (παραθέουσαν), not that it plays above it.
!note The eye: in the Phaedrus the stream of beauty enters the lover through the eyes (251b), and flows back to the beloved through his (255c-d). Plotinus' next chapter takes Eros' name from seeing.

@ch III.5.3 | Love born from seeing; the love of the world's soul
Love is a reality, born from a reality. The soul above looked at intellect, the first being, with such intensity and joy that she begot something worthy of herself and of the sight: an eye filled with what it sees, Eros, whose name may come from seeing. This love is separate, like the soul, and stays above. The soul of the All begot another love, who has to do with marriages, and who, as far as he touches the longing above, moves the souls of the young and turns soul back to the memory of what is there; for every soul longs for the good.

@p
That it is a reality and a being, from a being, less than the one that made it but a being all the same, we ought not to doubt. For that soul too was a being, born from the activity before it, and living, and of the being of the things that are, and looking towards what was the first being, and looking intently. This was her first sight, and she looked at it as at her own good, and rejoiced in looking; and the sight was such that the one who saw could not make the seeing a side matter, so that by her pleasure, as it were, and her straining towards it, and the intensity of her seeing, she begot from herself something worthy of herself and of the sight. So from what was intently active about the seen, and from what flows, as it were, from the seen, an eye was filled, a sight with its image, as it were, and Eros was born; perhaps his name too came from here, because he has his reality from seeing (horasis). For the passion would take its name from this one, if being comes before what is not being; and the passion is called loving, and if love holds someone, it is love of this or that; it would not be called love simply. Such, then, would be the Eros of the soul above, himself looking above, since he is her follower, born from her and by her, and content with the sight of the gods.
!flag That Love is a Hypostasis (a " Person ") | The Greek says love is a "reality" (ὑπόστασις) and a "being" (οὐσία); "Person" is MacKenna's.
!flag towards the very Highest | The Greek says the soul looks "towards what was the first being" (πρὸς ἐκεῖνο ... ὃ πρώτη ἦν οὐσία): intellect, the first being, not the One, which is beyond being.
!note Eros from horasis, "seeing": a play on ἔρως and ὅρασις. In the Cratylus (420a-b) Plato takes ἔρως from the flowing in (ἐσρεῖν) of beauty through the eyes. The "follower" (ὀπαδός) of a god is the Phaedrus' word for the souls that follow the gods round the heaven (248a, 252c).

@p
@greek χωριστὴν δὲ ἐκείνην τὴν ψυχὴν
If we say that that soul, which first lights up the heaven, is separate, we shall hold that this Eros is separate too, even though we did call the soul heavenly as much as we could; just as in our own case, when we say that the best in us is in us, we still hold that it is separate. So let him be only there, where the pure soul is.
!flag though not, perhaps, so loftily celestial a being as the Soul | The Greek says "even though we called the soul heavenly as much as could be" (εἰ καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα οὐρανίαν τὴν ψυχὴν εἴπομεν): her name does not tie her to the heaven, and so her love is separate too. No comparison is made between the love and the soul.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς
But since there had to be a soul of this All too, the other Eros came into being with her at once, he too her eye, he too born from longing. Being the world's, this Aphrodite, who is not only soul nor soul simply, begot the Eros in this world too, who already has to do with marriages himself, and who, as far as he too touches the longing above, so far moves the souls of the young, and turns back the soul with which he is ranked, as far as she too is of a nature to come to the memory of those things. For every soul longs for the good, the mixed one too, and the one that has become some one thing's; since this soul too comes next after that one, and from it.
!flag giving birth, therefore, to the Love concerned with the universal life | The Greek says that this Aphrodite, "not only soul nor simply soul", begot the love in this world, who has to do with marriages; MacKenna's "the Love concerned with the universal life", followed by "no", turns the Greek's statement into a denial.
!note The love of the common Aphrodite, who has to do with marriages and bodies: Symposium 180d-181c.

@ch III.5.4 | Each soul's love; many Aphrodites
Has each soul its own love, as the whole soul and the soul of the All have? Yes: this love is the daemon that goes with each, putting in the desires that suit its nature, as worthy as the soul that begets it. The whole soul has the whole love, the partial souls their own, and as the souls are one, so are the loves; the love in the All appears everywhere in it. So there are many Aphrodites in the All, daemons, hanging from one whole Aphrodite: soul is love's mother, Aphrodite is soul, love is a soul's activity reaching for the good. The love of the soul above is a god, the love of the mixed soul a daemon.

@p
Does each soul, then, have such a love too, in being and in reality? Or why should the whole soul, and the soul of the All, have love as a reality, and the soul of each of us not, and the soul in all the other animals too? And this love, then, is the daemon that, they say, goes along with each, each one's own love. For this would be the one that puts in the desires according to the nature of each soul, each soul reaching out in proportion to its own nature and begetting the love that answers to its worth and its being.
!flag the Spirit which, as we are told, walks with every being | The Greek has ὁ δαίμων, "the daemon" that goes with each, Plato's daemon allotted to each of us (Phaedo 107d, Republic X 617e; III.4); MacKenna's "Spirit" hides the reference.
!flag the guiding spirit realising its worth and the quality of its Being | The Greek says the soul begets the love "answering to its worth and its being" (εἴς τε ἀξίαν καὶ πρὸς οὐσίαν): the love is as worthy as the soul that begets it. It is the soul that begets, not the guiding spirit that realises.
!note Plotinus' III.4 made the daemon allotted to each the power of the soul just above the one by which we live; here it is each one's own love.

@p
@greek ἐχέτω δὴ ἡ μὲν ὅλη ὅλον
So let the whole soul have the whole love, and the partial souls each its own. And as each soul stands to the whole, not cut off from it but contained in it, so that all are one, each love too would stand to the whole love; and the partial love would be with the partial soul, and that great love with the whole soul; and the love in the All would be everywhere in the All, and this one love would become many and be many, appearing everywhere in the All where he wishes, shaping himself in his parts and showing himself, if he wishes.
!note All souls one: IV.9, and IV.3.1-8, where the partial souls are not cut off from the whole soul.

@p
@greek οἴεσθαι δὲ χρὴ καὶ Ἀφροδίτας
We must think too that there are many Aphrodites in the whole, daemons that have come to be in it with love, flowed from some whole Aphrodite, many partial ones hanging from her with loves of their own; if soul is the mother of love, and Aphrodite is soul, and love is the activity of a soul reaching for the good. So this love, who leads each soul to the nature of the good: the love of the soul above would be a god, who always joins the soul to that good; the love of the mixed soul a daemon.
!flag the Love in the mingling Soul will be a celestial spirit | The Greek says the love of the mixed soul is "a daemon" (δαίμων), as the love of the soul above is "a god": Plato's distinction between gods and daemons, which "celestial spirit" hides.

@ch III.5.5 | Love is not the world
What is the nature of daemons, which the Symposium speaks of, and of Eros, born from Poverty and Resource? Some take Plato's Eros to be the world. But the world is a blessed and self-sufficient god, and Eros, Plato says, is neither god nor self-sufficient, but always in need. If the world is soul and body, Aphrodite would be the ruling part of Eros; if the world is its soul, Eros would be Aphrodite. Why would this daemon be the world and the others not? How could the world be overseer of beautiful boys, or homeless and barefoot?

@p
But what is the nature of a daemon, and of daemons altogether, of which the Symposium speaks too: the nature of the others, and that of Eros himself, who was born from Poverty and Resource, the son of Cunning, at Aphrodite's birthday feast? To suppose that Plato means by Eros this world, and not the Eros that has grown up in the world, has much against it. For the world is said to be a blessed god and self-sufficient, while this Eros is agreed by Plato to be neither a god nor self-sufficient, but always in need.
!flag Poros — Possession — who is son of Metis — Resource | Μῆτις is "cunning", practical wisdom, the mother of Πόρος (Symposium 203b), and it is Poros himself who is "resource"; MacKenna gives the son's name to the mother.
!flag the passage has been misunderstood | The Greek says only that to suppose Plato meant the world "has much against it"; MacKenna's bracket says who misunderstood.
!note Plutarch had read the myth so: in On Isis and Osiris 57 (374c-d) Poros is the first and self-sufficient, Penia is matter, and Eros, born of them, is the world. The world a blessed god: Timaeus 34b; self-sufficient: 33d. Eros neither god nor self-sufficient: Symposium 202b-d, 203c-d.

@p
@greek εἶτα ἀνάγκη, εἴπερ ὁ κόσμος
Then, if the world is from soul and body, and the soul of the world is Aphrodite to Plato, Aphrodite must be the ruling part of Eros; or, if the world is its soul, as a man is the soul of a man, Eros must be Aphrodite. Then why will this one, being a daemon, be the world, and the other daemons, who are plainly of the same being, not be the world too? And the world will be a compound made of just this, of daemons. And how could the one said to be the overseer of beautiful boys be the world? And how could "without bed, barefoot and homeless" fit it, except meanly and out of tune?
!flag Our only escape would be to make the Kosmos a complex of Supernals | The Greek says "and the world will be a compound made of just this, of daemons" (ἔσται σύστασις αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐκ δαιμόνων): one more absurdity, not an escape; "Supernals" is MacKenna's word for daemons.
!flag Love, again, is called the Dispenser of beautiful children | The Greek has ἔφορος καλῶν παίδων, "overseer of beautiful boys" (Phaedrus 265c): not a giver of children.
!note A man is his soul: Alcibiades I 130c. Eros "hard and dry, barefoot and homeless, always lying on the ground without a bed": Symposium 203c-d.

@ch III.5.6 | Gods, daemons, and intelligible matter
How do daemons differ from gods? The gods are without passion; daemons, everlasting and next to the gods, have passions, between gods and men. There is no daemon in the intelligible: even a daemon itself would be a god; the visible gods down to the moon are second gods, like the radiance round a star. A daemon is the trace of a soul that has come into the world; the loves are born from soul's longing for the good, the other daemons from the other powers of the soul of the All, to govern it. They do not share in bodily matter, but they must share in some matter, an intelligible one, through which they come to bodies.

@p
What, then, must we say about Eros and his so-called birth? Plainly we must grasp what Poverty is and what Resource is, and how they suit being his parents. And plainly we must make them suit the other daemons too, if daemons, as daemons, are to have one nature and one being, and not only a common name. Let us grasp, then, how we distinguish gods from daemons, even if we often call daemons gods too, at least when we say that the one is one kind, and the other another. We say and hold that the kind of the gods is free from passion, but we give passions to daemons, saying that they are everlasting, next after the gods, but already towards us, between gods and our kind.
!flag distinguish the Gods from the Celestials | The Greek has δαίμονες, "daemons", throughout; MacKenna's "Celestials", "Spirits" and "Supernals" change from sentence to sentence for one Greek word.
!note Daemons between gods and men: Symposium 202d-203a. The Epinomis (984d-985b) gives daemons pleasure and pain, which the gods do not feel.

@p
@greek πῇ δὴ οὖν οὐκ ἔμειναν ἀπαθεῖς
How, then, did these not stay free from passion? How did they come down by nature to the worse? And this too must be looked at: whether there is not even one daemon in the intelligible, and only daemons in this world, while god is set apart in the intelligible; or whether there are gods here too, and the world is a god, the third, as it is usual to say, and each of those down to the moon is a god. It is better not to call any in the intelligible a daemon, but, even if there is a daemon itself, to call him a god too; and again, in the sensible, to call those down to the moon, the visible gods, second gods, after those intelligible ones and in accord with them, hanging from them, like the radiance round each star.
!note The world as a god: Timaeus 34a-b, 92c; the "third" after the first god and intellect, as Numenius counted them (fr. 21 des Places). The visible gods, the stars, born: Timaeus 40d, 41a.

@p
@greek τοὺς δὲ δαίμονας τί;
What, then, are daemons? Is each the trace of a soul that has come into the world? And why of a soul in the world? Because a pure soul begets a god, and we said that the love of this soul is a god. First, then, why are not all daemons loves? And then, how are these not pure of matter too? Or: those are loves that are begotten when a soul longs for the good and the beautiful, and all the souls here beget this daemon; but the other daemons, also from a soul, the soul of the All, are begotten by other powers, and fill out the All and help to govern each thing in it, according to the need of the whole. For the soul of the All had to be sufficient for the All, begetting the powers of daemons, those fitted to its own whole.
!flag A Celestial is the representative generated by each Soul when it enters the Kosmos | The Greek asks (ἆρά γε ...;) whether daemons are "the trace" (ἴχνος) of a soul that has come into the world: a trace left behind, not a representative sent out, and a question, not an answer.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ πῶς καὶ τίνος ὕλης
But how, and in what matter, do they share? Not bodily matter, or they will be animals of sense.
