For even if they take on bodies of air or of fire, their nature must first be different, so that they can share in body too; for what is pure in every way does not mix with body straight off, although many think that the being of a daemon, in so far as it is a daemon, goes with some body, of air or of fire. But why does one mix with body and another not, unless there is some cause in the one that mixes? What, then, is the cause? We must posit an intelligible matter, so that what shares in it may come through it into this matter too, the matter of bodies.
!note Daemons with bodies of air: Epinomis 984b-985b, and Apuleius, On the god of Socrates 8-11. Intelligible matter, the matter of the forms: II.4.2-5, after Aristotle's "intelligible matter" (Metaphysics VII.10, 1036a9-12).

@ch III.5.7 | Resource, Poverty, and what love is
So Resource was drunk with nectar before there was wine: love was born before the sensible, and Poverty shared in the intelligible, with the indefiniteness the soul has before it reaches the good. A reason-principle in what is not reason, a sufficient reason and an indefinite longing, made a love that is lacking, never filled, like a gadfly: helpless by its need, resourceful by its reason. Every daemon is such. The good love the good simply; others live by other daemons; the bad fetter their loves with evil desires. Natural loves are beautiful and real; loves against nature are passions, not beings. Our love is for the simple things, as our thoughts are.

@p
That is why Plato, in telling of Eros' birth, says that Resource was drunk with nectar, "for there was no wine yet": as if Eros was born before the sensible, and Poverty shared in the nature of the intelligible, not of an image of the intelligible pictured from there, but came to be there and was mixed with Resource, as from form and indefiniteness: the indefiniteness the soul has before it reaches the good, while it divines that there is something, by an indefinite and boundless image. So she bore the reality of Eros.
!flag Penia (Poverty) had participation in the Intellectual before the lower image of that divine Realm had appeared | The Greek says Poverty shared in the intelligible nature, "not of an image of the intelligible" pictured from there: the contrast is between the intelligible and its image, not one of time; "before" is MacKenna's.
!note Symposium 203b-c: on the day Aphrodite was born the gods feasted, Poros among them; when they had dined, Penia came to beg at the door. Poros, drunk with nectar, "for there was no wine yet", went into the garden of Zeus and, weighed down, fell asleep; and Penia, plotting because of her own helplessness to have a child by Poros, lay down beside him and conceived Eros.

@p
@greek λόγος οὖν γενόμενος ἐν οὐ λόγῳ
So a reason-principle, coming to be in what is not reason, but in an indefinite longing and a dim reality, made what was born neither complete nor sufficient, but lacking, since it was born from an indefinite longing and a sufficient reason-principle. And this reason-principle is not pure, since it has in itself a longing that is indefinite, unreasoning and boundless; for it will never be filled, as long as it has in itself the nature of the indefinite. It hangs from soul, since it was born from her as from its origin; but it is a mixture of a reason-principle that did not stay in itself but was mixed with indefiniteness, not by blending itself with it, but by what comes from it. And love is like a gadfly, without resource by its own nature; so even when it gets what it wants, it is without resource again. For it cannot be filled, because it is a mixture; only what is already full by its own nature is truly filled; but what longs because of the need that is with it, even if it is filled for the moment, does not hold it. So its helplessness comes from its need, and its resourcefulness from the nature of the reason-principle.
!flag Love, therefore, is like a goad | The Greek οἶστρος is a "gadfly", the insect whose sting drives cattle wild, and so a frenzy: Plato's word for the lover driven by desire (Phaedrus 240d); a goad is the herdsman's, used from outside.
!note Eros, by his mother, is without resource (ἄπορος), and by his father resourceful (πόριμος): what he gains always slips away, so that he is never without resource nor rich (Symposium 203d-e).

@p
@greek δεῖ δὲ καὶ πᾶν τὸ δαιμόνιον
And we must think that every daemon is such, and from such parents. For each is resourceful for what it is set over, and longs for it, and in this is akin to Eros; and it is not full either, but longs for one of the partial things, as goods.

@p
@greek ὅθεν καὶ τοὺς ἐνταῦθα ἀγαθοὺς
So the good here, having the love they have of the good simply and truly, do not have some particular love; and those who are ranked under other daemons are ranked under one daemon or another: they have left idle the daemon they had simply, and act by another daemon, which they chose in accord with the part of soul that is active in them. Those who long for evils have fettered all the loves in them with the evil desires that have come to be in them, just as they have fettered the right reason, which is born with them, with the evil opinions that have come on top.
!flag but this is mere blank possession when they ignore their own | The Greek says they "have left idle" (ἀργὸν ἀφέντας) the daemon they had simply, and act by another they chose: as in III.4.3, where the daemon above stands over us idle while the one below acts.
!flag merged all the Love-Principles within them in the evil desires | The Greek says they "fettered" (ἐπέδησαν) all the loves in them with evil desires, as they fettered the right reason, "which is inborn" (σύμφυτος), with evil opinions; "merged", "which belongs to our kind" and "from another source" are MacKenna's.
!note The choice of a daemon by the part of the soul that is active: III.4.3, after Republic X 617e.

@p
@greek οἱ μὲν οὖν φύσει ἔρωτες
The loves, then, that are by nature and according to nature are beautiful: those of a lesser soul lesser in worth and power, those of a greater soul greater, but all of them in being. But those against nature are the passions of those who have slipped, and in no way beings or realities with being, no longer born from soul, but coming into existence along with the vice of a soul that begets things like itself, in dispositions and states, by now.
!flag All the natural Loves, all that serve the ends of Nature, are good | The Greek calls the natural loves "beautiful" (καλοί), the word of the whole treatise, not "good"; "that serve the ends of Nature" is MacKenna's for "according to nature".

@p
@greek καὶ γὰρ ὅλως κινδυνεύει
For on the whole it seems that the true goods, when the soul is active according to nature within what is defined, are being, and the others, when it is not active from itself, are nothing but passions; just as false thoughts do not have beings beneath them, as the true ones do, which are truly everlasting and defined, having together thinking, the intelligible and being, not only in what is simply, but in each one, about what is truly intelligible, and the intellect in each form. And we must posit in each of us, purely, thinking and the intelligible, though we are not this together and simply. So our love too is of the simple things, for so are our thoughts; and if it is of some partial thing, it is by accident, as if one saw that this triangle has angles equal to two right angles in so far as it is simply a triangle.
!flag a given triangular figure is made up of two right angles | The Greek has the old theorem: this triangle has its angles equal to "two right angles" (δύο ὀρθάς), and one sees it in this triangle in so far as it is simply a triangle. A triangle is not "made up of" right angles.
!note The triangle's two right angles were the schools' example of what belongs to a thing as such, not by accident (Aristotle, Posterior Analytics I.4, 73b30-74a3; I.24, 85b5-15).

@ch III.5.8 | Zeus and his garden
Who is Zeus, into whose garden Resource went? Not soul, which is Aphrodite. Plato calls Zeus the great leader in the Phaedrus, the third elsewhere, and in the Philebus says there is in Zeus a royal soul and a royal intellect. So Zeus is intellect, and Aphrodite, his, from him and with him, is his soul, named for the beauty, splendour, innocence and delicacy of soul. The male gods are intellects, the female their souls; priests and theologians make Hera and Aphrodite one, and call Aphrodite's star Hera's.

@p
But who is Zeus, whose garden he speaks of, the garden into which Resource went? And what is this garden? For Aphrodite, we said, was soul, and Resource was said to be the reason-principle of all things. What must we take these to be, Zeus and his garden? We must not take Zeus to be soul, since we took Aphrodite to be that. Here too we must take Zeus from Plato: in the Phaedrus he calls this god a great leader, and elsewhere, I think, the third; and more plainly in the Philebus, where he says that in Zeus there is a royal soul and a royal intellect.
!flag though elsewhere he seems to rank him as one of three | The Greek says that elsewhere Plato calls Zeus "the third, I think" (τρίτον, οἶμαι): a rank, not one of three.
!note Zeus "the great leader in heaven": Phaedrus 246e. "The third" is probably Zeus the Saviour, to whom the third libation was poured (Republic IX 583b, Philebus 66d); Plotinus' "I think" shows he quotes from memory. "In the nature of Zeus a royal soul and a royal intellect": Philebus 30d.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν ὁ Ζεὺς νοῦς ἐστι μέγας
If, then, Zeus is a great intellect and soul, and is ranked among the causes, and must be ranked by the better in him, both for other reasons and because the royal and leading is a cause, he will be on the side of intellect; and Aphrodite, being his, and from him, and with him, will be ranked on the side of soul, called Aphrodite for the beautiful, the splendid, the innocent and the delicate (habron) in soul. For if we rank the male gods with intellect and call the female ones their souls, since a soul is with each intellect, in this way too the soul of Zeus would be Aphrodite; and priests and theologians bear witness to this account again, who bring Hera and Aphrodite to the same, and call Aphrodite's star in the heaven Hera's.
!flag he must be the highest for several reasons | The Greek says Zeus must be ranked "by the better" (κατὰ τὸ κρεῖττον) of what is in him, intellect rather than soul, so "he will be on the side of intellect"; not that he is the highest.
!note Aphrodite and ἁβρός, "delicate": the play is Plotinus'; Plato takes her name from the foam (ἀφρός) she was born from (Cratylus 406c-d). Hera's star: the morning star, "which some call Aphrodite's and others Hera's" ([Aristotle], On the cosmos 2, 392a27-28; Pliny, Natural History II.37).

@ch III.5.9 | The myth read whole
@older 9 10
Resource is the reason-principle of the intelligible, unfolded, coming into soul: drunk because his fullness is brought in from outside, as intellect's is not. The garden of Zeus is the adornments that come from his intellect into soul; the nectar is the reason-principle that the divine receives. Myths divide into times and births what is always together; put together again, soul with intellect, filled with reason-principles, is Aphrodite, her reason-principles Resource, her adornments the garden where he sleeps, and the gods' feast their blessed life. Love has always been, from soul's longing for the good: mixed, needy and resourceful. His mother Poverty is matter, the indefiniteness of desire; so love is something like matter, a daemon born from soul.

@p
Resource, then, being the reason-principle of the things in the intelligible and in intellect, and more poured out, and unfolded, as it were, would come to be about soul and in soul. For what is gathered together in intellect does not come into it from another; but to Resource, drunk, the filling is brought in from outside. And what would the one filled there with nectar be, but a reason-principle fallen from a better principle to a lesser? So this reason-principle is in the soul from intellect, when Aphrodite is said to have been born, having flowed into his garden.
!flag being more diffused, kneaded out as it were | The Greek has ἁπλωθείς, "unfolded", "spread out", as against what is "coiled together" (συνεσπειραμένον) in intellect; "kneaded" is MacKenna's.
!flag breaking into the garden of Zeus | The Greek says the reason-principle "flowed into" (εἰσρυείς) his garden: nothing breaks in.

@p
@greek κῆπος δὲ πᾶς ἀγλάισμα
Every garden is an adornment and a show of wealth. Zeus' garden is adorned by Zeus' reason-principle, and its ornaments are the adornments that have come from his intellect into the soul. Or what would the garden of Zeus be, but his statues and his adornments? And what would his adornments and ornaments be, but the reason-principles that have flowed from him? So the reason-principles together, Resource, the plenty and wealth of beautiful things, now showing forth: this is being drunk with nectar. For what is nectar to the gods, but what the divine receives? And what is below intellect receives a reason-principle. Intellect has itself in fullness, and is not drunk in having it, for it has nothing brought in. But the reason-principle, the offspring of intellect and a reality after intellect, no longer its own but in another, is said to lie in the garden of Zeus, who is intellect; and it lies there at the time when Aphrodite is said to come to be among the beings.
!flag what the god-nature essentially demands | The Greek asks "what is nectar to the gods but what the divine receives (κομίζεται)?", and answers that what is below intellect receives a reason-principle: what is received, not demanded.
!note Intellect "in fullness" (ἐν κόρῳ): Plotinus takes Kronos' name from κόρος, "fullness", and νοῦς (V.1.4, V.1.7), after the Cratylus (396b).

@p
@greek δεῖ δὲ τοὺς μύθους
Myths, if they are to be myths, must divide what they tell into times, and separate from one another many of the beings that are together but stand apart in rank or in powers; since reasoned accounts too make births of what is unborn, and they too divide what is together, and, having taught as well as they can, they let the one who has understood put it together again. Put together, it is this: soul, being with intellect, and having its reality from intellect, and filled in turn with reason-principles, beautiful and adorned with beautiful things, and filled with plenty, so that many adornments are to be seen in her, and images of all beautiful things, is Aphrodite as a whole; all the reason-principles in her are plenty and Resource, from the nectar there flowing from above; and the adornments in her, as lying in life, are called the garden of Zeus, and Resource is said to sleep there, weighed down by what he was filled with. And since life has shown itself and is always among the beings, the gods are said to feast, as being in such blessedness.
!flag breaking away from it | The Greek says soul "has its reality from intellect" (παρὰ νοῦ ὑποστᾶσα): it comes from intellect, and stays "with intellect"; it does not break away from it.
!note So the early Academy read the Timaeus' making of the world: told as a birth in time for the sake of teaching, as one draws a figure step by step (Aristotle, On the heavens I.10, 279b32-280a2).

@p
@greek ἀεὶ δὲ οὕτως ὑπέστη
And Eros has always come to be in this way, of necessity, from the soul's longing for the better and the good, and he always was, as long as soul was. He is a mixed thing, sharing in need, by which he wants to be filled, but not without a share in plenty, by which he seeks what is lacking to what he has; for what has no share at all in the good would never seek the good. So he is said to be from Resource and Poverty, in that the lack, the longing and the memory of the reason-principles, coming together in the soul, begot the activity towards the good, which is this love.

@p
@greek ἡ δὲ μήτηρ αὐτῷ Πενία
His mother is Poverty, because longing always belongs to what is in need. And Poverty is matter, because matter too is in need of all things, and because of the indefiniteness of the desire for the good: for there is no shape or reason-principle in what longs for it, and the longing makes what longs more like matter, as far as it longs. But what is turned towards itself is form alone, staying in itself; and when something longs to receive, it makes what is to receive matter for what comes upon it. So Eros is something like matter, and he is this daemon, born from soul in so far as it lacks the good, but longs for it.
!flag will leave it still unchanged in Kind | The Greek says that what is turned to itself is "form alone, staying in itself", and that what longs to receive makes the receiver matter for what comes: MacKenna's striving "(with attainment)" that leaves a thing "unchanged in Kind" is not in it.
!flag and at the same time a Celestial, sprung of the Soul | The Greek says love is "this daemon" (δαίμων οὗτος), born from soul: the daemon of the Symposium, whom the treatise set out to explain.
!note Matter as poverty: II.4.16, where Plotinus calls matter "Poverty" (πενία), and I.8.3. Plutarch too made Penia matter (On Isis and Osiris 57, 374c-d).

# Milestone E14: III.8 On nature, contemplation and the One, and III.9 Various considerations, beside MacKenna's vol. II
# (pp. 119-141). MacKenna has ten chapters of III.8 for Volkmann's eleven: his tenth begins with the Greek's tenth and
# runs on through the eleventh ("Another approach"), so the eleventh is shown with his 10 (@older 10). The Greek of
# III.9 is in three chapters, as MacKenna's are; his third is cut into lettered notes, (A) to (F), as the Greek's

@treatise III.8 | On nature, contemplation and the One
Plotinus proposes, half in play, that everything longs for contemplation and makes and acts for its sake. Nature makes without hands or levers: it is a forming principle that stays in itself, and its making is a silent contemplation, whose object is the visible world; it is the weakest contemplation, and its offspring is weak. Soul above nature contemplates more clearly, and makes nature as a weaker contemplation; human action is a contemplation too weak to see, and seeks by a detour what it cannot grasp directly, and the good man has turned all inward. In intellect, seer and seen are one: its contemplation is alive, the first life and the first thought, and it became many by wanting to have all. Beyond intellect, since intellect is two and number, there must be the simple One, neither intellect nor intelligible, the power of all things, like a spring that gives itself to all the rivers and stays as it was, or the life of a great tree that stays in the root. It is known by what is like it in us, when intellect turns back; it is the Good, which needs nothing, not even thinking, and is the maker of intellect, the beautiful child.

@ch III.8.1 | Everything longs for contemplation
A playful thesis, before the serious work: everything, rational and irrational animals, the nature in plants and the earth that bears them, longs for contemplation and attains it as far as it can, some truly and some in imitation. Even our play, and every action, necessary or voluntary, is done for the sake of contemplation. Action is left for later: first, how nature, said to be without imagination or reason, has contemplation, and makes through it.

@p
Suppose, playing at first, before we set about being serious, we were to say that all things long for contemplation and look to this as their end: not only rational animals but also irrational ones, and the nature in plants, and the earth that begets them; and that all things attain it as far as they can, in their natural state, some contemplating and attaining it in one way and some in another, some truly, and some taking an imitation and an image of it: would anyone put up with the strangeness of the argument? But since the argument is among ourselves, there will be no danger in playing with what is our own. Are we, then, contemplating now, as we play? Or do we, and all who play, do this, and play because we long for it? It may be that, whether a child or a man plays or is serious, one is serious and the other plays for the sake of contemplation, and that every action is earnest about contemplation: necessary action drawing contemplation more towards what is outside, and the action called voluntary less, but it too coming to be from a longing for contemplation.
!flag a light handling of our own ideas | The Greek says there is no danger "in playing with what is our own" (ἐν τῷ παίζειν τὰ αὐτῶν): the treatise's own word "play" (παίζειν), which comes back in the next sentences, where Plotinus asks whether we are contemplating "as we play"; "a light handling" loses the link.
!note "Contemplation" is θεωρία, beholding or looking at, the life of the mind turned on what it sees; its object is the θεώρημα, "what is contemplated". The treatise makes these the cause of all making and doing. The "play" of the opening recalls Plato, who calls man a plaything of god and our life a play (Laws VII 803c-804b), and his own dialogues a serious game (Phaedrus 276d-e).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ὕστερον
But this later. Now let us say, about the earth itself and trees and plants in general, what their contemplation is, and how we shall lead back what is made and begotten by it to the activity of contemplation; and how nature, which they say is without imagination and without reason, has contemplation in itself, and how it makes what it makes through a contemplation that it does not have.
!flag The case of Man will be treated later on | The Greek says only "but this later" (ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ὕστερον): what is put off is the question of action, voluntary and necessary, which the treatise takes up in chapters 4 and 6; man is not named.
!flag held to be devoid of reason and even of conscious representation | The Greek ἀφάνταστον is "without imagination" (φαντασία), the power of forming images, which the Stoics and Aristotle denied to nature; "conscious representation" is MacKenna's.
!note "They say": the Stoics, for whom nature (φύσις) is the power in plants that holds and grows them, without impulse or imagination, unlike the soul of animals (compare Philo, Allegory of the Laws II.22-23).

@ch III.8.2 | Nature makes as a forming principle that stays
Nature has no hands, feet or tools, and does not make by pushing and levering: no lever makes colours and shapes, and even the wax-modellers have to bring their colours from elsewhere. As in the craftsman, something must stay in nature and make without hands; nature is not partly at rest and partly moved, since only matter is moved. Nature is a forming principle, a form and not a compound of form and matter; matter becomes fire not by fire coming to it but by a forming principle. The principle in the visible shape is last and dead; the living one, brother of the one that made the shape, makes in what is born.

@p
That there are no hands here, nor feet, nor any tool brought in or grown on, but that there is need of matter, on which nature will make and which it will make into form, is plain, I suppose, to everyone. And one must also take leverage away from nature's making. For what thrust or what levering makes colours, varied and of every kind, and shapes? Not even the wax-modellers, to whom people looked when they thought that the craft of nature was of this kind, can make colours, unless they bring colours from elsewhere to what they make. But they ought to have reflected that, in those who practise such crafts, something must stay in them, by which, as it stays, they will make their works through their hands; and they ought to have gone up to something of this kind in nature too, and understood that here too the power that makes, not through hands, must stay, and stay whole. For it does not need some parts of itself that stay and others that are moved. Matter is what is moved, and nothing of nature is moved; or else that will not be what moves first, nor will nature be this, but what is unmoved in the whole.
!flag Nature need possess no outgoing force as against that remaining within | The Greek says nature "does not need some parts that stay and others that are moved" (οὐ γὰρ δὴ δεῖται τῶν μὲν ὡς μενόντων, τῶν δὲ ὡς κινουμένων): it is not split into a resting and a moving part. There is no "outgoing force" in the Greek.
!note The wax-modellers: the Stoics compared nature to an artist working from within (Cicero, On the nature of the gods II.57-58, "nature is a craftsmanlike fire"), and Aristotle compared the making of an animal to a craftsman's (Generation of animals I.22, 730b5-32). Plotinus' point is that a craftsman working with hands and tools cannot be the model of a power that makes colours and shapes themselves.

@p
@greek ὁ μὲν δὴ λόγος, φαίη ἄν τις
"The forming principle," someone might say, "is unmoved; but nature itself is something other than the forming principle, and moved." But if they say that the whole of nature is moved, the forming principle is too; and if some of it is unmoved, this is the forming principle. For nature must be a form, and not something made of matter and form. What need has it of hot or cold matter? The matter that lies under it and is worked on comes bringing this, or else matter that has no quality becomes such when it is given a forming principle. For it is not fire that must come for matter to become fire, but a forming principle. This is no small sign that in animals and plants it is the forming principles that make, and that nature is a forming principle, which makes another forming principle, its offspring, giving something to the substrate but staying itself. The forming principle in the visible shape is already last, and dead, and can no longer make another; but the one that has life, being the brother of the one that made the shape, and having the same power itself, makes in what is born.
!flag brother, no doubt, to that which gives mere shape, but having life-giving power | The Greek says the living principle is the brother "of the one that made the shape" (ὁ τοῦ ποιήσαντος τὴν μορφὴν ἀδελφός), and "has the same power" (τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν ἔχων): it is the brother of nature, the maker, not of the dead principle in the shape, and its power is the same, not a different, "life-giving" one.
!note "Forming principle" is λόγος, the reason or formula of a thing that shapes matter from within: the Stoic "seminal principles" (σπερματικοὶ λόγοι), which Plotinus makes a power of soul. The "substrate" (ὑποκείμενον) is matter, what lies under the form.

@ch III.8.3 | Making is contemplation
How does nature contemplate? Because it makes while staying, and a forming principle that stays in itself is a contemplation: action is according to a principle but other than it. Every forming principle comes from contemplation; the last, in the thing made, is a contemplation as something contemplated. Nature does not contemplate by reasoning, which is looking into what one does not yet have; it has, and so it makes. Its being what it is, a contemplation, an object of contemplation and a forming principle, is its making; so making is contemplation.

@p
How, then, when it makes, and makes in this way, could it have anything to do with contemplation? Well, if it makes while staying, and is a forming principle staying in itself, it would itself be a contemplation. For action would come about according to a forming principle, being plainly other than the forming principle; but the forming principle itself, which is with the action and presides over it, would not be action. If, then, it is not action but a forming principle, it is contemplation. And in every forming principle the last comes from contemplation, and is a contemplation in the sense that it has been contemplated; while all that is before it is contemplation in one way or another: one not as nature but as soul, the other in nature, and is nature. Does nature itself, too, come from contemplation? Wholly from contemplation. But has it, too, contemplated itself? Or how? It is the result of a contemplation, and of something that contemplated.
!flag above it stands the total Logos with its two distinguishable phases | The Greek says only that every forming principle before the last is contemplation "in one way or another" (ὁ μὲν ἄλλος ἄλλως), one as soul, one in nature and as nature; "the total Logos" is MacKenna's.
!flag Wholly and solely ? | The Greek πάντως μὴν ἐκ θεωρίας is an answer, "wholly from contemplation", not a question; and the next question asks whether it "has contemplated itself" (τεθεωρηκὼς αὑτόν).

@p
@greek πῶς δὲ αὐτὴ ἔχει θεωρίαν
But how does nature have contemplation? It does not have the contemplation that comes from reasoning; by "from reasoning" I mean looking into what is in it. Why not, when it is a life and a forming principle and a power that makes? Is it because to look into something is not yet to have it? But nature has, and because it has, it also makes. For nature, its being what it is, is its making; and it is contemplation and object of contemplation, for it is a forming principle. So by being contemplation, object of contemplation and forming principle, by this it makes, in so far as it is these. Making, then, has been shown to us to be contemplation: it is the result of a contemplation that stays a contemplation, that has done nothing else, but has made by being contemplation.
!flag The Contemplation springing from the reasoning faculty — that, I mean, of planning its own content, it does not possess | The Greek says nature lacks contemplation "from reasoning" (ἐκ λόγου), "I mean looking into what is in it" (τὸ σκοπεῖσθαι περὶ τῶν ἐν αὑτῇ): examining, not "planning". The point is that to look into a thing is not yet to have it.

@ch III.8.4 | Nature speaks: my making is silent contemplation
Asked why it makes, nature would answer: you should not ask, but understand in silence, as I am silent; what comes to be is what I see in silence, an object of contemplation born by nature, and I make as I contemplate, as geometers draw while they contemplate, except that I do not draw, and the lines of bodies fall out of my contemplation. My parents, too, made me by contemplating themselves. Nature is a soul, the offspring of a stronger soul, contemplating quietly, in a kind of self-awareness like sleep beside waking; its contemplation is dim, its offspring weak. So too men too weak for contemplation turn to action, a shadow of contemplation, to see with their eyes what they could not see with intellect; the duller children take to crafts.

@p
And if someone were to ask nature why it makes, and it were willing to listen to the one who asks and to speak, it would say: "You ought not to ask, but to understand, you too, in silence, as I am silent and am not used to speaking. Understand what? That what comes to be is my sight, mine in my silence, an object of contemplation that comes to be by nature; and that, since I came to be from contemplation of this kind, I have a nature that loves to contemplate. And what contemplates in me makes an object of contemplation, as geometers draw as they contemplate; but I do not draw: I contemplate, and the lines of bodies come into being as if they fell out of it. And I have what my mother and those who begot me have: they too are from contemplation, and my birth came about without their doing anything; they are greater forming principles, and as they contemplate themselves I have been born."
!flag The mathematicians from their vision draw their figures | The Greek has "geometers" (γεωμέτραι), who "draw as they contemplate" (θεωροῦντες γράφουσιν): the drawing goes with the contemplating, it is not drawn "from" it, and nature's figures are "the lines of bodies" (αἱ τῶν σωμάτων γραμμαί).
!flag As with my Mother (the All-Soul) and the Beings that begot me | The Greek says nature "has the experience" (πάθος) of its mother and parents: they too came from contemplation. "The All-Soul" is MacKenna's gloss; the Greek names only the mother and parents.
!note Nature's speech is in the manner of Plato's personifications, as of the Laws speaking to Socrates (Crito 50a-54d). Its "silence" recurs: the soul and nature contemplate "without noise" (ἄψοφος).

@p
@greek τί οὖν ταῦτα βούλεται
What does this mean? That what is called nature is a soul, the offspring of an earlier soul that lives more powerfully, and has its contemplation quietly in itself, turned neither upwards nor again downwards, but standing still where it is, in its own stillness and a kind of self-awareness; and by this understanding and self-awareness it saw what comes after it, as far as it could, and no longer looked for anything else, having brought to completion an object of contemplation, splendid and graceful. And if one wants to give it some understanding or perception, it is not such as we mean by perception or understanding in other things, but as if one were to compare the awareness of sleep with that of one awake. For it rests as it contemplates its own object of contemplation, which came to be for it from its staying in itself and with itself and being an object of contemplation; and its contemplation is noiseless, but dimmer.
!flag we are applying to sleep a word borrowed from the wake | The Greek says nature's awareness is to ours "as if one were to compare that of sleep with that of one awake" (οἷον εἴ τις τὴν τοῦ ὕπνου τῇ τοῦ ἐγρηγορότος προσεικάσειε): a likeness between two states, sleep and waking, not a word borrowed.
!flag It is a Vision silent but somewhat blurred | The Greek says nature's contemplation is "noiseless" (ἄψοφος) "but dimmer" (ἀμυδροτέρα δέ); "blurred" is MacKenna's.
!note Self-awareness (συναίσθησις) is the awareness a thing has of itself, together with what it perceives. Plotinus gives nature a dim one, like the awareness of one asleep compared with one awake. The "earlier soul" is the soul of the All, of which nature is the lowest part (IV.4.13).

@p
@greek ταύτῃ δὴ καὶ τὸ γεννηθὲν
For there is another, clearer contemplation, for sight, and nature's is an image of another contemplation. That is why what it begets is altogether weak, because a weak contemplation makes a weak object. So too men, when they are too weak for contemplation, make action a shadow of contemplation and of reason. Because contemplation is not enough for them, from weakness of soul, since they cannot grasp the sight well enough and so are not filled, but long to see it, they are carried towards action, to see with their eyes what they could not see with intellect. At any rate, when they make something, they want to see it themselves, and to contemplate and perceive it, and want others to, whenever their purpose is, as far as possible, action. Everywhere we shall find that making and action are either a weakness of contemplation or a consequence of it: a weakness if one has nothing more after what was done; a consequence if one has something else, better than what was made, to contemplate before it. For who, if he can contemplate what is true, goes first to the image of the true? The duller children bear witness too: unable to manage learning and contemplation, they sink to crafts and manual work.
!flag find in action their trace of vision and of reason | The Greek says such men "make action a shadow of contemplation and of reason" (σκιὰν θεωρίας καὶ λόγου τὴν πρᾶξιν ποιοῦνται); MacKenna's "trace" softens the shadow.
!flag when the result shall prove fairly well equal to the plan | The Greek says they want others to see "when their purpose is, as far as possible, action" (ὅταν ἡ πρόθεσις αὐτοῖς ὡς οἷόν τε πρᾶξις ᾖ): there is no matching of result to plan.
!flag an attenuation or a complement of vision | The Greek's second word is παρακολούθημα, "a consequence" of contemplation, something that follows on it, not "a complement".
!note The image of the true: Plato's cave, where the prisoners see shadows of images (Republic VII 514a-517a). On those who turn from learning to crafts, compare Republic VI 495d-e.

@ch III.8.5 | Soul's contemplation, and its overflow
Soul before nature, by its contemplation, love of learning and fullness, became wholly an object of contemplation and made another, as a full craft makes a small one in a child. Its first part stays above, filled and lit; the part that shares goes forth, life from life, leaving its first part where it was. What goes forth is weaker, yet still contemplation; so even what seems action is the weakest contemplation, for the offspring is akin. All goes in silence; contemplation has no limit and is everywhere, but not equally. The charioteer gives the horses what he saw, and they long for it and act for its sake.

@p
Having said, then, about nature, in what way its begetting is contemplation, let us come to the soul that is before it and say how its contemplation, its love of learning and of inquiry, its birth-pangs from what it had come to know, and its fullness, made it, when it had become wholly an object of contemplation, make another object of contemplation: as craft does, when each craft is full, making another, a small craft as it were, in a child who has an image of it all. But these, the sights and objects of contemplation of the second, are dim, as it were, and unable to help themselves.
!flag a given science, complete in itself, becomes the source and cause of what might be called a minor science in the student | The Greek speaks of "craft" (τέχνη), not science, which makes a small craft "in a child" (ἐν παιδίῳ) who has "an image of it all" (ἴνδαλμα ἁπάντων); MacKenna turns the child into a student who has "some partial knowledge of all its divisions".
!flag dim and helpless by the side of the content of the Soul | The Greek says the sights of the second are "unable to help themselves" (οὐ δυνάμενα βοηθεῖν ἑαυτοῖς), Plato's phrase for the written word, which cannot defend itself (Phaedrus 275e); "by the side of the content of the Soul" is MacKenna's.
!note The birth-pangs (ὠδίς) of the soul full of what it knows are Plato's: the soul pregnant with wisdom longs to give birth (Symposium 206c-e, 209a-c), and Socrates is midwife to young men in labour (Theaetetus 148e-151d).

@p
@greek τὸ πρῶτον οὖν αὐτῆς ἄνω
The first part of soul, above, always being filled and lit by what is above, stays there; but the part that shares by the first sharing of what shared goes forth always, life from life. For the activity of life reaches everywhere, and there is nowhere that it is absent. But as it goes forth it lets the part of itself that was in front stay where it left it; for if it abandoned what was in front, it would no longer be everywhere, but only where it ends. But what goes forth is not equal to what stayed. If, then, it must come to be everywhere, and there must be nowhere without its activity, and what is earlier must always be different from what is later, and activity comes from contemplation or action, but action did not yet exist, for it cannot be before contemplation: then one activity must be weaker than another, but all must be contemplation. So the action that seems to be according to contemplation is the weakest contemplation; for what is begotten must always be of the same kind, but weaker, by fading as it comes down.
!flag for energy runs through the Universe and there is no extremity at which it dwindles out | The Greek says "the activity of life" (ζωῆς ἐνέργεια) "reaches everywhere" (πανταχοῦ φθάνει): it is life's activity, not "energy" in general.
!flag act, however, is not at this stage existent since it depends upon contemplation | The Greek says "action did not yet exist, for it cannot be before contemplation" (οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε πρὸ θεωρίας): action cannot come before contemplation; MacKenna's "depends upon" turns an order into a dependence.

@p
@greek ἀψοφητὶ μὲν δὴ πάντα
All, then, goes noiselessly, because it needs no visible or outward contemplation or action; and it is soul that contemplates, and what has contemplated in this way, being further out and not like what is before it, makes what comes after it; and contemplation makes contemplation. For contemplation has no limit, nor has its object. That is why it is everywhere: for where is it not? Since in every soul it is the same; for it is not bounded by magnitude. But it is not alike in all, so that it is not alike in every part of soul either. That is why the charioteer gives the horses what he saw, and they, having received it, would plainly long for what they saw, for they did not receive all of it. And if they act in longing, they act for the sake of what they long for; and that was an object of contemplation and contemplation.
!flag Vision is not cabined within the bournes of magnitude | The Greek says "it is not bounded by magnitude" (οὐ γὰρ περιγέγραπται μεγέθει) of what is the same "in every soul"; MacKenna's archaism keeps the sense but the subject is contemplation in soul.
!flag they, taking that gift, showed that they were hungry for what made that vision | The Greek says the horses "would plainly long for what he saw" (δῆλον ὅτι ὀρέγοιντο ἂν ὧν εἶδεν), because "they did not receive all of it" (ἔλαβον γὰρ οὐ πᾶν): they long for the seen, not for "what made that vision", and the reason is that the gift was partial.
!note The charioteer and the horses are from Plato's Phaedrus (246a-254e): the charioteer sees the plain of truth, and feeds his horses ambrosia and nectar when he comes home (247e). Plotinus reads the horses' longing as action for the sake of a sight they only partly received.

@ch III.8.6 | Action returns to contemplation; the good man
So action is for the sake of contemplation: what people could not take directly they try to catch by a detour. When they get what they wanted, they want to know it and see it present in the soul; they act for a good, which they want to have in the soul, so action bends back to contemplation. The surer the conviction, the quieter the contemplation, and the knower becomes one with the known: a forming principle that is not one with the soul does nothing. Soul makes its contents its own and brings them out to look at as something other, because it lacks; it is quieter than nature but still looks into itself; the good man has reasoned already and is wholly turned inward.

@p
Action, then, is for the sake of contemplation and its object; so that for those who act too, contemplation is the end, and what they could not take in a straight line they seek to catch by going round. For again, when they attain what they wanted, what they wished to come about, it is not so that they may not know it, but so that they may know it and see it present in the soul, plainly lying there to be contemplated. For they act for the sake of a good, and this not so that it may be outside them, nor so that they may not have it, but so that they may have the good that comes from the action. And where is this? In the soul. So action has bent back again to contemplation; for what one receives in the soul, which is a forming principle, what else could it be but a silent forming principle? And the more so, the more it is received. For then the soul is at rest and seeks nothing, as having been filled; and the contemplation in one so placed lies within, because it is confident that it has.
!flag the more certainly such a principle as the impression made is the deeper | The Greek says only "and the more so, the more it is" (καὶ μᾶλλον, ὅσῳ μᾶλλον): the more fully one receives it, the more silent it is. "The impression made is the deeper" is MacKenna's.
!flag This vision achieved, the acting instinct pauses | The Greek says the soul, having been filled, "is at rest and seeks nothing" (ἡσυχίαν ἄγει καὶ οὐδὲν ζητεῖ); there is no "acting instinct".

@p
@greek καὶ ὅσῳ ἐναργεστέρα ἡ πίστις
And the clearer the conviction, the quieter the contemplation, in so far as it leads more into one; and what knows, in so far as it knows (now we must be serious), comes into one with what is known. For if they are two, one will be one thing and the other another; so they lie side by side, as it were, and this doubleness has not yet been made at home, as when forming principles are in the soul and do nothing. That is why the forming principle must not be outside, but made one with the soul of the learner, until he finds it his own.
!flag as when Ideal-Principles laid up in the mind or Soul remain idle | The Greek says the doubleness "has not yet been made one's own" (οὔπω ᾠκείωται), as when forming principles in the soul "do nothing" (μηδὲν ποιῶσι); and the soul is the soul, not "the mind or Soul".
!note "Now we must be serious" answers the play of the opening (III.8.1). The doctrine that the knower in act is one with the known is Aristotle's (On the soul III.4-5, 430a2-5, 430a19-20; III.7, 431a1-2).

@p
@greek ἡ μὲν οὖν ψυχή, ὅταν οἰκειωθῇ
So the soul, when it has made it its own and is disposed in like manner, brings it forth and puts it before itself; for what it had first it also comes to learn thoroughly, and by putting it forward it becomes, as it were, other than itself; and as it thinks it through it looks at it as one thing looking at another. Yet it too was a forming principle, and a sort of intellect, but one that sees another. For it is not full, but falls short of what is before it; yet it too sees quietly what it brings forth. What it has once brought forth it no longer brings forth; what it brings forth, it brings forth because of its lack, to look it over, learning thoroughly what it has. In practical matters it fits what it has to things outside. And by having more, it is quieter than nature, and by having more, it is more contemplative; but by not being perfect, it longs more to have a thorough learning of what it has contemplated, and a contemplation that comes from looking it over. And when it leaves itself and comes to be among other things, and then comes back again, it contemplates with the part of itself it left behind; but the soul that stands still in itself does this less. That is why the good man has done his reasoning already, and shows to another what is from himself; but towards himself he is sight. For he is already turned to the one and to the quiet, not only of things outside but also towards himself, and all is within.
!flag informed as it now is by the purely intellectual, it sees (in its outgoing act) as a stranger looking upon a strange world | The Greek says the soul, putting its contents before itself, "thinks them through and looks at them as one thing looks at another" (διανοουμένη βλέπει ὡς ἄλλο ὂν ἄλλο): it is the soul's discursive thinking, not anything "purely intellectual", and there is no "strange world".
!flag but its function is to see a (lower) realm which these do not see | The Greek says the soul is a forming principle and a sort of intellect, "but one seeing another" (ἀλλ’ ὁρῶν ἄλλο): it sees something other than itself, not a "lower realm" that intellect does not see.
!flag The Sage, then, is the man made over into a Reason-Principle | The Greek says the good man (σπουδαῖος) "has done his reasoning already" (λελόγισται ἤδη): he has finished reasoning, not been "made over into a Reason-Principle".
!note The good man (σπουδαῖος) is the Stoics' sage, whom Plotinus describes in I.4.4-16; his life within, "all is within", is that of the man who has become one with intellect.

@ch III.8.7 | Everything is contemplation and for contemplation
What truly is, is contemplation and comes from contemplation; what comes from it is an object of contemplation, perceived or known or believed; actions aim at knowledge, begettings at form, and every image makes forms. Reasoning and perception aim at seeing, and nature makes the object of contemplation in it. Since the first things are in contemplation, all else longs for it: the beginning is the end of all. Animals beget because the forming principles move within, a birth-pang to fill all with forms; mistakes come from swerving away from what is contemplated, the bad craftsman makes ugly forms, and loves are of those who saw and hasten to a form.

@p
That all things, then, both the things that truly are, come from contemplation and are contemplation, and those that come to be from them, as those contemplate, are themselves objects of contemplation, some by perception, some by knowledge or belief; and that actions have their end in knowledge, and their longing is the longing for knowledge; and that begettings start from contemplation and end in the completion of a form and another object of contemplation; and that in general, all things, being imitations of what makes them, make objects of contemplation and forms; and that the realities that come to be, being imitations of what is, show that what makes them makes as its end not the makings or the actions, but the result, so that it may be contemplated; and that thinking things through wants to see this, and before it perception, whose end is knowledge, and before these nature, which makes the object of contemplation in itself, and the forming principle, completing another forming principle: of these some could be grasped at once, and some the argument has brought to mind. That much, I suppose, is clear.
!flag manifest to sensation or to true knowledge or to surface-awareness | The Greek has "perception" (αἴσθησις), "knowledge" (γνῶσις) and "belief" (δόξα), opinion; "surface-awareness" is MacKenna's.
!flag brings into being the vision and Idea that we know in it | The Greek says nature "makes the object of contemplation in it and the forming principle, completing another forming principle" (τὸν λόγον ποιεῖ ἄλλον λόγον ἀποτελοῦσα): nature makes a forming principle that completes another, as in chapter 2; there is no "Idea that we know".

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ κἀκεῖνο δῆλον
For this too is clear: since the first things are in contemplation, all other things too must necessarily long for it, if the beginning is the end for all. For when animals beget, it is the forming principles within that move them, and this is an activity of contemplation, a birth-pang to make many forms and many objects of contemplation, and to fill all things with forming principles, and as it were always to contemplate. For to make something be is to make a form, and this is to fill all things with contemplation. And the mistakes too, both in what comes to be and in what is done, are a swerving away, by those who contemplate, from what is contemplated; and the bad craftsman is like one who makes ugly forms. And loves too belong to those who have seen and are hastening to a form.
!flag in the end the sorriest craftsman is still a maker of forms, ungracefully | The Greek says "the bad craftsman is like one who makes ugly forms" (ἔοικεν αἰσχρὰ εἴδη ποιοῦντι): the stress is on the ugliness of his forms, a swerving from what he contemplates, not that he is "still a maker of forms".
!flag So Love, too, is vision with the pursuit of Ideal-Form | The Greek says "loves" (οἱ ἔρωτες), in the plural, belong "to those who have seen and hasten to a form" (ἰδόντων καὶ πρὸς εἶδος σπευδόντων); "Love" is not personified.
!note "The beginning is the end for all": what comes from a principle longs to return to it. Love as the longing of those who have seen beauty is III.5.1, written later (the fiftieth treatise in Porphyry's order, this one the thirtieth).

@ch III.8.8 | In intellect, seer and seen are one, a living contemplation
Contemplation rises from nature to soul to intellect, its objects ever more one's own; in the good soul the known comes near to the knower, but in intellect the two are one by being, since to be and to think are the same. This is a living contemplation, the first life and the first thought; every life is a kind of thought, dimmer or clearer. How is the one also many? Intellect, beginning as one, did not stay as it began, but became many without noticing, wanting to have all, like a circle unfolding into figure, centre and lines. Intellect is of all, and each part of it is all; so it is unlimited, and nothing is lessened by what comes from it.

@p
So much for that. As contemplation rises from nature to soul and from soul to intellect, and the contemplations become ever more one's own and more one with those who contemplate, and in the good soul what is known goes towards being the same as the subject, since it hastens towards intellect, in intellect it is plain that both are now one, not by being made one's own, as in the best soul, but in being, and because to be and to think are the same. For there is no longer one thing and another; for then again there will have to be something else that is no longer one thing and another. This, then, must be truly both in one; and this is a living contemplation, not an object of contemplation like what is in something else. For what is in something else is alive by that, not alive of itself. If, then, an object of contemplation and an object of thought is to live, it must be a life that is not the life of growth, nor of perception, nor the rest of soul's life.
!flag we cannot stop at a principle containing separate parts ; there must always be a yet higher | The Greek says that if seer and seen were two, "there will again be another, which is no longer one and another" (πάλιν γὰρ αὖ ἄλλο ἔσται, ὃ οὐκέτι ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο): a regress that intellect itself must stop by being one; MacKenna's "a yet higher" points beyond intellect, which is not the argument here.
!flag it will, therefore, be a Seeing that lives | The Greek says "a living contemplation" (θεωρία ζῶσα), "not an object of contemplation like what is in something else"; MacKenna's "The Supreme" for its subject is his: the subject is intellect.
!note "To be and to think are the same" (τὸ γὰρ αὐτὸ νοεῖν ἐστίν τε καὶ εἶναι) is Parmenides (fragment B3), which Plotinus quotes for intellect (V.1.8, V.9.5).

@p
@greek νοήσεις μὲν γάρ πως
For the others are thoughts, in a way, too: but one is a thought of growth, one of perception, one of soul. How, then, are they thoughts? Because they are forming principles. And every life is a kind of thought, but one dimmer than another, as life is too. But this one is clearer, and is the first life and one first intellect. So the first thought is the first life, and the second life is the second thought, and the last life is the last thought. Every life, then, of this kind is also thought. But people might perhaps speak of differences of life, but do not speak of differences of thoughts: they say some are thoughts and others not thoughts at all, because they do not look into what life is at all. But this at least must be marked: that again the argument shows all things that are to be a by-product of contemplation. If, then, the truest life is life by thought, and is the same as the truest thought, the truest thought lives, and contemplation and its object, being such, are living and life, and the two are one together.
!flag Thus every Life, of the order strictly so called, is an Intellection | The Greek says "every life of this kind" (ἡ τοῦ γένους τούτου), of the kind just described, every life in the scale from growth up, is thought; "strictly so called" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἓν οὖν ὂν τὰ δύο
The two, then, being one, how again is this one many? Because what it contemplates is not one. For even when it contemplates the One, it does not do so as one; otherwise intellect does not come to be. It began as one, but did not stay as it began; without noticing, it became many, as though weighed down, and unrolled itself, wanting to have all things. It would have been better for it not to want this, for it became second. It is like a circle that has unrolled itself and become figure and surface and circumference and centre and radii, some parts above and some below. Better is where it starts from, worse what it goes to; for the starting point was not such as the starting point together with what it goes to, nor again is the starting point with what it goes to such as the starting point alone. And in another way, intellect is not the intellect of some one thing, but is all, and being all it is of all. So it must, being all and of all, have the part of itself as all and all things; otherwise it will have some part that is not intellect, and it will be put together from what is not intellect, and will be a heap gathered together, waiting to become intellect from all things. That is why it is unlimited, and if anything comes from it, there is no lessening, neither of what comes from it, because it too is all, nor of that from which it comes, because it was not a putting together of parts.
!flag The explanation is that in a unity there can be no seeing (a pure unity has no room for vision and an object) ; and in its Contemplation the One is not acting as a Unity | The Greek says intellect is many "because it does not contemplate as one" (ὅτι οὐχ ἓν θεωρεῖ), and that "even when it contemplates the One" (ὅταν τὸ ἓν θεωρῇ), it does not do so as one. The subject is intellect looking at the One, not the One contemplating.
!flag The Highest began as a unity but did not remain as it began | The subject of "began as one" is intellect, as the rest of the sentence shows ("otherwise intellect does not come to be"; "it became second"); MacKenna makes it "the Highest", which would make the One fall into multiplicity.
!flag it grew, as it were, pregnant | The Greek says intellect became many "as though weighed down" (οἷον βεβαρημένος), heavy, not "pregnant".
!flag The Intellectual-Principle on the other hand was never merely the Principle of an inviolable unity | The Greek says "intellect is not the intellect of some one thing" (οὐχ ἑνός τινος νοῦς), but of all; there is no "inviolable unity".
!note The circle that unfolds: the centre is the point from which the radii and the circumference come. Plotinus often pictures the One as the centre and intellect as a circle around it (VI.8.18, VI.9.8). The "heap" (σωρός) is the Stoic and Aristotelian term for a mere aggregate with no unity (Aristotle, Metaphysics VII.17, 1041b11-12).

@ch III.8.9 | Beyond intellect: the simple first
Intellect is not first: it is a number, and two, intellect and intelligible together, and before two there must be one. The first is neither intellect nor intelligible, but that from which both come. If it thinks, it is intellect; if not, is it ignorant even of itself? Saying it is the Good and simplest says nothing clear until we have something to rest the mind on. It is grasped by what is like it in us: as a voice filling a desert is heard whole by every ear, so wherever you set what can receive it, you have it. Intellect must step back, two-faced, and not be all intellect. Intellect is the first life, the unrolling of all things; it needs a beginning of unrolling, simpler than it, which is not all things or any of them, but before them all.

@p
This, then, is what intellect is like. That is why it is not first, but there must be what is beyond it, for whose sake the earlier arguments too were made. First, because the many comes after the one; and this is a number, and the beginning of number, and of such a number, is what is truly one. And this is intellect and intelligible at once, so two at once. But if two, we must take what is before the two. What, then? Intellect alone? But the intelligible is yoked with every intellect; if, then, the intelligible must not be yoked with it, it will not be intellect either. If, then, it is not intellect, but will escape the two, what is prior to these two must be beyond intellect. What, then, prevents it from being the intelligible itself? That the intelligible too is yoked with intellect. If, then, it is neither intellect nor intelligible, what would it be? We shall say: that from which intellect and the intelligible with it come. What, then, is this, and what shall we imagine it to be like? For again, it will either be something that thinks or something without thought. If it thinks, it is intellect; if without thought, it will be ignorant even of itself: so what is there majestic about it? For not even if we were to say that it is the Good and is the simplest, shall we be saying anything plain and clear, though we speak the truth, as long as we do not have something on which to rest our thinking when we speak.
!flag the source of a number such as this must be the authentically One | The Greek says "the beginning of number, and of such a number, is what is truly one" (ἀριθμοῦ δὲ ἀρχὴ καὶ τοῦ τοιούτου τὸ ὄντως ἕν): the One is the beginning of number in general and of this one; MacKenna gives only the second.
!flag the Prior demanded by that duality must be something on the further side of the Intellectual-Principle | The Greek says that what is first "will escape the two" (ἐκφεύξεται τὰ δύο) and so "must be beyond intellect" (ἐπέκεινα δεῖ νοῦ εἶναι): ἐπέκεινα, "beyond", Plato's word for the Good "beyond being" (Republic VI 509b).
!note Intellect as number: in VI.6 (On numbers) Plotinus makes being and intellect a number, the first plurality; the one before it is not a number. "Beyond" (ἐπέκεινα) is Plato's word for the Good, "beyond being in dignity and power" (Republic VI 509b).

@p
@greek καὶ γὰρ αὖ τῆς γνώσεως
For again, since knowledge of other things comes through intellect, and we can know something by intellect when we think, by what direct grasp could this be caught, which has gone beyond the nature of intellect? To which we must say, as far as we can point to it: by what is like it in us. For there is something of it with us too; or rather, there is nowhere that it is not, for those who can share in it. For wherever you set what can have it, you have it from there, from what is everywhere. As if a voice filled a desert, and men in it with the desert, and in whatever part of the desert you set an ear, it would take in the whole voice, and again not the whole.
!flag nay, nothing, ripe for that participation, can be void of it | The Greek says "there is nowhere that it is not" (οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅπου μὴ ἔστιν) "for those who can share in it" (οἷς ἔστι μετέχειν αὐτοῦ): the point is about place, it is everywhere, as the next sentence says, not about things "void of it".
!flag imagine a voice sounding over a vast waste of land, and not only over the emptiness alone but over human beings | The Greek says a voice "filled a desert" (φωνῆς κατεχούσης ἐρημίαν), the desert and the men in it, and that an ear set anywhere in the desert would take "the whole voice and again not the whole"; "a vast waste of land" is MacKenna's.
!note "By what is like it in us": like is known by like, Empedocles' principle (fragment B109), which Plotinus uses of the eye that must become sunlike to see the sun (I.6.9) and of the One here.

@p
@greek ἔστι μὲν γὰρ αὐτὸς ζωὴ πρώτη
What, then, is it that we shall take in, when we set intellect beside it? Intellect must, as it were, withdraw backwards, and as it were give itself up to what is behind it, since it faces both ways, and there, if it wants to see that, it must not be wholly intellect. For intellect is the first life, being an activity in an unrolling of all things: an unrolling not one that is still unrolling, but one that has unrolled. If, then, it is life and unrolling and has all things exactly and not in the gross, for then it would have them imperfectly and unjointed, it must come from something else, which is no longer in an unrolling, but the beginning of unrolling and the beginning of life and the beginning of intellect and of all things. For all things are not a beginning, but come from a beginning; and the beginning is no longer all things nor any of all things, so that it may beget all things, and so that it may not be a multitude, but the beginning of multitude: for everywhere what begets is simpler than what is begotten. If, then, this begot intellect, it must be simpler than intellect. And if someone were to think that it is itself the one and all things, either it will be each one of all things by one, or all together. If all together, gathered up, it will come after all things; if before all things, all things will be one thing, and it another, distinct from all; if it and all things are at once, it will not be a beginning. But it must be a beginning and be before all, so that all things too may be after it. And to be each of all things by one, first, will make anything the same as anything, and then all will be together, and nothing will be distinguished. So it is none of all things, but before all things.
!flag essentially a thing facing two ways, it must deliver itself over to those powers within it which tend upward | The Greek says intellect must "give itself up to what is behind it" (ἑαυτὸν ἀφέντα τοῖς εἰς ὄπισθεν αὐτοῦ), "since it faces both ways" (ἀμφίστομον): what is behind it is the One, its source, not "powers within it".
!flag the outflow, that is, of the first moment, not that of the continuous process | The Greek says intellect's unrolling (διέξοδος) is not one "that is still unrolling, but one that has unrolled" (οὐ τῇ διεξιούσῃ, ἀλλὰ τῇ διεξελθούσῃ): its going-through of all things is complete, not "the first moment".
!note "Facing both ways" (ἀμφίστομος, with two mouths, like a two-mouthed jar) is Plotinus' word for intellect turned both to the One and to itself. On the One as "all things and none of them", see V.2.1 and VI.7.32.

@ch III.8.10 | The power of all things: the spring and the root
The first is the power of all things, without which there would be no intellect, the first life; it is above life and its cause, as a spring that has no other source gives itself to all the rivers and is not used up, or the life of a great tree stays in the root. Everywhere the leading back is to one, and at last to the simply One. If the One of each thing is its most powerful and valued part, shall we doubt the One of what truly is, or think it nothing? It is none of what it is the beginning of; take away being and you will have a wonder: reach for it, rest in it, and understand it by its greatness in what comes after it.

@p
What, then, is it? The power of all things. If it did not exist, neither would all things exist, nor intellect, the first life and all life. What is above life is the cause of life; for the activity of life, which is all things, is not first, but is as it were poured out itself, as from a spring. Think of a spring that has no other beginning, but gives itself to all the rivers and is not used up by the rivers, but stays quietly itself; while those that have gone out of it, before each flows its own way, still go together for a while, yet each already knows, as it were, where it will let its streams go. Or think of the life of a huge plant, which goes through all of it, while its beginning stays and is not scattered over all of it, being as it were settled in the root. This beginning gave the plant all its life, the life that is many, but stayed itself, not many, but the beginning of the many life. And there is no wonder. Or rather there is a wonder too: how the multitude of life came from what is not a multitude, and how the multitude would not be, if before the multitude there were not what was not a multitude. For the beginning is not divided into the whole; if it were divided, it would destroy the whole too, and the whole would not still come to be, if the beginning did not stay by itself, being different.
!flag the tides that proceed from it are at one within it before they run their several ways | The Greek says the rivers, "having gone out of it, before each flows its own way, still go together" (τοὺς δὲ ἐξ αὐτῆς προεληλυθότας πρὶν ἄλλον ἄλλῃ ῥεῖν ὁμοῦ συνιόντας ἔτι): they have already come out of the spring; they are together outside it, not "within it".
!flag And this surprises no one : though it is in fact astonishing | The Greek says "and no wonder. Or rather a wonder too" (καὶ θαῦμα οὐδέν. ἢ καὶ θαῦμα): Plotinus corrects himself; it is not that "no one" is surprised.
!flag nothing would come into being if its cause, thus broken up, changed character | The Greek says nothing would come to be "if the beginning did not stay by itself, being different" (μὴ μενούσης τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆς ἑτέρας οὔσης): the beginning must stay apart and other, not "change character".
!note The spring that gives itself to all the rivers and is not used up is one of Plotinus' images of the One's giving without loss (compare the sun and its light, V.1.6, V.3.12). The life settled in the root is the image of III.3.7, where the principle of the All is like the root of a great plant.

@p
@greek διὸ καὶ ἡ ἀναγωγὴ
That is why the leading back is everywhere to one. And in each thing there is some one to which you will lead it back; and this whole to the one before it, not the simply one, until one comes to the simply One; and this no longer leads back to another. If one takes the one of the plant, which is the beginning that stays, and the one of the animal, and the one of the soul, and the one of the All, he takes in each case what is most powerful and most valued. But if he takes the one of the things that truly are, their beginning and spring and power, shall we lose faith, and suspect it is nothing? It is none of the things of which it is the beginning; yet it is such that nothing can be said of it, not being, not substance, not life, being what is above all these. But if you grasp it by taking away being, you will have a wonder. And casting yourself towards it, and reaching it, resting in what is its, understand it more, knowing it by touching it, and seeing its greatness together in the things after it that are because of it.
!flag the All has its One, its Prior but not yet the Absolute One | The Greek says each whole is led back "to the one before it, not the simply one" (εἰς ἓν τὸ πρὸ αὐτοῦ, οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἕν), "until one comes to the simply One": "the All" (τὸ πᾶν) here is "the whole" of each thing, and the One at the end is "simply one", not "Absolute".
!flag seek to grasp it more and more — understanding it by that intuitive thrust alone | The Greek says "understand it more, knowing it by touching it" (συννόει μᾶλλον τῇ προσβολῇ συνείς): the grasp is by direct contact (προσβολή), a touching, as in VI.9.
!note "None of the things of which it is the beginning": the negative theology of the First hypothesis of Plato's Parmenides (137c-142a), where the One is not, has no name, and nothing is said of it, which Plotinus reads as the One beyond being (V.1.8).

@ch III.8.11 | The Good, intellect's fulfilment; intellect, its beautiful child
@older 10
Intellect is a seeing, a power come to act: it has matter and form, as sight does, and is filled by the Good, as sight by the visible. If intellect were the Good, it would not need to see. Say "the Good" and add nothing, not even thinking: intellect longs for the Good and is made like the Good by it; the Good longs for nothing. Intellect is beautiful, in pure light, and the world is its shadow; as one who sees the stars seeks their maker, so whoever has seen the intelligible world must seek who made it, who begot such a child, intellect, a beautiful boy, a fullness born of him. He is neither intellect nor fullness, but before them, and neither needs nor has.

@p
And in this way too: since intellect is a kind of sight, and a sight that sees, it will be a power that has come to activity. So one part of it will be matter and the other form, as also with sight in act; but matter in intelligibles. For sight in act too has a double nature: before seeing, at any rate, it was one. So the one has become two, and the two one. For sight, its filling and its perfecting, as it were, comes from the perceptible; but for the sight of intellect, it is the Good that fills it. For if intellect itself were the Good, what need would it have of seeing, or of being active at all? For other things have their activity about the Good and because of the Good, but the Good needs nothing; so there will be nothing for it but itself. When you have uttered "the Good", then, think of nothing more to add: for if you add anything, by whatever you have added you will make it lacking. That is why you should not add thinking either, so that you may not add something other, and make two, intellect and the Good. For intellect needs the Good, but the Good does not need it. So, when it attains the Good, intellect becomes like the Good, and is perfected by the Good, the form upon it coming from the Good and making it like the Good.
!flag The Intellectual-Principle is a Seeing, and a Seeing which itself sees | The Greek says intellect is "a kind of sight" (ὄψις τις), "and a sight that sees" (ὄψις ὁρῶσα): MacKenna's "itself sees" reads in self-seeing, which the Greek does not say here.
!flag for The Good is the centre of all else | The Greek says other things "have their activity about the Good and because of the Good" (περὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ διὰ τὸ ἀγαθόν); "the centre" is MacKenna's image.
!flag Do not even say that it has Intellection | The Greek says do not add "thinking" (τὸ νοεῖν) either, "so that you may not add something other" (ἵνα καὶ μὴ ἄλλο); MacKenna drops the reason, that thinking would be one thing more added to the Good.
!note "Becomes like the Good" (ἀγαθοειδής, "good-formed") is Plato's word: knowledge and truth are "like the Good" but not the Good (Republic VI 509a). The sight-and-sun analogy of Republic VI (507b-509b) lies behind the whole chapter.

@p
@greek οἷον δὲ ἐνορᾶται
As a trace of the Good is seen upon intellect, so we should think the archetype to be, conceiving the true nature of that from the trace that plays upon intellect. The Good, then, gave intellect, as it looks into it, to have the trace of itself upon it; so that in intellect there is longing, and it is always longing and always attaining; but there, there is neither longing, for what would it long for? nor attaining, for it did not long. So it is not intellect either; for in intellect too there is longing, and a converging upon its form.
!flag the concentrated strain towards its Form | The Greek says in intellect there is "a converging" (σύννευσις), an inclining together, towards its form; "concentrated strain" is MacKenna's, and it hides that the longing is intellect's leaning towards the form it receives.

@p
@greek τοῦ δὴ νοῦ καλοῦ ὄντος
Intellect, then, being beautiful, and the most beautiful of all, lying in pure light and pure radiance, and embracing the nature of what is, of which this beautiful world too is a shadow and an image; lying in all splendour, because there is nothing without intellect in it, nothing dark, nothing without measure; living a blessed life: wonder would seize whoever saw this too, and, as one should, went into it and became one with it. As one who looks up to the heaven and sees the light of the stars thinks of and seeks the one who made them, so whoever has beheld and looked into and wondered at the intelligible world should seek its maker too: who it is that brought such a thing into being, or where, or how, who begot such a child, intellect, a beautiful boy, and a fullness that came from him. Surely he is neither intellect nor fullness, but before intellect and fullness; for intellect and fullness come after him, needing both to have been filled and to have thought. These are near to what needs nothing and needs no thinking, but they have true fullness and thinking, because they have them first. But what is before them neither needs nor has; or it would not be the Good.
!flag this lovely abundance so abundantly endowed | The Greek plays on κόρος, which means both "boy" and "fullness": intellect is "a beautiful boy" (κόρον καλόν) and "a fullness that came from him" (παῤ αὐτοῦ γενόμενον κόρον). The pun alludes to Kronos, child of Ouranos and father of Zeus, whom Plotinus makes intellect; "abundance" keeps one sense and loses the boy.
!flag must overwhelm with awe any that has seen it, and penetrated it, to become a unit of its Being | The Greek says wonder would seize whoever saw it and, "as one should, went into it and became one with it" (αὐτοῦ γενόμενον ἕνα); "a unit of its Being" is MacKenna's.
!note Kronos as "fullness" (κόρος) and "intellect" (νοῦς): Plato's Cratylus etymologises Kronos as "pure intellect" (396b), and Plotinus reads Kronos, son of Ouranos, as intellect, the full child of the One, who holds his offspring in himself (V.1.4, V.1.7, V.8.13).

@treatise III.9 | Various considerations
Not a treatise but a set of notes, put together by Porphyry from Plotinus' jottings, the last of the Third Ennead. The first reads the Timaeus, where intellect sees the Forms in the Living Being and the Craftsman thinks that this world must have them too: are the Living Being, intellect and the one who thinks it through three, or one? Intellect and the intelligible are one, distinguished only in thought; the division into many, the work of thinking things through, belongs to soul. The second: as a science is whole in each theorem, a man must make his beginnings his ends; the soul of the All never came anywhere, the body came to it, while the partial soul is lit when it turns upwards and, turning to itself, makes an image of itself, dark and indefinite, and goes into it with delight. The third is a string of short notes: how the one, everywhere and nowhere, makes all; soul is a sight whose object is intellect; in thinking ourselves we think a nature that thinks, and we are the intelligible; the first is beyond motion and rest, beyond thinking and self-awareness, and does not even live, since it gives life.

@ch III.9.1 | The Living Being, intellect, and the one who thinks it through
Plato says intellect sees the Forms in the Living Being, and the Craftsman thought that this All must have them too. Are the Forms before intellect, and the Living Being other than intellect? If so, intellect would have images, not the truth. But nothing prevents the two being one, divided only in thought: the intelligible is intellect at rest, and the intellect that sees it is its activity. What "thought it through" to make the four kinds of living beings may seem a third; but the division into many is soul's, which has a divided activity.

@p
"Intellect," he says, "sees the Forms that are in what Living Being is"; "then the Craftsman thought," he says, "that what intellect sees in what Living Being is, this All too must have." Does he not say, then, that the Forms are already before intellect, and that intellect thinks them as already being? First, then, we must look into that, I mean the Living Being, to see whether it is not intellect but other than intellect. For what contemplates is intellect; so we shall say that the Living Being itself is not intellect but intelligible, and we shall say that intellect has what it sees outside itself. It has, then, images and not the true things, if the true things are there; for he says that truth too is there, in what is, where each thing is itself. Or, even if each of the two is other, they are not apart from each other, but only by being other. Next, as far as what is said goes, nothing prevents both being one, but divided by thinking, if indeed it is only so that one is intelligible and the other thinking: for he does not say that what intellect beholds is wholly in another, but that it has the intelligible in itself.
!flag though, in a unity, admitting that distinction, of the intellectual act (as against passivity) | The Greek says only that the two may be one but "divided by thinking" (διαιρούμενα δὲ τῇ νοήσει); there is nothing of act "as against passivity".
