Men are like constitutions: bad, democratic, aristocratic, and in the best man one ruler, as a city above and a city below.

@older 16
@p
But why, in us too, are not the soul's thoughts and forming principles like this, and why here does the later come in times, and our inquiries in this way? Is it because there are many things that rule and are moved, and no one thing controls? Or also because one thing and another come for the need and the present, which are not determined in themselves but always directed to one thing and another outside: hence the deliberation is different and for the occasion, when the need is present. And this happens to us from outside, and then this. And because many things rule, the images too must be many, acquired and new, one from one thing, another from another, and hindering the motions and activities of each.
!note The "images" (φαντασίαι) are the impressions that, for the Stoics, set impulse going, and to which reason gives or refuses assent.

@p
@greek ὅταν γὰρ τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν κινηθῇ
For when the desiring part is moved, its image comes, like a perception announcing and declaring the affection, and demanding that we follow and procure what is desired; and what is necessarily in perplexity, whether it follows along and procures or resists. And spirit, calling for revenge, does the same when it is moved; and so do the needs of the body; and the affections make us hold now one opinion and now another; and the ignorance of what is good, and the soul's not knowing what to say, being led in every direction; and from the mixture of these, other things again.
!flag is necessarily thrown out of equilibrium | The Greek says what is called on is necessarily "in perplexity" (ἐν ἀπόρῳ), at a loss whether to follow or resist; the word for the treatise's whole question.
!note Desire (τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν) and spirit (θυμός) are the lower parts of the soul of Plato's Republic (IV 439d-441c).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ τὸ βέλτιστον
But does the best part itself hold now one opinion and now another? Or the perplexity and the change of opinion belong to the common part; and from the best, the right reason is given to the common part, weak by being in the mixture, not by its own nature: as in the great tumult of an assembly the best of the counsellors speaks and does not prevail, but the worst of those who make a din and shout; and he sits in silence, able to do nothing, beaten by the din of the worse.
!flag the doubt and the change of standard are of the Conjoint | The Greek has "the common" (τοῦ κοινοῦ), the compound of soul and body, and ἀλλοδοξία, holding different opinions at different times; "change of standard" is MacKenna's.
!note The crowd's din in the assembly, which drowns the voice of reason, is Plato's (Republic VI 492b-c).

@p
@greek καὶ ἔστιν ἐν μὲν τῷ φαυλοτάτῳ
And in the worst man the common part, the man made up of all of these, is like a bad constitution; in the middle man it is like a city in which something good might control a democratic constitution that is not wholly unmixed; in the better man, the life is aristocratic, since he is already fleeing the common part of the man and giving himself to the better; and in the best, the one who separates himself, the ruler is one, and the order comes from it to the rest: as if the city were double, one city above, and the other the city of those below, set in order according to those above. But that in the soul of the All there is the one, the same and the like, and in the others otherwise, and why, has been said. So much for this.
!flag a demotic constitution not out of control | The Greek says a democracy "not unmixed" (οὐκ ἀκράτου), tempered by something better; the word means "unmixed", like undiluted wine, and so "unbridled", but the point is the mixture.
!flag the city of the lower elements | MacKenna's chapter ends here, leaving out the Greek's last sentence: that in the soul of the All there is one, the same and the like, and in the other souls otherwise, which sums up the chapters on memory and reasoning.
!note The man as a city, and the constitutions from the worst to the best, are Plato's (Republic VIII-IX 544d-592b); the city above is "a pattern laid up in heaven" (IX 592b), and here the ruling part of the soul.

@ch IV.4.18 | Does the body have a life of its own?
The living body is not like lit air but like warmed air: it has a shadow of soul, and bodily pleasure and pain belong to a body of this kind, while they come to us as knowledge, unaffected. The body is ours, though it is not us, and we care for it; the weaker we are, the more we take it for the man. Such affections belong to the compound: a single thing is self-sufficient, but when a worse nature takes only a trace of a better and the two become one, the unsteady partnership breeds pain when it is drawn down and pleasure when it is drawn up.

@p
We must consider whether the body has something on its own, and, when the soul is present, lives already having something of its own; or whether what it has is nature, and this is what keeps company with the body. Or the body itself, in which there are soul and nature, must not be like what is soulless, nor like air that has been lit, but like air that has been warmed: the body of an animal, and of a plant too, has as it were a shadow of soul; and being in pain, and taking pleasure in the pleasures of the body, concern a body of this kind. But to us the pain of this body, and pleasure of this kind, come as knowledge, without our being affected. By "us" I mean the other soul, since a body of this kind is not foreign to us either, but ours: and that is why we care for it, as ours. For we are not this, nor are we clean of it: it hangs from us and depends on us. We are the ruling part; this is ours in another way, but ours all the same. That is why we care when it feels pleasure and pain; and the more, the weaker we are, and the less we separate ourselves. Instead we set this down as the most honoured part of us, and as the man, and as it were sink ourselves into it.
!flag the most honourable phase of our being, is what we think of as the true man and into this we are penetrating | The Greek says "we set this down as the most honoured part of us, and as the man, and as it were sink into it" (τοῦτο ἡμῶν τὸ τιμιώτατον καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον τιθέμεθα καὶ οἷον εἰσδυόμεθα εἰς αὐτό). "This" is the body we care for: Plotinus is blaming our mistake of taking it for ourselves. MacKenna makes it the higher part, and our going into it a good.
!note "The shadow of soul" (σκιὰ ψυχῆς) is the trace that nature leaves in the body (IV.4.14, IV.4.20); "the man" set in the body is the question of I.1 (E1), What is the living being, and what is the human being.

@p
@greek χρὴ γὰρ τὰ πάθη
For we must say that affections of this kind do not belong to the soul at all, but to a body of this kind and to something common, made of both. For when a thing is one, it is as it were self-sufficient to itself. What, for example, could body alone suffer, being soulless? When it is divided, it is not it that suffers but the unity in it. And soul alone does not even suffer division, and being as it is, it escapes everything. But when two want to be one, using a oneness brought in from outside, it is reasonable that they find the origin of pain in not being allowed to be one. I do not mean two in the sense of two bodies: they have one nature. I mean when one nature wants to share with another nature, of another kind, and the worse takes something from the better, and cannot take that, but only some trace of it; and so it becomes two and one, coming to be between what it was and what it could not have. Then it has bred a perplexity for itself, having got a partnership that is perishable and not secure, but always carried towards opposites. So, hanging between down and up, when it is carried down it announces its own pain, and towards what is up, its own pleasure, through its longing for the partnership.
!flag by its very nature is immune from evil | The Greek says soul alone "escapes everything" (ἐκφεύγει πᾶν): it suffers neither division nor anything else. "From evil" is MacKenna's.
!flag in the mere fact that they were inapt to partnership | The Greek puts the origin of pain in their "not being allowed to be one" (τῷ οὐκ ἐᾶσθαι εἶναι ἕν): two that want to be one, held together by a oneness brought in from outside, and kept apart by their natures; it says nothing of their being unfit to share.
!flag directed to the above, of longing for unison | The Greek says that, turned upward, the compound announces "its own pleasure" (τὴν αὑτοῦ ἡδονήν), as it announced its pain when carried down; the longing for the partnership is the reason for the pleasure. MacKenna leaves the pleasure out, though the chapter is about pleasure and pain.

@ch IV.4.19 | Pain is knowing that the body is losing soul's image
Pain is knowing that the body is being drawn away from the image of soul; pleasure, knowing that it is fitted back. The affection is in the body; the perceiving soul next to it knows it and reports it. The whole soul feels it and says where it is, so it is not itself affected: if it were, it would hurt all over. The finger hurts, and the man because the finger is his. Perception is knowledge of pain, unaffected, so that it can report soundly: an affected messenger is no messenger.

@p
This, then, is what is meant when it is said that pleasure and pain are: pain is knowing that a body is being drawn away as it is deprived of the image of soul; pleasure is knowing that the animal is being fitted together again with the image of soul in the body. The affection is there, in the body; the knowledge belongs to the perceiving soul, which perceives it by being its neighbour, and announces it to that in which the perceptions end. And that, the body, was pained: by "was pained" I mean that it was affected. In a cutting, for example, when the body is cut, the division is in the bulk; but the distress is in the bulk because it is not only bulk, but bulk of a certain kind; and the inflammation is there too. The soul perceived it, taking it over because it lies, as it were, next to it.
!flag the principle, the imaging faculty, into which the sensations finally merge | The Greek names no faculty: the perceiving soul announces the affection "to that in which the perceptions end" (τῷ εἰς ὃ λήγουσιν αἱ αἰσθήσεις). MacKenna identifies it as the imaging faculty, which Plotinus makes the seat of memory in IV.3.29-31, but not here.
!note "Image of soul" (ἴνδαλμα ψυχῆς) is the trace or shadow of soul in the living body of the last chapter.

@p
@greek πᾶσα δὲ ᾔσθετο
The whole soul perceived the affection there, without being affected itself. For perceiving as a whole, it says the affection is there, where the blow and the pain are. If it were itself affected, being whole in the whole body, it would not say or indicate that it is there: it would suffer the pain all of it, and be pained as a whole, and would not say or show that it is there, but would say it is wherever it is itself; and it is everywhere. As it is, the finger hurts, and the man hurts, because the finger is the man's. The man is said to hurt in his finger, as the grey-eyed man is called grey-eyed for the grey in his eye.
!flag just as we class him as fair from his eyes being blue | The Greek says the man is called grey-eyed (γλαυκός) for the grey in his eye: the same word is used of the man and of his eye, as "hurts" is said of the man and of his finger. "Fair" loses the point that the whole is named from its part.

@p
@greek ἐκεῖνο μὲν οὖν τὸ πεπονθὸς ἀλγεῖ
So it is the affected part that is in pain, unless one takes pain to include the perception that follows it; and taking it so, one plainly means pain together with its not escaping the perception. But the perception itself must not be called pain: it is knowledge of pain; and being knowledge, it is unaffected, so that it may know and report soundly. For an affected messenger, taken up with what he suffers, either does not report, or is not a sound messenger.

@ch IV.4.20 | Where bodily desire begins
Bodily desires begin in the body as nature has shaped it, not in any body whatever nor in soul itself: in body that wants to be more than body. As with pain, perception learns, and nature, the soul nearby that gave the trace, gives the clear desire, and perception the image; then the soul whose task it is either provides or resists. Desire begins not in nature but in the shaped body that suffers and longs for the opposite; nature, like a mother guessing what a sick child wants, tries to set it right, and the desire is finished in her. So there is a pre-desire of the body, a desire of nature, and a soul that provides or not.

@p
And we must hold that the beginning of the bodily desires too follows from what is common in this way, and from a bodily nature of this kind. For the beginning of appetite and eagerness must not be given to a body in any state whatever, nor the search for salt or sweet things to the soul itself, but to what is body, but wants not to be only body, and has acquired more movements than the soul itself, and because of what it has acquired has been forced to turn to many things. So, in one state, it wants salt things, and in another sweet, and to be moistened and warmed: none of which would have mattered to it if it were alone.

@p
@greek ὥσπερ δὲ ἐκεῖ ἐκ τῆς
Just as there, with pain, the knowledge came from the pain, and the soul, wishing to lead the body away from what was causing the affection, made it flee, and what was first affected taught this, itself fleeing in a way by shrinking: so here too perception learns, and so does the soul nearby, which we call nature, the one that gave the trace. Nature gives the clear desire, which is the end of the one that began in the body; perception gives the image; and from the image the soul whose task it is to provide either provides, or resists and holds out, and pays no attention either to what began the desire or to what desired after it.
!flag the soul, which alone is competent, acts upon it | The Greek says it is "the soul whose task it is to provide" (ἧς τὸ πορίζειν) that provides or resists: it is marked out by its task of providing, not by being alone competent.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ διὰ τί δύο
But why two desires, and why is it not only that body of this kind that desires? Because nature is one thing, and the body of this kind, which came from nature, another: for nature is before the body of this kind comes to be, since it makes this body, moulding and shaping it. So it must not be nature that begins the desire, but the body of this kind, affected in these ways and pained, longing for the opposite of what it suffers, pleasure after toil and filling after want. And nature, like a mother, guessing as it were at the wishes of the one that suffers, tries to set it right and bring it back to herself; and, as she searches for what will heal it, she joins to her search the desire of the one that suffers, and its completion comes from it to her. So one might call the desiring that comes from the body itself a pre-desire, and perhaps a pre-wanting; the desiring from another and for another, nature's; and the soul that provides, or does not, yet another.
!flag makes the child's experience her own | The Greek says "the completion comes from that to her" (τὴν περάτωσιν ἀπ’ ἐκείνου πρὸς αὐτὴν ἥκειν): the desire begun in the body is finished in nature, which is why the clear desire of the last paragraph is "the end of the one that began in the body".
!note The play is on ἐπιθυμία (desire), προεπιθυμία (pre-desire) and προθυμία (eagerness, here "pre-wanting"), as if "eagerness" were desire before desire.

@ch IV.4.21 | Desire changes with the body
That desire begins in the body is shown by age and health: the desiring part is the same, but children, youths and men, the healthy and the sick, desire differently. Desire may stir in the body before reasoning while nature does not join it, when the body is not out of its natural state. And a changing body is not enough to explain different desires in another part, which gains nothing from food or warmth.

@p
That this is what the beginning of desire is about the different ages also witness. For the bodily desires of children, of youths and of men are different, and those of the healthy and of the sick, while the desiring part is the same: for it is clear that it is because it is bodily, and a body of a certain kind, turned through changes of every kind, that it has desires of every kind too. And the fact that the whole desire is not always roused along with what are called the pre-wantings, even when the bodily one persists to its end, and does not want to eat or drink before reasoning comes in, tells that desire went forward to some point, as far as it was in a body of this kind, but that nature did not join itself to it, nor take its side, nor want it: since, as the body was in its natural state, there was nothing to bring back to nature; for nature presides over what is against nature and what is according to it.
!flag it may refuse assent to the idea of eating or drinking until reason gives the word | The Greek does not make the whole desire wait on reason: it says the desire "does not want to eat or drink before reasoning comes in" (πρὸ τοῦ τὸν λογισμὸν εἶναι), because nature has not joined the body's pre-desire; reason is not yet in the picture.

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις πρὸς τὸ πρότερον
If someone, against the first point, were to say that the body, becoming different, is enough to make the desires in the desiring part different, he does not say enough to explain how, when one thing is affected one way, the other has different desires on the first one's behalf, when what is provided does not even come to it. For food, warmth and moisture do not go to the desiring part, nor movement, nor relief when it is emptied, nor filling when it is full: all of these belong to the body.

@ch IV.4.22 | Does the earth have a soul, and does it perceive?
Is the growing soul in plants an echo of a soul that supplies it, in the earth? First: what soul is in the earth, a shining from the soul of the All, or its own, since Plato calls the earth the first and oldest god within the heaven? The earth grows plants and animals: why not an animal, with intellect, a god, as each star is? Its sluggishness only means that it does not move from its place. Perception needs no flesh: soul is given to body to keep it, and judges from its affections. But what would the earth perceive, through what, and for what need? Sense has a delight beyond need, as in seeing the sun and the sky; but first we must ask, in general, whether there is perception without organs, and whether it is for need.

@p
In plants, is what is as it were echoed in their bodies one thing, and what supplied it another, what in us is the desiring part and in them the growing part? Or is this in the earth, since there is soul in it, and in the plants what comes from it? But one might first ask what soul is in the earth: whether it comes from the sphere of the All, which alone Plato seems to ensoul first, as a shining into the earth; or whether, again, when he calls it the first and oldest of the gods within the heaven, he gives it too a soul such as the stars have. For how could it be a god if it did not have that soul? So it turns out that it is hard to find how the matter stands, and that from what Plato has said the perplexity becomes greater, or not less. But first, how might the matter reasonably seem to stand?
!note Plato sets the soul in the middle of the body of the All and stretches it through the whole (Timaeus 34b); he calls the earth "the first and eldest of the gods that have come to be within the heaven" (Timaeus 40c).

@p
@greek τὴν μὲν οὖν φυτικὴν ψυχὴν
That the earth has a growing soul one might judge from what grows out of it. And if many animals too are seen to come from the earth, why might one not say that it is an animal too? And, being so great an animal, and no small part of the All, why might one not say that it has intellect too, and so is a god? If each of the stars is one, why should the earth not be an animal too, being a part of the whole animal? For we must not say that it is held together from outside by a soul foreign to it, and has none inside, as if it could not have one of its own as well. For why can the fiery bodies have one, and the earthy not? Each is body; and there are no sinews there, no flesh, no blood, no moisture; and yet the earth is more varied, and made of all the bodies. If it is because it is hard to move, one might say that this bears only on its not moving from its place.
!flag they lack the flesh, blood, muscle, and pliant material of earth | The Greek says there are no sinews, flesh, blood or moisture "there", in the fiery stars, and yet they have soul; it does not give the earth flesh and blood, but says it is "more varied, made of all the bodies".

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι πῶς
But perception, how? How do the stars perceive? For perceiving does not belong to flesh either; nor must a body be given to the soul so that it may perceive, but a soul to the body, so that the body may be and be kept; and the soul, being able to judge, can look to a body and make its judgement from the body's affections. What then are the earth's affections, and what are its judgements of? For plants, in so far as they are of earth, do not perceive. Of what, then, are its perceptions, and through what? Or must we not dare to say that perceptions come about even without organs? And for what need would perceiving be to it? Not for knowing: for those who have no need that comes from perceiving, the knowledge that belongs to wisdom is perhaps enough.

@p
@greek ἢ τοῦτο μὲν οὐκ ἄν τις
Or one would not grant this. For apart from need there is in perceptible things a knowing that is not without grace, as of the sun and the rest, and of the heaven and the earth: for the perceptions of these are pleasant in themselves. This must be looked at later. Now again: if the earth has perceptions, the perceptions of what living things are they, and how? Or must we first take up again the difficulties, and take them in general: whether it is possible to perceive without organs, and whether perceptions are for need, even if something else comes about besides the need.
!note "Not without grace" is ἄμουσος with a negative: "not without the Muses". The delight of the senses apart from use is the opening of Aristotle's Metaphysics (I.1, 980a21-27), and of sight above all.

@ch IV.4.23 | Perception needs a bodily organ
Perceiving is the soul's grasp of the qualities of bodies, taking the impression of their forms. Alone, soul knows only what is in it: it cannot be made like the perceptible, as a point cannot be made like a line. There must be a third thing, which is affected: of one matter with the object, a mean between perceptible and intelligible, receiving and reporting, an organ, as a ruler stands between the straight in the craftsman's soul and the straight in the wood. Whether contact or a medium is needed is another question; perception belongs to soul in body and comes through body.

@p
We must lay it down that perceiving perceptible things is a grasp, by the soul or by the animal, in which the soul understands the quality that belongs to bodies and takes the impression of their forms. Either, then, it will grasp alone and by itself, or with something else. Alone and by itself, how? For by itself it grasps only what is in it, and that is thinking. If it is to grasp other things too, it must first have taken hold of them as well, either by being made like them, or by being with something that has been made like them. To be made like them while staying by itself is not possible: for how could a point be made like a line? Not even the intelligible line would fit the perceptible line, nor intelligible fire or man the perceptible fire or man. Not even nature, which makes the man, comes to be one with the man that comes to be. Alone, even if it could reach out to the perceptible, the soul will end in understanding the intelligible, since the perceptible escapes it and it has nothing with which to take hold of it.
!flag it has the faculty of dealing with the sensible, but it remains isolated | The Greek returns to the soul alone (μόνη), and puts its reaching for the perceptible as a supposition, "even if it could" (κἂν οἷόν τε); MacKenna makes it nature, with a faculty it has.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ ὁρατόν
For with the visible too, when the soul sees from far off, however much a form comes to it, beginning, in what reaches it, as something without parts, it ends in the underlying colour and shape, as large as it is there, for the soul that sees. So these must not be the only two, the thing outside and the soul, since then there would be no affection: there must be a third, which will be affected, and this is what will receive the shape. It must, then, share the affection and be affected in the same way, and be of one matter with the object; and one must be affected, and the other know. And the affection must be such as to keep something of what made it, yet not be the same: being between what made it and the soul, the affection lies between perceptible and intelligible, a mean in proportion, joining the extremes to each other in some way, able at once to receive and to report, fitted to be made like each. For, being the organ of some knowledge, it must be the same neither as the knower nor as what will be known, but fitted to be made like each: like the thing outside by being affected, and like the knower inside by its affection becoming form.
!flag an object whose complete detail of colour and form is known | The Greek says the form ends "in the underlying colour and shape, as large as it is there" (ὅσον ἐστὶν ἐκεῖ): seeing reaches the object at its own size, though what first comes from far off is without parts. That distant things look small is the question of II.8 (E9).
!note The mean "in proportion" (μέσον ἀνὰ λόγον) that binds the extremes is the Timaeus' (31c-32a), where the best bond makes three terms into one by proportion.

@p
@greek εἰ δὴ τοίνυν ὑγιὲς λέγομεν
If, then, what we say is sound, perceptions must come about through bodily organs. And this also follows from the fact that the soul, when it has come wholly outside body, grasps nothing perceptible. The organ must be either the whole body, or some part marked off for some work, as with touch and sight. One can see that the tools of the crafts too come between those who judge and what is judged, and report to the one who judges the particular character of what lies before him: for the ruler, joining the straight in the soul and the straight in the wood, set in between them, gave the craftsman the judging of his work. Whether what is to be judged must touch the organ; or whether it can be judged through something between, at a distance from the perceptible thing, as when the fire is far from the flesh; or even when what is between is not affected at all, as if there were a void between sight and colour, it being possible to see when the organ is there with its power: that is another discussion. But that perception belongs to soul in body, and comes through body, is clear.
!note Whether sight needs an affected medium is the question of IV.5 (E18), against Aristotle's account (On the soul II.7, 419a12-21), for whom in a void nothing at all would be seen.

@ch IV.4.24 | Is perception only for need? Does the All perceive?
If perception comes only with body, it is given for the body's sake: either following of necessity, as a strong affection reaches the soul, or contrived so that we guard against harm before it comes. Then it is for need, and for knowledge only to one who has forgotten. This widens the question to the stars and the whole cosmos. The whole, with nothing outside it, has awareness of itself, not perception. Yet, as in us part perceives part, why should the fixed sphere not see the wandering stars and the earth, like an eye reporting to the soul of the All? Plato says it needed no eyes; but it has things inside to see, and sight may follow from its nature.

@p
Whether perception is only for need must be considered in this way. If perception would not come about for soul alone, but perceptions come with body, it would be for the sake of body, from which the perceptions also come, and given because of the partnership with body: either following of necessity, for whatever the body suffers, the affection, when it is greater, reaches as far as the soul; or else contrived, so that we may guard against what acts on us even before it becomes greater, so as even to destroy it, or guard against it before it comes near. If so, perceptions would be for need. For even if they are for knowledge too, it is for one who is not in knowledge, but has become ignorant through misfortune, so that he may be reminded because he has forgotten; not for one who is neither in need nor in forgetting.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τοῦτο, οὐ περὶ τῆς γῆς
But if this is so, we would have to consider not only the earth but all the stars, and above all the whole heaven and the cosmos. For parts in relation to parts, to which being affected belongs, might have perception, on the present account; but the whole in relation to itself, unaffected in every way towards itself, what perception could it have? For if the organ must belong to the one who perceives, and what is perceived must be another thing besides the organ, while the All is a whole, it could not have one thing through which, and another of which, there is perception. We must grant it awareness of itself, as we too are aware of ourselves; but not perception, which is always of another thing. For even when we grasp something in the body that is out of its settled state, we grasp it as something that has come from outside.
!note "Awareness of itself" (συναίσθησις) is not perception of an object: the word for being aware together with oneself, which Plotinus uses for the self-awareness of intellect and of the whole (V.3.13).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ἐφ̓ ἡμῶν
But just as in us the grasp is not only of things outside, but also of part by part, what prevents the All too from seeing the wandering sphere with the unwandering one, and with this the earth and what is on it? And if these are not free from the other affections, why should it not have perceptions in another way too, and its sight belong to the unwandering sphere not only by itself, but as an eye reporting to the soul of the All what it saw? For even if it is free from the other affections, why will it not see as an eye does, being ensouled and of the nature of light?
!flag by means of what is stationary in it, perceive that region of itself which is in movement, that is to say the earth | The Greek says the All sees "the wandering sphere with the unwandering one, and with this the earth and what is on it": the fixed stars (ἀπλανής, "unwandering", not "stationary": they turn with the heaven) see the planets, and through them the earth. MacKenna makes the earth the moving region.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ὀμμάτων, φησίν
"But it had no need of eyes," he says. But if that was because nothing visible was left outside, still there was something inside, and nothing prevented it from seeing itself; and if it was because seeing itself would have been in vain, let it be that it did not come to be as it is for the sake of seeing, as its first purpose, but that seeing follows of necessity from its being so. And why should seeing not belong to a body of this kind?
!note Timaeus 33c: the All "had no need of eyes, for nothing visible was left outside it".

@ch IV.4.25 | The soul of the All looks to the intelligible, not to sense
An organ is not enough: the soul must incline towards perceptible things, and the soul of the All is always with the intelligibles; we too, when we are wholly there, miss sights and sounds. To look at a part of oneself is idle, and to want to see something else as beautiful belongs to one in need. Smell and taste are distractions; the sun and the stars might see and hear incidentally, and if they turn to us through these they will remember: how could they do good without memory?

@p
Or it is not enough that there is something through which to see, and to perceive at all: the soul must be so disposed as to incline towards perceptible things. But it belongs to the soul of the All to be always with the intelligibles; and even if it could perceive, it would not, because it is with better things. So too, when we are intensely with the intelligibles, at the times when we are there, sights and the other perceptions escape us; and in general, when one is wholly with one thing, the others escape one. For wanting to grasp a part with some part, as if one were to look down at oneself, is idle even in us, and in vain unless it is for some purpose; and to see something else as beautiful belongs to one who is affected and in want.
!flag Now it is the soul's character to be ever in the Intellectual sphere | The Greek says this of "the soul of the All" (τῇ τοῦ παντὸς ψυχῇ); our souls are with the intelligibles only "at the times when we are there", as the next words say.

@p
@greek ὀσφραίνεσθαι δὲ καὶ γεύεσθαι
Smelling, and tasting flavours, one might count as distractions and draggings about of the soul; but the sun and the other stars might see, and hear too, incidentally. And if they were to turn towards us through both, the position is not unreasonable. But if they turned, they will remember too: or it would be strange for them not to remember those they do good to. How do they do good, if they will not remember?
!flag means by which they apply themselves to their function | The Greek says "if they turn (ἐπιστρέφεσθαι) through both", sight and hearing: turn towards us and the earth, whose prayers they hear; "their function" is MacKenna's.
!note That the stars have no memory and do not reason was argued in IV.4.6-8 (E15); here the prayers bring the question back, and chapter 30 takes it up.

@ch IV.4.26 | Prayer, magic and the senses of the earth
Prayers are known and answered through a linking and sympathy, as everything in magic is. So why not grant the earth perception: first touch, of great movements, which cannot escape a soul within; perhaps for men's sake too, hearing prayers, and smell and taste, not in our way and not with our organs, as some animals hear without ears. Even sight: its growing power is in pneuma, which is transparent and lit by the heaven's circle. So the soul in the earth can see; and it must be thought a good soul, and a god.

@p
Knowledge of prayers comes about by a kind of linking, and by a certain relation of things fitted together; and so do the deeds that answer them; and in the arts of the magicians everything looks to this linkage: these things come about by powers that follow in sympathy. If so, why will we not grant that the earth too perceives? But what perceptions? Why not, first, touch: both of part by part, sent up to the ruling part of perception, and by the whole, of fire and the rest? For even if its body is hard to move, it is not unmoved. But its perceptions will be not of small things but of great ones. Why? Because, if there is soul in it, the greatest movements cannot escape it.
!note The sympathy of the All, by which magic and prayer work without the gods being moved by them, is the theme of IV.4.40-45 (E17).

@p
@greek κωλύει δ’ οὐδὲν καὶ
And nothing prevents perceiving from coming about for this reason too: that it may set well what concerns men, as far as men's affairs depend on it; and set them well as by sympathy; and hear those who pray, and nod assent to prayers, not in our way; and be affected by the other perceptions too, towards itself and towards other things, as with smells and with what is tasted, all that is smelt by the scents of juices, for the care of living things and the building and repairing of their bodies. And we must not demand the organs we have: not all animals have the same ones either; not all have ears, for example, and those that do not still grasp sounds.

@p
@greek περὶ δὲ ὄψεως, εἰ φωτὸς δεῖ
As for sight, if light is needed, how? For we must not demand eyes. If, then, granting the growing power, we had to grant that it is, first of all, in pneuma, since that is how it is, why disbelieve that this pneuma is also transparent? Rather, if it is pneuma, it is transparent too, and lit by the circle of the heaven, transparent in act. So it is neither strange nor impossible that the soul in the earth sees. And we must also consider that the soul belongs to no mean body, so as to be a god too: for in every way the soul must always be good.
!flag the earth is primarily of the spiritual order | The Greek says the growing power is first "in pneuma" (ἐν πνεύματι), the warm breath that the doctors and the Stoics put in living bodies: a fine body, and it is because it is a body that it can be transparent and lit. "The spiritual order" makes it bodiless.
!note "Transparent in act": light, for Aristotle, is the actuality of the transparent (On the soul II.7, 418b9-11).

@ch IV.4.27 | The earth's soul: Hestia and Demeter
The earth gives plants the generative soul, or a trace of it, which makes a plant differ from cut wood. The earth's own body receives something too: stones grow while they are attached and stop when cut out. So each part has a trace; over it lies the growing power of the whole earth, then the perceiving nature, riding on the body, then the rest of soul and intellect, which men, divining by a voice from the gods, call Hestia and Demeter.

@p
If, then, it gives the plants the generative soul itself; or the generative soul is in the earth and a trace of it is in the plants: so too the plants would be like flesh that is already ensouled and has received soul, if the plants also have the generative power in themselves. Being in the plant, it gives the plant's body what is better, by which it differs from what has been cut off and is no longer a plant, but only wood.
!flag at once the earth is ensouled, as our flesh is | The comparison is of the plants, not the earth: if they hold the generative power in themselves, they are "like flesh already ensouled" (ὡς ἡ σὰρξ ἔμψυχος ἤδη).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ γε τῷ σώματι
But what does the soul give to the body of the earth itself? We must think that an earthy body cut off from the earth is not the same as one that stays continuous with it, as stones show, which grow as long as they are attached, and stay the size they were when they were cut, once they have been taken away. So we must think that each part has a trace, and that over this lies the whole growing power, which is no longer this part's or that part's, but the whole earth's; then the nature of the perceiving power, no longer mixed into the body, but riding upon it; then the rest of soul, and intellect, which men call Hestia and Demeter, divining such things by a voice from the gods and by nature.
!flag Hestia (Earth-Mind) and Demeter (Earth-Soul) | The Greek names Hestia and Demeter together for the earth's higher soul and intellect; it does not assign intellect to one and soul to the other. The glosses in brackets are MacKenna's.
!note Hestia, the hearth, who stays at home when the gods ride out (Phaedrus 247a), was taken for the earth at the centre of the All; Plato's Cratylus reads Demeter's name as "the mother who gives" (404b).

@ch IV.4.28 | Where anger comes from
Is anger, like the start of desire, in the body as nature shaped it, about the heart or the bile? Desire begins at the liver, where the growing power is most active. We are angry at wrongs to others too, so anger needs perception and understanding; yet it follows the body's states: hot blood and bile, illness, hunger. So the affected body stirs blood or bile, the image joins the soul to this state and it rushes at the cause; from above, reasoning soul, seeing an injustice, takes this ready spirit as its ally. Both come from the growing power, which made the body bilious and bitter. Those who despise the body are less angry, and trees, with no blood or bile, are never angry. Desire and spirit are divided as appetites, not by the being they come from; the trace of anger may be set about the heart, as the source of such blood.

@p
So much for this. We must go back again and ask about the spirited part: whether, as we set the beginning of the desires, and pains and pleasures (the affections, not the perceptions), in the body so disposed, made as it were alive, so we will set the beginning of anger too; or whether we will set all of anger in the body so disposed, or in some part of the body, such as the heart in that state, or the bile, in a body that is not dead; and whether, if what gives the soul-trace is something else, anger here is some one thing, no longer coming from a spirited or a perceiving part.
!note The spirited part (τὸ θυμοειδές) is the middle part of the soul in Plato's Republic (IV 439e-441c), between reason and desire.

@p
@greek ἐκεῖ μὲν οὖν καθ̓ ὅλον
There, then, the growing power, being throughout the whole body, gave the trace to all the body, and pain was in all of it, and pleasure, and the beginning of the desire to be filled was in all of it. The desire for sex was not spoken of, but let it be about the parts that accomplish such things. And let the region about the liver be the beginning of desire, because the growing power is most active there, which gives the soul-trace to the liver and to the body; there, because the activity begins there. But about anger: what it is itself, and what soul it is, and whether a trace from it is about the heart, or something else supplies the movement that ends in the compound, or here it is not a trace, but anger itself that is supplied.
!note Plato's Timaeus (70a-71b) houses spirit about the heart, between midriff and neck, and desire below the midriff, with the liver.

@p
@greek πρῶτον οὖν σκεπτέον
First, then, we must consider what it is. That we are angry not only at what the body suffers, but also at what one of those close to us suffers, and in general at what anyone does against what is fitting, is clear enough: so in being angry there must be perception, and some understanding too. And so, looking to these things, one would seek the origin of anger not as starting from the growing power but from something else. But when readiness for anger follows the states of the body; and those boiling with blood and bile are ready to be angry, while those called bile-less and cold are slack to anger; and beasts are angry according to their temperaments, at nothing else but at what they think has harmed them: then again one would refer anger to what is more bodily, and to what holds together the frame of the animal. And when the same men are more irritable sick than well, and fasting than fed, they show that anger, or the beginnings of anger, belong to a body of this kind, and that bile or blood, as if ensouling it, supply such movements.
!flag they pay attention to no outside combinations | The Greek says beasts are angry "according to their temperaments" (πρὸς τὰς κράσεις), the blends of their bodies, and at nothing else, but at what they think has harmed them: κρᾶσις is the body's own mixture, not anything outside.
!note "Bile-less" (ἄχολος) is the word of the doctors' humours: the man without bile is mild. Aristotle defines anger both ways, as the desire to pay back pain and as the boiling of the blood about the heart (On the soul I.1, 403a29-b1).

@p
@greek ὥστε παθόντος τοῦ τοιοῦδε
So, when the body of this kind is affected, the blood or the bile is at once moved; and when perception has come about, the image, having made the soul share in the state of this kind of body, rushes now at what caused the pain. And from above, again, the soul that uses reasoning, when an injustice has appeared, even one that is not about the body, takes as its ally this spirited part, which is ready to be angry in that way, since it is its nature to fight the opponent that has been shown to it. And there is one anger that rises without reason and draws reason after it by the image, and another that begins from reason and ends in what is naturally made to grow bilious. Both come from the growing and generative power, which builds the body as able to grasp pleasant and painful things; and by having made it bilious and bitter, and since the soul-trace is in such a thing, it is moved in such ways, peevish and angry; and, having been harmed first, it seeks in some way to harm the others too, and as it were make them like itself.
!flag the phase not inbound with body | The Greek's "not about the body" (μὴ περὶ τὸ σῶμα) goes with the injustice: reason is angered by a wrong that does not touch the body, which is why anger was said to need understanding. MacKenna takes it of the soul.
!note Spirit as reason's ally against desire is the Republic's (IV 440b-441a).

@p
@greek μαρτύριον δὲ τοῦ ὁμοούσιον
A witness that this is of the same being as the other soul-trace: those who long less for the body's pleasures, and in general despise the body, are less moved to anger and to unreasoning affections. That trees have no anger, though they have the growing power, need not surprise us: they have no share in blood or bile. If these were in them without perception, there would be only a boiling and a kind of indignation; but when perception is in them too, there would at once be an impulse against the wrongdoer as well, so as to defend oneself.
!note "Of the same being" is ὁμοούσιος, the word the creed of Nicaea (325) would use of the Son and the Father.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τὸ ἄλογον τῆς
But if the unreasoning part of the soul were divided into the desiring and the spirited, and the one were the growing power, and the spirited a trace from it, about blood or bile or both, the division would not be a true one, since one would be prior and the other posterior. Or nothing prevents both from being posterior, and the division being of what has come to be from the same source: for it is a division of appetites, as appetites, not of the being from which they have come. That being in itself is not appetite; but perhaps it perfects the appetite, joining to itself the activity that comes from it. And it is not strange to say that the trace that has fallen into anger is about the heart: not that the soul is there, but let the beginning of blood of this kind be said to be there.
!note Things divided against each other from the same genus are "simultaneous by nature" (Aristotle, Categories 13, 14b33-15a7), so one cannot be prior to the other.

@ch IV.4.29 | Does the body's life go when the soul goes?
If the body is like warmed air, why does nothing living remain when the soul leaves? Some does, for a little: hair and nails grow on corpses, and cut animals move. Going together is no proof of sameness: when the sun goes, the light thrown on other things goes too. Does such light go with its source, or perish? Colour is not like shape but like sweetness, which might pass into other bodies unnoticed; unless we see by convention. Perhaps light moves with its body unseen; whether the lower soul follows the higher is for elsewhere, and whether the body's life can be without soul.

@p
How then, if the body is like what has been warmed and not like what has been lit, does it have nothing living left when the other soul has gone out? Or it does, for a little while, but it fades away fast, as with things that have been warmed when they have moved away from the fire. Hairs bear witness too, growing on dead bodies, and nails growing, and animals cut in pieces that go on moving for a long time: for this is perhaps what is still lying in them. And if it goes away together with the other soul, that is no proof that it is not something else. For when the sun goes away, not only the light that is next to it, going with it and hanging from it, goes away, but also the light that comes from this and is seen outside it, in the things that lie beside it, which is other than that, goes away along with it.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν συναπέρχεται
Does it go away with it, then, or perish? This must be asked both of light of this kind and of the life in the body, which we say is the body's own. That nothing of the light is left in the things that were lit is clear; but whether it falls back into what made it, or simply is not, is what the argument asks. How then could it simply not be, being something before? But what was it, at all? We may say that what is called colour belongs to the bodies themselves from which the light comes, and when the bodies are perishable and change, it is no more, and no one asks where the colour of a fire that has gone out is, any more than where its shape is. Or the shape is a kind of arrangement, like the closing and opening of the hand, but colour is not so, but like sweetness. For what prevents the sweetness of a sweet body, when the body has perished, from not being lost, and the fragrance of a fragrant one, but coming to be in another body, and not being perceptible, because the bodies that have taken a share are not such that the qualities that come to be in them press against the perception? So too the light of bodies that have perished might remain, while the resistance, which was made of them all, does not remain.

@p
@greek εἰ μή τις λέγοι νόμῳ ὁρᾶν
Unless someone were to say that we see by convention, and that the so-called qualities are not in the underlying things. But if so, we will make the qualities imperishable, and not coming to be in the formations of bodies; and the forming principles in the seeds will not make the colours, as in the many-coloured birds, but gather them, being there already; or they make them, but use as well those in the air, which is full of such things: for they are in the air too, though not such as they appear in bodies, when they have come to be there. But let this difficulty be left lying here.
!flag the seeing is merely the sequel to some law | "To see by convention" (νόμῳ ὁρᾶν) is Democritus' word: "by convention colour, by convention sweet; in truth atoms and void" (fragment B9, B125). The colours we see are not in the things. MacKenna's "law (of our own nature)" loses the reference.
!flag the full store of colours in the sky | The Greek says "in the air" (ἐν τῷ ἀέρι), which is full of such things, and that in the air they are not such as they appear in bodies; not the sky or the heavens.
!note The forming principles in the seeds (λόγοι σπερματικοί) are the Stoics', which Plotinus takes over for nature's making (compare III.8.2, E14).

@p
@greek μενόντων δὲ τῶν σωμάτων
But if, while the bodies remain, the light is joined to them and not cut off, what prevents the light, when the body moves away, from moving away with it, both the light next to it and whatever is joined to that next light, even if it is not seen going away, as it is not seen coming either? But as for the soul, whether the second things follow the prior, and the next always follow those before them; or whether each is on its own, deprived of those before it and able to stay by itself; or whether no part of the soul is cut off at all, but all souls are one and many, and in what way: that is for elsewhere. But what is the trace of soul that has already become the body's? If it is soul, it will follow, if it is not cut off, the account of soul; if it is like a life of the body, the same account holds there as was raised as a difficulty about the light that is an image; and we must consider whether life can be without soul, unless indeed it is by the soul's lying near and acting on something else.
!flag on the dissolution of the body | The Greek says "when the body is moved away" (μετακινουμένου τοῦ σώματος): the case now is of bodies that remain, and move, and their light moving with them; the perishing of bodies was the case just left lying.
!note That all souls are one and many is IV.9, Whether all souls are one (E19), and IV.3.1-8.

@ch IV.4.30 | Do the stars remember our prayers?
We denied the stars memory but gave them perception, and said that they hear prayers; and it is believed that they do much for men, and so easily that they help even in unjust deeds and in lust. This raises old difficulties about gods made accomplices in strange deeds, and above all about memory: if they answer prayers later, they remember. We must show how memory fits our view, defend the gods in the heaven, ask whether the whole heaven is bewitched by human art, and how daemons serve.

@p
Now, we set down that memories are superfluous in the stars, but gave them perceptions, hearing as well as sight, and said that they hear prayers, which we make to the sun, and some other men to the stars too; and it is believed that many things are done for men through them, and so very easily that they are helpers not only in the just among their deeds, but also in many of the unjust. So we must inquire into these matters too, which have fallen in our way. For in themselves they hold very great difficulties, much talked about among those who cannot bear that gods should become fellow-workers in, and causes of, strange deeds, among others in love affairs and in licentious couplings. For these reasons, then, and above all for the sake of what our account was about from the beginning, their memory.
!note "What our account was about from the beginning": memory, the question with which IV.3 ended and IV.4 began (IV.4.1, E15).

@p
@greek δῆλον γὰρ ὅτι, εἰ εὐξαμένων
For it is clear that, if they act when men have prayed, and do it not at once but later, and very often after long times, they have memory of what men pray to them for. Our account before did not grant this; though for benefits to men too it would have been of this kind, like those of Demeter and Hestia, unless one were to say that only the earth does good to human things.
!flag such a memory as we ascribed to Demeter and Hestia | The earlier account gave Demeter and Hestia no memory (chapter 27 only names them). The Greek says that memory would be needed too for benefits to men such as Demeter's and Hestia's, the earth's, "unless one were to say that only the earth does good to human things".

@p
@greek ἀμφότερα οὖν πειρατέον
So we must try to show both things: how we will place what belongs to memory in these, which concerns us, not the views of the others, who are not prevented from granting memories; and, about the deeds that seem to come about strangely, which it is philosophy's task to examine, whether there is any way to answer the difficulties raised against the gods in the heaven; and indeed about the whole cosmos itself, since a charge of this kind reaches it too, whether those are to be believed who say that even the whole heaven itself is bewitched by men's daring and art. And the account will also ask about daemons, how they are said to serve in such things, unless from the solution of the first questions it gets theirs too.
!note "Bewitched" (γοητεύεσθαι): the claim of the magicians, which Plotinus answers in IV.4.40-44 (E17); the Gnostics' incantations to the higher powers he mocks in II.9.14.

@ch IV.4.31 | Every action and affection in the cosmos
Take all actions and affections in the cosmos, by nature and by art: from the whole to the parts, from parts to the whole, from part to part; and arts that end in their products, that help nature, like medicine and farming, or that change souls, like rhetoric and music. The revolution of the heaven plainly acts on the earth, on bodies and on souls. But not by hot and cold alone: these cannot explain envy, fortune, wealth, birth or treasure found. Nor by the stars' choice: gods would not contrive thieves and temple-robbers, which not even decent men would do.

@older 30
@p
In general, then, we must take all the actions and affections that come about in the whole cosmos, both those called natural and those that come about by art. Of the natural, we must say that some come from the All to the parts, and from the parts to the All, or from parts to parts; of those that come about by art, either the art, as it began, ends in the products of art, or it uses natural powers as well, for the making and suffering of natural works. By those of the whole I mean all that the whole revolution does to itself and to its parts: for as it moves it disposes in some way both itself and its parts, both those in the revolution itself and all that it gives to the things on earth. The affections of parts by parts are, I suppose, plain to everyone: the relations of the sun and its actions both towards the other stars and towards things on earth, and those in the other elements, both of the sun itself and of the other stars and of the things on earth; each of these must be examined.
!flag Our problem embraces all act and all experience throughout the entire kosmos | MacKenna's chapter 30 runs on here without a break: the Greek's chapter 31 begins with these words (the OCR lost his number 31).

@p
@greek τέχναι δὲ αἱ μὲν οἰκίαν
Of the arts, those that make a house and the other products of art have ended in a thing of that kind; medicine and farming and the arts of that kind are servants, and bring help to natural things, so that they may be in their natural state; and rhetoric and the musical art and every leading of souls change them, leading them to the better or the worse. In these we must ask how many the arts are and what power they have; and, if it is possible, in all these, so far as they bear on our present need, we must work out the why as well, as far as we can.
!note "Leading of souls" (ψυχαγωγία) is the Phaedrus' word for rhetoric (261a, 271c).

@p
@greek ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἡ φορὰ ποιεῖ
That the revolution acts, first disposing itself in different ways, and what is within it; and beyond dispute acts on earthly things, not only on their bodies but also on the dispositions of the soul; and that each of its parts acts on earthly things, and in general on what is below: this is plain in many ways. Whether these act on those too, later. For now, leaving as they are the things granted by all or by most, as far as they will appear through reasoning, we must try to tell the manner, taking it from the beginning of the acting.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ μόνον θερμὰ καὶ ψυχρὰ
For we must not say that only hot and cold things act, and things of that kind, which are called the first qualities of the elements, nor those that come from their mixture; nor that the sun does everything by heat, and another star by cold: for what could be cold in the heaven, and in a fiery body? Nor another by moist fire: for in that way it would not be possible to grasp their difference either. And many of the things that come about cannot be traced back to any of these. For even if one were to grant them the differences of characters, according to the mixtures of bodies, being such through a prevailing cold or heat, how could one trace envies, jealousies or villainies back to these? And even if these, how could one trace fortunes at least, worse and better, rich men and poor, the nobility of fathers, or the finding of treasures? One could name thousands of such things, leading far from the bodily quality that comes from the elements into the bodies and souls of living things.
!note The astrologers gave the planets the qualities of the elements: Saturn cold, Mars hot and dry, the moon moist (Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos I.4). Plotinus' fuller answer to them is II.3, Whether the stars are causes (E8).

@p
@greek οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ προαιρέσει
Nor again must what befalls each of the things below them be referred to the choice of the stars, and to the judgement of the All, and to their reasonings. For it is strange that they should contrive human affairs so that some become thieves, others kidnappers, house-breakers and temple-robbers, others unmanly, womanish in what they do and suffer, doing shameful things. For to do and contrive such things belongs not only not to gods, but not even to decent men, and perhaps not to anyone at all, when no benefit at all would come to them from it.
!flag a doom from the All | The Greek has "the judgement of the All" (τῇ τοῦ παντὸς γνώμῃ): the mind and will of the All, set with the stars' choice and reasonings; not a doom laid on us.
!note The same argument against stars that will evil is in II.3.6 (E8) and III.1.5-6 (E10).

# Milestone E17: IV.4 On difficulties about the soul, second part, chapters 32 to 45, beside MacKenna's vol. III (1924,
# pp. 85-101), which completes the treatise. MacKenna's chapters are the Greek's, except that his 37 runs on into the
# Greek's 38 and his 40 into the Greek's 41 (the OCR lost his numbers 38 and 41), so those are shown with his 37 and 40
# (@older 37, @older 40).

@ch IV.4.32 | The All is one living being, in sympathy with itself
If the stars act neither by bodily causes nor by choice, what is left? The All is one living being with one soul reaching all its parts; each thing is a part of it by body, and by soul as far as it shares in the soul of the All. So the whole is in sympathy with itself, and the far is near, as in an animal, where like parts apart feel together. Parts harm and feed on one another, as bile and anger do in us; but all this coming to be and perishing makes the unhindered life of the one living being, whose staying is its moving.

@p
If, then, we are to refer neither to bodily causes nor to choices all that comes from outside, from the heaven, to us and to the other living beings and in general to the things on earth, what cause would be left that is reasonable? First, then, we must lay down that this All is one living being, embracing all the living beings within it, and having one soul that reaches all its parts, so far as each is a part of it. Each thing in the perceptible All is a part of it: in its body wholly; and so far as it also shares in the soul of the All, to that extent in this way too. Those that share in this soul alone are parts in every way; those that share in another soul as well have, by this, the power of not being parts in every way. But they are affected no less by the others, so far as they have something of the All, and according to what they have.
!flag material agencies (blind elements) | The Greek says only "bodily causes" (σωματικαῖς αἰτίαις), the hot and cold of chapter 31; "blind elements" is MacKenna's.
!flag partial where there is also a union with a lower soul | The Greek says those that share in "another" soul as well (ἄλλης), a soul of their own such as ours, are by this not wholly parts; nothing says that the other soul is lower.

@p
@greek συμπαθὲς δὴ πᾶν τοῦτο τὸ ἕν
This one All, then, is in sympathy with itself, as one living being, and what is far is near: as in one single animal a nail, a horn, a finger, or some other part that is not next to it; the part between is passed over and is not affected at all, while what is not near has been affected. For when like things do not lie next to each other, but are separated by others between, and feel together by their likeness, what is done by the one not lying beside must reach the far one too. And since it is a living being, and goes to make one, nothing is so far in place as not to be near, by the nature of the one living being, so as to feel together. What has likeness to the agent, then, has an affection that is not foreign to it; but when the agent is unlike, what is affected has the affection as foreign and not agreeable.
!note Sympathy (συμπάθεια, "feeling together") of the parts of the cosmos is the Stoics' word (Posidonius; Cicero, On divination II.34), which Plotinus takes over and grounds in the one soul of the All. Like acting on like goes back to Empedocles and to Plato's Timaeus (45b-d), where like fire meets like in sight.

@p
@greek βλαβερὰν δὲ ποίησιν
That one thing should do harm to another, though it is one living being, need not surprise us: for in us too, in our own activities, one part might be harmed by another, since bile and anger, it seems, press and sting something else. And in the All too there is something analogous to anger and bile, and one thing to another; and in plants too one thing will be a hindrance to another, so as even to wither it. This All is seen to be not only one living being but also many: so that, so far as each is one, it is kept safe by the whole; but so far as they are many, and meet one another, they have often done harm by their difference. One thing has harmed another for its own need, and has even made food of what is akin and at the same time different. And each, hastening for itself according to nature, takes into itself as much of the other as is its own, and does away with as much as was foreign, by its goodwill towards itself.
!flag bile and animal spirit seem to press and goad | The Greek has "bile and anger" (χολὴ καὶ ὁ θυμός), anger with its seat in the bile (IV.4.28); "animal spirit" is the physiology of MacKenna's day.
!flag by sucking the moisture from it | The Greek says only that among plants one is "a hindrance" (ἐμπόδιον) to another, "so as even to wither it"; nothing of sucking moisture.
!flag whatever is becoming a menace to it | The Greek says each does away with what was "foreign" (ἀλλότριον) to it, "by its goodwill towards itself" (εὐνοίᾳ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ), as food is made its own; not what threatens it.

@p
@greek ἔργον τε τὸ αὑτοῦ ποιοῦν
And each, doing its own work, has benefited whatever could enjoy something of its works, and has done away with or harmed whatever could not withstand the rush of the work, as things would wither when a fire goes by, or smaller animals would be swept aside by the running of greater ones, or even trampled underfoot. The coming to be of all these, and their perishing, and their change to the worse or the better, complete the unhindered life, according to nature, of that one living being: since it was not possible for each thing to be as if it were alone, nor for the end to be for them, and for them to look to it, being parts, but to look to that of which they are parts; and being different, they could not always have all that is theirs in one life. Nor could anything remain wholly the same, if the All was to remain, which has its remaining in being moved.
!flag for the permanence of an All demands varying forms | The Greek says the All "has its remaining in being moved" (ἐν τῷ κινεῖσθαι τὸ μένειν ἔχον): its permanence is its motion, not a variety of forms.
!note "Changing, it rests" is Heraclitus' (fragment B84a); the parts that serve the whole are Plato's (Laws X 903b-d: "you were made for the sake of the whole, and not the whole for you").

@ch IV.4.33 | The cosmos as a dance
The revolution is not random but moves by the reason of the living being, so agent and patient are in concord, and each figure of the heaven brings a new disposition below, as in a varied choral dance. A dancer's limbs bend and rise as each figure requires, not by their own choice: so the heavenly bodies act, and also signify. Better: the whole cosmos lives its life in act, changing the figures of its great parts, and the rest follow; the cause is not the figured but the one who figures, and it is itself all that comes to be.

@p
Since the revolution has nothing random about it, but is carried on by the reason that belongs to the living being, there had to be concord too between what acts and what is affected, and an order that ranges things to one another and towards one another, so that at each relation of the revolution, and of the things in turn under the revolution, there is one disposition and then another, as of those who make one dance in a varied choral dance. For in our own dances too, why should one speak of the things outside, which plainly change differently at each movement, the things that contribute to the dance, pipes and songs and the rest joined to it?

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ τὰ μέρη τοῦ τὴν
But the parts of the one who performs the dance could not, of necessity, be the same at each figure, as the limbs of the body follow along and bend, one pressed, another let go, one labouring, another taking a breath in the change of figure. The dancer's choice looks to something else; but the limbs are affected in following the dance, serve the dance, and help complete the whole of it, so that one skilled in dancing could say that in such a figure this limb of the body is lifted high, this one bends, this one is hidden, and another is made low: not because the dancer chose otherwise to do this, but because in the dance of the whole body this part, which carries the dance through, holds this position of necessity.
!flag The dancer's mind is on his own purpose | The Greek says the dancer's choice "looks to something else" (πρὸς ἄλλο βλέπει), to the dance as a whole, while the limbs follow; not to a purpose of his own.

@p
@greek τοῦτον τοίνυν τὸν τρόπον
In this way, then, we must say that the things in the heaven act, so far as they act, and that some things they also signify. Or rather, that the whole cosmos lives its whole life in act, moving its great parts within itself and always changing their figures; and that the relations of the parts to one another and to the whole, and their different positions, bring the other things after them, as when one living being moves: holding one way according to these relations, positions and figurings, another way according to those. So it is not the figured that act, but the one who figures; and the one who figures is not doing one thing and making another, for it is not acting on something else, but is itself all that comes to be: there the figures, here the affections that follow the figures of necessity, in the living being moved in this way, and again in the one so composed and constituted by nature, both affected and acting on itself by necessities.
!flag a living being (an All) thus by its nature conjoined | MacKenna's "(an All)" is his own addition: the Greek speaks of one living being only, moved in this way and composed in this way, which acts on itself and is affected by itself.
!note That the stars signify more than they cause is the theme of II.3, Whether the stars are causes (E8), where they are letters written in the heaven (II.3.7). The cosmic dance is the Timaeus' (40c), "the choral dances" of the stars.

@ch IV.4.34 | Figures and the things figured
We give the part of us that belongs to the body of the All to be affected by it, but not the whole of us, like sensible hired men, who are not wholly another's. The figures differ because the stars run at different speeds. Do things here follow those there in concord, or do the figures have powers? The same figure means different things for different things, so the power is in both, the figures and the figured: as in a dance the hands, the figures and what follows them each have power. Some figures both act and signify, others only signify.

@p
We, however, giving the part of ourselves that was ours of that body to be affected, and not thinking that the whole of us belongs to it, should be affected by it within measure: as sensible men among those in service serve their masters with a part of themselves, but with a part are their own, and for this reason receive more measured orders from the master, since they are not slaves and not wholly another's.
!flag in part retain their personality | The Greek says that with a part "they are their own" (τὸ δ’ αὑτῶν ὄντες); "personality" is a modern word.
!flag are thus less absolutely at beck and call | The Greek says that for this reason they "receive more measured orders" (μετριωτέρων ... ἐπιταγμάτων) from the master: it is the master's orders that are moderated.
!note Those "in service" (θητεύοντες) are hired men, free men working for a wage, set against slaves (ἀνδράποδα). That we are not wholly of the All is III.1.8-10 (E10), and the "other soul" of chapter 32.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ τῶν σχηματισμῶν διάφορον
The difference of the figures had to come about, as it does now, since the runners are not of equal speed. And since they are carried by reason, and the relations of the living being become different, and then here too the things among us become sympathetic with what comes about there, it is reasonable to ask whether we should say that these follow along, in concord with those, or that the figures have the powers of what is done; and whether the figures simply, or the figures of these things. For the same figure of the same thing does not produce the same signification or effect upon one thing and again upon others, since each, by itself, seems to have a different nature.
!note "The runners" (οἱ θέοντες) are the stars: Plato's Cratylus (397c-d) derives "gods" (θεοί) from "running" (θεῖν), since the first men saw the sun, moon and stars always running.

@p
@greek ἢ ὀρθῶς ἔχει λέγειν
Or it is right to say that the figuring of these things is this disposition and of this kind, and that of others, though it is the same in its figure, is another. But if so, we will give the powers no longer to the figures, but to the figured things themselves. Or to both together. At any rate, when the same things take a different relation, different results come, and when the same thing takes only a different place, different ones. But what results? Effects or significations? Or to the pair together, the figuring of these things, both, effects and significations, in many cases, but elsewhere significations only.
!flag changing the members, the relationship remains the same | The Greek says the opposite: the figuring of other things, though the same in figure, is "another" disposition (τὴν δὲ ἄλλων τὴν αὐτὴν οὖσαν ἐν σχηματισμῷ ἄλλην): change the members and the same figure means something else.

@p
@greek οὗτος τοίνυν ὁ λόγος
This account, then, gives powers to the figures, and powers to the figured too: since in dancers too each hand has some power, and so do the other limbs, and the figures have much; and third come the things that follow along, both the parts of the limbs taken into the dance and the things these are made of, such as the squeezed parts of the hand, and the sinews and veins that feel with them.
!flag the clutched fingers and the muscles and veins following suit | The Greek has "sinews" (νεῦρα) and veins "feeling with them" (συμπαθοῦντα), the same sympathy as in the All; not muscles that follow suit.

@ch IV.4.35 | How the figures have power
We gave the effects neither to the stars' bodies nor to their choices. But the All is one living being, in sympathy with itself, whose life runs in one harmony and order by reason, its parts dancing by numbers: the figures and the figured parts are the activity of the All, which lives so. Choice is outside these powers; the parts desire one another, but the whole seeks the Good, or rather looks at it, and so does right choice. The sun looks upward, and gives its warmth and its power without choosing. Figures have powers here too: some frighten and some move by beauty, for whatever is acts or is acted on. And there are powers besides figures, in stones and herbs.

@p
How, then, are these powers? We must say it more clearly again. What difference does one triangle have from another triangle? And what does this star do to that one, and by what does it act, and how far? For we gave the effects neither to their bodies nor to their choices: not to the bodies, since what comes about was not the work of body only; not to the choices, since it was absurd for gods to do absurd things by choice.
!flag How can there be the exercise of power from man to man | The Greek "this one towards that one" (ὁδὶ πρὸς τονδί) is masculine because it speaks of the stars (ἀστήρ), one star in relation to another, as the triangles before it are their figures; no men are in it.
!note The triangle is the astrologers' trine, two planets a third of the zodiac apart; II.3.4 (E8) asks the same of the square and the opposition.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ μνημονεύοιμεν
But if we were to remember that we laid down that the All is one living being, and that, being so, it had of necessity to be in sympathy with itself; and that the course of its life, being by reason, is all in concord with itself; and that there is nothing random in its life, but one harmony and order; and that the figures are by reason, and each thing is by numbers, and so are the parts of the living being that dance in the chorus: then we must agree to both, that the activity of the All is both the figures that come about in it and its parts that are figured, and what follows on these; and that the All lives in this way, and the powers contribute to this, just as they came to be, having them, when they were made by the one who made them in forming principles.
!flag the producing agency within the Reason-Principles | The Greek says the powers were made "by the one who made them in forming principles" (ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν λόγοις πεποιηκότος): a maker, who made them by forming principles, not an agency within the principles.

@p
@greek καὶ τὰ μὲν σχήματα οἷον λόγους
And the figures are like forming principles, or distances of the living being, its rhythms and relations according to reason, and the members set apart and figured are another thing. And the living being has, apart from choice, other powers, those that are like parts of the living being, since choice is outside them and does not contribute to the nature of this living being. For the choice of one living being is one, but its other powers, directed to itself, are many. And all the choices in it look to the same thing to which the one choice of the All looks too. For desire is of one of the things in it towards another: one part wants to take something of the others, being in need of it; and anger is against another, when something pains it; and growth is from another, and generation into another of the parts. But the whole, in these, does these things, but itself seeks the Good, or rather looks at it.
!flag the anger of a moment of annoyance | The Greek says anger is "against another, when something pains it" (ὅταν τι παραλυπῇ), one part of the All against another, like desire before it; not a passing annoyance.
!note "The whole seeks the Good, or rather looks at it": the soul of the All contemplates, and its making follows (III.8.4, E14; IV.4.12 and 16).

@p
@greek τοῦτο τοίνυν καὶ ἡ ὀρθὴ προαίρεσις
This, then, is what right choice too seeks, the choice that is above the affections, and in this it contributes to the same end. For of those in service with another, too, many of their works look to what the master has ordered, but their longing for the good is towards the same thing as the master's. If, then, the sun and the other stars do something to the things here, we must think that the sun itself is looking upward (for we must make the account about one); but that something is done from it, as the warming of things on earth, and so too anything after this, by the giving out of soul, as much as is in it, since its growing soul is abundant; and that another star likewise, as if shining out, gives a power from itself without choice; and that all things, having become one in being figured so, give one disposition and then another, so that the figures too have powers: for by being so or so, things are this way or that. And something comes about through the figured things themselves too: for from these comes one thing, and from others another. That figures by themselves have something like powers one could see in the things here too.
!flag intent upon the Supreme | The Greek says the sun is "looking upward" (ἄνω βλέποντα); "the Supreme" is MacKenna's.
