!flag the vastly efficacious soul of Nature | The Greek says the sun's "growing soul" (φυτικῆς ψυχῆς), the soul that makes things grow, "is abundant" (πολλῆς οὔσης); not the soul of nature.

@p
@greek διὰ τί γὰρ τὰ μὲν
For why are some figures frightening to those who see them, though those who fear have suffered nothing from them before, while others do not frighten when seen? And why do some frighten these men, and others those? Or because these act on a man of this kind and those on that one, since they cannot fail to act on what is by nature fit for it; and figured in this way a thing moved the sight, and figured in that way it did not move the same sight. For even if one were to say that it is beauty that moves, why did it move this man by this and that man by another, unless the power lies in the difference of figure? For why shall we say that colours have power and act, and not say so of figures? Since in general it is absurd for something to be among the things that are and yet have nothing it can do. For what is, is such as either to act or to be affected; and in some we must grant acting, in the others both.
!note "What is, is such as either to act or to be affected": the Eleatic Stranger's mark of being, "power" to act or to be acted on (Sophist 247d-e).

@p
@greek καὶ ἐν τοῖς ὑποκειμένοις
And in the underlying things there are powers besides the figures; and in the things among us there are many that hot or cold things do not give, but things that have come to be with different qualities, given form by forming principles and sharing in a power of nature, as the natures of stones and the activities of herbs give many wonderful things.
!flag shaped to ideal-quality by the action of Reason-Principles | The Greek says such things are "given form" (εἰδοποιηθέντα) by forming principles, as every natural thing is; "ideal-quality" is MacKenna's.
!note The powers of stones and herbs were the matter of the lapidaries and herbals, and of the magic that used them; chapter 40 comes to it.

@ch IV.4.36 | Everything in the All lives
The All is most varied, full of forming principles and of powers without limit: as every part of a man has its own power, so, and much more, in the All, which is a trace of the intelligible, and above all in the heavenly bodies. It is not a soulless house of stones and timber, but awake everywhere, each thing living in its own way. This answers how there can be something soulless in an ensouled living being: each thing lives, but hiddenly. The All acts without needing choice, being older than choice.

@p
For the All is most varied, and all the forming principles are in it, and powers without limit and varied. As they say that in a man too the eye has one power and this bone another, and that bone another; this part of the hand one, and the toe another; and that there is no part that has no power, and none that has the same power, though we do not know it, unless someone has learned such things: so too, and much more so, in the All; or rather, because these things here are a trace of those, in the All there must be an untold and wonderful variety of powers, and above all in the things carried round the heaven.
!flag since all this order is but a representation of the higher | The Greek says these things here are "a trace of those" (ἴχνος ταῦτα ἐκείνων), the word Plotinus uses of nature as the last trace of soul (IV.4.13, 20); not a representation.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ δή, ὥσπερ ἄψυχον
For it should not have come to be a cosmos like a great soulless house, large and roomy besides, made of a few kinds easily counted, stones and timbers, say, and some others if you like; but it must be awake everywhere, and living, one thing in one way and another in another, and nothing can be that is not in it. So here too the difficulty might be solved, how in an ensouled living being there is something soulless: for this account says that one thing lives in one way and another in another in the whole, and that we do not say a thing lives when it is not moved by itself perceptibly; but each of these lives hiddenly, and what lives perceptibly is made of things that do not live perceptibly, but give wonderful powers for living to such a living being.
!note "Awake" (ἐγρηγορός) answers the sleeping life of nature (III.8.4, E14). The cosmos as one ensouled living being is the Timaeus' (30b-d).

@p
@greek μὴ γὰρ ἂν κινηθῆναι
For a man would not be moved to so many things if he were moved by powers in him that were wholly soulless; nor again would the All live so if each of the things in it did not live its own life, even if choice is not present to it. For it acts without needing choice too, being older than choice; and so many things serve its powers.
!flag Man would never have reached to his actual height | The Greek says a man "would not be moved to so many things" (ἐπὶ τοσαῦτα), so many kinds of movement, if the powers in him were soulless; nothing of his height.

@ch IV.4.37 | Each thing has its power, without choice
Nothing in the All is to be thrown away. If we ask what fire's acting is, we cannot say, unless we grant it a power from its being in the All. We do not wonder at the familiar, but would, if someone showed us their powers. Each thing, shaped in the All and sharing in its soul, has a power in proportion, the heavenly more than the earthly; and much comes about by these powers, not by choice, and without the givers turning to it, as a living thing is born of a living thing without choosing or knowing it.

@p
Nothing, then, of the All is to be thrown away. For fire too, and the things of that kind that we say act: if someone among those who now seem to know were to ask what their acting is, he would be at a loss, unless he granted that this power is theirs by their being in the All, and spoke in the same way of the other things in use. But the familiar things we neither think fit to inquire into nor disbelieve; the other powers, outside the familiar, we disbelieve, as to how each is, and add wonder to the unfamiliar; though we would wonder at these too if someone brought out each of them to us who had no experience of them, and explained their powers.

@p
@greek ἔχειν μὲν οὖν ἕκαστον
We must say, then, that each thing has some power in proportion, having been moulded and shaped in the All, and having shared somehow in soul from the whole, which is ensouled, and being embraced by such a thing, and being a part of something ensouled (for there is nothing in it that is not a part); some things being more powerful than others for acting, and the heavenly more than the earthly, since they have a clearer nature; and that many things come about by these powers, not by the choice of those from whom what is done seems to come: for there is acting in things that have no choice too; nor need they turn to the giving of the power, even if something of soul goes from them.
!flag Some such power, not necessarily accompanied by reason | The Greek says each thing has "some power in proportion" (δύναμίν τινα ἀνάλογον), as its place in the All allows; MacKenna seems to have read ἄλογον, "without reason".
!flag even attention is not necessary to the communication of power | The Greek says the givers need not even "turn" (ἐπιστραφέντων) to the giving of the power: the word for the soul's turning towards something.
!flag since they draw upon a purer nature | The Greek says the heavenly things have "a clearer" or "more vivid" nature (ἐναργεστέρᾳ φύσει), not a purer one.

@p
@greek γένοιτο γὰρ ἂν καὶ ζῷα
For living things might come from a living thing too, without its choice making them, and without its being lessened, or even being aware of it: for its choice, if it had one, would either be the living thing itself, or would not be what made them. And if a living thing has no choice, still less is it aware.
!note Being aware (παρακολουθεῖν) is following along with oneself, self-consciousness (I.4.10, E2; IV.3.30). That the begetter is not lessened is the image of the One's giving (III.8.10, V.1.6).

@ch IV.4.38 | All is woven into one, but virtue has no master
What comes from the All, of its own life or moved by prayers and spells, is to be referred to the nature of what is done. The useful things are its giving, from a greater part to a lesser; harm comes where the subject cannot take in what is useful; mixtures add, and we add much ourselves. Yet all is woven into one, in a wonderful concord; what falls short is matter not mastered. Since all is ordered together, all is signified; but virtue has no master, and its works too are woven in, since the things here hang from the divine.

@older 37
@p
The things, then, that come from the All with nothing moving it, from the rest of its life, and in general all that come from it, and those that come when something else moves it, as by prayers, either simple or sung with art: these are to be referred not to each of those, but to the nature of what is done. And whatever is useful for life or for some other need is to be referred to the giving, going from a greater part to another, lesser one; and whatever harmful thing is said to go from them into the births of living things, is so because the subject cannot receive what is useful: for what comes about does not come about simply, but into this thing and in this way, and what is affected and what will be affected must have some underlying nature of a certain kind.
!flag Whatever springs automatically from the All | MacKenna's chapter 37 runs on here without a break: the Greek's chapter 38 begins with these words (the OCR lost his number 38, shown only as "38. -").
!flag a certain natural tendency in the product | The Greek says only that these things are to be referred to "the nature of what is done" (τὴν τοῦ δρωμένου φύσιν), not to each of the powers; the "tendency to exist with its own quality" is MacKenna's gloss.

@p
@greek πολλὰ δὲ καὶ αἱ μίξεις
Mixtures too do much, each thing giving something useful for living. And something might befall someone though the things that profit do not suit his nature; and the ordering of the wholes does not always give each what it wants; and we ourselves add much to what is given. But all the same, all is woven together into one, and has a wonderful concord, different things coming from different sources, even if they come from opposites: for all are of one.

@p
@greek καὶ εἴ τι δὲ ἐλλεῖπον
And if something among the things that come about falls short of the better, not formed to its end, because the matter was not mastered, it is as if falling short of the noble, deprived of which it falls into ugliness: so that some things are made by those above, the underlying nature brings in others, and others the things themselves add of their own. And since all things are always being ordered together, and all contribute to one, all things are signified; but virtue has no master; and its works too are woven into the order, since the things here hang from there, those in this All from the more divine, and this All too shares in those.
!flag whose absence brings to shame | The Greek says that, deprived of the noble, the thing falls "into ugliness" (εἰς αἰσχρότητα): the form was not mastered in the matter; not shame.
!flag this does not make virtue a matter of compulsion | The Greek says "virtue has no master" (ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀδέσποτον), the words of Lachesis in Plato's myth of Er; MacKenna's paraphrase loses the quotation.
!note "Virtue has no master; as each honours it or dishonours it, he will have more or less of it": Republic X 617e. The same answer to fate is in II.3.9 (E8) and III.1.10 (E10).

@ch IV.4.39 | Like a lawgiver who knows what the citizens will do
Things come about not by seed principles but by principles that embrace them, prior to those of the seeds. The reason of the All is like a lawgiver who knows what the citizens will do and why, and weaves their deeds, honours and dishonours into the laws. Signifying is not the aim: one thing is known from another because all is one. So the difficulty about evils given by the gods is solved: no choice acts, but natural necessity; we add much; good gifts mix into something else; life is for the whole; and matter cannot master what it is given.

@p
The things in the All, then, come about not according to seed principles, but according to principles that embrace them, and those prior to the principles of the seeds. For there is not, in the seed principles, any of the things that come about apart from the seed principles themselves, nor of what matter contributes to the whole, nor of what the things that have come to be do to one another. But the principle of the All would rather be like one who sets the order of a city by reason, and lays down its law, already knowing what the citizens will do and why they will do it, and legislating with a view to all this, and weaving into the laws all their affections and deeds, and the honours and dishonours for their deeds, all things going to concord as if by a road of themselves.
!flag to the principles by which that seed itself takes shape | The Greek says principles "that embrace" (περιληπτικούς) the things that come about, "and of prior things": wider principles that take in matter and chance as well, not those that shape the seeds.
!flag in perfect adaptation of law to custom | The Greek says the lawgiver legislates "with a view to all this" (πρὸς ταῦτα πάντα), what the citizens will do and why; nothing of custom.
!note The seed principles (λόγοι σπερματικοί) are the Stoics' (IV.4.29). The lawgiver who foresees is Plato's (Laws X 903b-905c), where the "king" arranges each soul's place so that virtue wins and vice loses.

@p
@greek ἡ δὲ σημασία οὐ τούτου χάριν
The signifying is not for this, that it should signify as its first aim; but as things come about in this way, some are signified from others. For because all is one and of one, one thing could be known from another, the cause from the caused, what follows from what went before, and the composite from one of its parts, since the one and the other are together.
!flag the compound from the constituents which must make themselves known in the linked total | The Greek says the composite is known "from one of its two parts" (ἀπὸ θατέρου), "since the one and the other are together": from one part we know the whole.

@p
@greek εἰ δὴ ταῦτα ὀρθῶς
If this is rightly said, the difficulties would now be solved, among them the one about the giving of evils by the gods: because it is not choices that act, but what comes from there comes by natural necessities, as of parts to parts, and following on the life of one; because we add much of our own to what comes about; because, of the things given by each, which are not evil, something else comes about in the mixture; because the life is not for the sake of each, but for the sake of the whole; and because the underlying nature, receiving one thing, is affected as another, and cannot even master what is given.
!note That evil comes from the mixture with matter, not from the givers, is III.2.2-3 (E11) and II.3.10-11 (E8).

@ch IV.4.40 | Magic works by sympathy
Sorcery works by sympathy, the natural concord of like things and opposition of unlike, and by the variety of powers in one living being. The true magic is the love and strife in the All, the first sorcerer, whom men watch and copy: love-charms join souls as one ties plants together; the magician uses figures, and figures himself, drawing powers within the one, and outside the All he could draw nothing. Song, sound and gesture lead the unreasoning soul, as music does. Prayers are not heard by choice: the one bewitched by a snake knows it only after, and the sun does not hear.

@p
And sorceries, how do they work? By sympathy, and because there is by nature a concord of like things and an opposition of unlike, and by the variety of the many powers that go to make one living being. For many things are drawn and bewitched with no one else contriving it; and the true magic is the love in the All, and the strife too. This is the first sorcerer and enchanter, whom men have observed, and on one another they use his drugs and his sorceries.
!flag its attractions and, not less, its repulsions | The Greek has "love" and "strife" (φιλία καὶ τὸ νεῖκος), Empedocles' two powers that join and part the elements; MacKenna's physics hides the reference.
!note Love and Strife are Empedocles' (fragment B17). The magicians of Plotinus' day claimed to draw down the gods; Porphyry tells how Olympius tried his star-spells on Plotinus and had them turned back on himself (Life 10).

@p
@greek καὶ γάρ, ὅτι ἐρᾶν
For since things are by nature such as to love, and what makes them love draws them to one another, an art of drawing lovers by sorcery has come about, of men who add by contact natures that draw others together and have love lying in them; and they join one soul to another, as if tying together plants that stand apart. And they make use of figures that have powers, and, figuring themselves so, they bring powers on themselves without a sound, being in one and acting on one: since if someone supposed such a man outside the All, he could neither draw nor bring down by invocations or binding spells; but as it is, because he does not lead as from somewhere else, he can lead, knowing where in the living being one thing is led towards another.
!flag by the force of contact implant in others | The Greek says they "add by contact" (προστιθέντων ἐπαφαῖς) natures, substances or charms that draw together and "have love lying in them"; they do not implant a temperament.

@p
@greek πέφυκε δὲ καὶ ἐπῳδῆς
The soul is of a nature to be led, too, by the melody of a spell, by such a sound, and by the figure of the one who acts: for such things draw it, as pitiable figures and voices do. For it is not choice, nor reason, that is charmed by musical sounds, but the unreasoning soul; and magic of this kind is not wondered at. And yet men love to be enchanted, even if they do not ask this of those who practise the musician's art. And other prayers too we must not think are heard by a choice: for those charmed by spells are not so either, nor, when a snake bewitches men, does the one bewitched understand or perceive, but he knows that he has been affected only after he has been, while his ruling part itself is unaffected. And from the one to whom he prayed, something came to him, or to another; but the sun or another star does not hear.
!flag is welcomed, exacted, from the performers | The Greek says men love to be charmed "even if they do not ask this" (κἂν μὴ τοῦτο αἰτῶνται) of those who use music: the charm comes whether asked for or not.
!flag his highest mind is never caught | The Greek says "the ruling part itself is unaffected" (ἀπαθὲς δ’ αὐτὸ τὸ ἡγούμενον), the Stoics' ruling part of the soul, which knows the affection afterwards.
!note Music that charms the unreasoning soul: Republic III 398c-401a and Laws II 659d-e, where songs are "charms" (ἐπῳδαί) for souls.

@ch IV.4.41 | One string sounds with another
A prayer is fulfilled because part is in sympathy with part, as on one stretched string, moved below, which moves above. One string moved makes another tuned with it perceive, as it were; and if a movement goes from one lyre to another, the All too has one harmony, though of opposites, for all in it are akin. What harms men, like spirit drawn with bile to the liver, comes not in order to harm, as when one takes fire from a fire and burns another without meaning to.

@older 40
@p
And what is prayed for comes about because part is in sympathy with part, as on one stretched string: moved from below, it has the movement above as well. And often, when one string is moved, another has, as it were, a perception of it, by their concord, and by their being tuned to one harmony. And if the movement goes even from one lyre to another, so far as the sympathy reaches, then in the All too there is one harmony, even if it is of opposites: and it is of like things too, and all are akin, even the opposites.
!flag The prayer is answered by the mere fact | MacKenna's chapter 40 runs on here: the Greek's chapter 41 begins with these words (the OCR read his number 41 as "4*.").
!flag for it contains its unisons as well | The Greek says the harmony of the All is "of like things too" (ἐξ ὁμοίων), and all its members are akin, even the opposites; not unisons.
!note The sympathetic string answers IV.4.8, where the music of the stars is "like strings in a lyre moved in sympathy". The harmony of opposites is Heraclitus' (fragment B51, "as of the bow and the lyre").

@p
@greek καὶ ὅσα λωβᾶται
And the things that maim men, such as the spirited part drawn with bile into the nature of the liver, came not as things that would maim: as if someone took fire from a fire and harmed another without contriving that it should go to him. Or the one who took it does act, at least by having given something, transferring it as it were from one to another; and so does what has come, if the one to whom it was carried could not receive it.
!flag blundered in taking it | The Greek says only that the one to whom the fire was carried "could not receive it" (μὴ οἷός τε ἐγένετο δέξασθαι), as matter cannot master what it is given (chapter 39); no blunder.
!note The liver as the seat of desire, and bile with anger, are the Timaeus' (70a-71d); spirit with bile is IV.4.28.

@ch IV.4.42 | The stars give without knowing; the All is unaffected
So the stars need no memory, nor perceptions sent up to them, nor do they nod to prayers by choice: something comes from them with prayer or without, since they are parts of one. As in one living being, the arts of doctors and enchanters force one part to give another some of its power, so the All gives to a part when another draws on it. A bad man may receive, as bad men draw water from rivers; but if he takes what he should not, justice follows him by necessary law. The ruling part of the All is unaffected; the stars are affected as parts, but their choices, bodies and natures are unharmed, and their soul is not lessened.

@p
So the stars will not need memory for this, which is what all this has been worked out for, nor perceptions sent up to them; nor do they nod assent to prayers in this way, by some choice, as some think; but we must grant that something comes from them both with prayer and without prayer, in that they too are parts of one. And there are many powers without choice, both without contrivance and with art, as in one living being: one thing enjoys another, and is harmed by it, by being of such a nature; and by the arts of doctors and of enchanters one thing is forced to give another something of its own power.
!flag any sense of petitions addressed to them | The Greek says the stars need no "perceptions sent up" to them (αἰσθήσεων ἀναπεμπομένων), as if our prayers had to be carried up to their senses.

@p
@greek καὶ τὸ πᾶν δὲ ὡσαύτως
And the All too gives to its parts in the same way, both of itself and when another draws on it for some part of it that lies there: to its own parts, by the same nature, since the one asking is nothing foreign to it. If the one asking is bad, we need not wonder: for bad men draw water from rivers too, and what gives does not itself know what it gives, but only gives; but all the same it has been ordered together with, and given to, the nature of the All. So if someone has taken from what lies there for all, when he should not, justice follows him by a necessary law.
!flag There is, therefore, no necessity by ineluctable law | The Greek is better read "if someone took what he should not" (οὐ δέον) "from what lies there for all, justice follows him by a necessary law": the gift is not withheld, but punishment comes; MacKenna turns it into its opposite.
!note The justice "no one can escape" is Adrasteia (III.2.13, E11; Phaedrus 248c), and it closes the treatise in chapter 45.

@p
@greek οὔκουν δοτέον τὸ πᾶν πάσχειν
We must not grant, then, that the All is affected. Or we must grant that its ruling part is wholly unaffected; and that when affections come about in its parts, the affection reaches those, but since nothing is against its nature, what has come about is no affection as regards the All itself. For the stars too, so far as they are parts, have affections, but they themselves are unaffected: because their choices are unaffected, and their bodies and natures are unharmed; and because, even if they give something through their soul, their soul is not lessened, and their bodies stay the same, and if anything flows away, it goes away unperceived, and what comes to them, if anything comes, comes unnoticed.
!flag since nothing existent can be at strife with the total of existence | The Greek says "since nothing is against its nature" (παρὰ φύσιν δὲ μηδενὸς αὐτῷ ὄντος): what happens in the parts is natural to the All, and so no affection of it.
!note That the heavenly bodies lose nothing, and what flows from them is made up again, is II.1.3-5 (E7).

@ch IV.4.43 | The good man and the spells of nature
The good man is unaffected by sorcery in his soul, and his reason cannot be turned; his unreasoning part, which is of the All, can be affected, but he will not love by philtres, and he will undo spells by counter-spells, though death or illness may come. Daemons too are affected in their unreasoning part, may remember and perceive, and hear those who call. Everything turned towards another is bewitched by it: so all action and the whole practical life are bewitched, as by "the people of great-hearted Erechtheus". Nature gives the deception and the love-charms.

@p
And the good man, how is he affected by sorcery and drugs? In his soul he is unaffected by enchantment, and his reasoning part could not be affected, nor could he be brought to change his opinion; but by whatever unreasoning part of the All is in him he might be affected, or rather that might be affected. But he will not feel loves from drugs, if loving needs the other soul too to assent to the affection of the other. And as the unreasoning part is affected by spells, so he himself, singing counter-spells, will undo the powers there. But death from such things, or illnesses, or whatever is bodily, he might suffer: for the part of the All might be affected by another part, or by the All, but he himself is unharmed. And that the effect comes not at once, but later, is not out of keeping with nature.
!flag the Proficient (the Sage) | The Greek has "the good man" (ὁ σπουδαῖος), the serious, earnest man of the philosophers; "the Proficient" is MacKenna's word throughout.
!note Plotinus himself turned back the spells of Olympius, who tried star-magic on him (Porphyry, Life 10). That death and illness may touch the good man without harming him is I.4.7-8 (E2).

@p
@greek δαίμονες δὲ οὐκ
Daemons, too, are not unaffected in their unreasoning part: it is not absurd to give them memories and perceptions, and to have them charmed, being drawn by nature, and hearing those who call them; those of them that are nearer to the things here, and so far as they are concerned with the things here.
!flag Even the Celestials, the Daimones | The Greek says only "daemons" (δαίμονες), the powers between gods and men; "the Celestials" is MacKenna's.
!note Daemons are between gods and men, and carry prayers up and gifts down (Symposium 202e-203a); that they have memory and perception is IV.3.18.

@p
@greek πᾶν γὰρ τὸ πρὸς ἄλλο
For everything directed towards another is bewitched by another: for what it is directed to bewitches it and leads it; only what is directed towards itself is free of bewitchment. So every action is bewitched, and the whole life of the practical man: for he moves towards the things that charm him. Hence the line: "For fair of face is the people of great-hearted Erechtheus." For why does anyone stand towards another? He is drawn, not by the arts of magicians, but by nature, which gives the deception, and joins one thing to another, not in places, but by the love-charms it gave.
!flag the burgher of great-hearted Erechtheus | The Greek has "the people" (δῆμος) of Erechtheus, the Athenian people, not a citizen of the middle class.
!flag but you should see him naked | Not in the Greek: MacKenna adds, in brackets, the next words of Plato's dialogue, where Socrates says one should see the people stripped.
!note The line is Plato's Alcibiades I (132a), where Socrates fears that Alcibiades, in love with the people of Athens, will be corrupted by them; it echoes the Iliad (II.547), "the people of great-hearted Erechtheus".

@ch IV.4.44 | Only contemplation is free of magic
Only contemplation is unbewitched: the one turned to himself is one, and what he contemplates is himself. Action begins from the unreasoning and the proposals of the affections: care for children, marriage, pleasure, anger, love of rule, fear, gain, and the needs of nature. Whoever does fine actions as necessary, knowing that the truly fine is elsewhere, is not bewitched; whoever loves the fineness in actions, deceived by its traces, is. To pursue what is not good as good is to be led where one did not want: nature's magic. He alone is free who, though drawn by his other parts, calls nothing good but what he knows, not pursuing but having it.

@p
There remains, then, contemplation alone as unbewitched, because no one directed towards himself has been bewitched: for he is one, and what he contemplates is himself, and his reason is not deceived, but does what it should, and makes its own life and its work. But there, in action, it is not one's own self, and not reason, that gives the impulse; the unreasoning too is a beginning, and the premises are those of the affection. For cares for children and efforts towards marriage have a plain drawing, and so do all the things that lure men, becoming pleasant to their desires. Of actions, some are moved unreasoningly by anger, others likewise by desires; political life and the longing for office have the love of rule in us calling them out. And those done so as not to suffer have fear as their beginning, and those done for having more, desire. And those done for the sake of necessities, seeking to fill up nature's lack, plainly have the force of nature, which has made us at home with living.
!flag that unity is all he perceives | The Greek says "what he contemplates is himself" (τὸ θεωρούμενον αὐτός ἐστι): seer and seen are one, as in III.8.6-8 (E14).
!flag this is the first condition of the misfortune | The Greek speaks of "the premises of the affection" (αἱ τοῦ πάθους προτάσεις): action reasons from what affection proposes, as from a premise; πάθος here is affection, not misfortune.
!note "Making us at home" (οἰκείωσις) is the Stoics' word for nature's first gift, which makes each living thing its own and dear to itself (Cicero, On ends III.16).

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις λέγοι
And if someone were to say that actions for fine things are unbewitched, or else that contemplation too, being of fine things, must be called bewitched: if one does even the so-called fine actions as necessary ones, having the truly fine as something else, he is not bewitched; for he knows the necessity, and does not look to what is here, nor is his life directed to other things; but he acts by the force of human nature, and by its being at home in the life of others, or even his own (for it seems reasonable, perhaps, not to take oneself out of life because of this being at home in it); because in this way he was bewitched.
!flag rather than to withdraw from it | MacKenna ends the sentence here and leaves out its last words, "because in this way he was bewitched" (ὅτι οὕτως ἐγοητεύθη): staying in life for its sake is itself nature's spell, though one that the good man sees through.
!note "To take oneself out" (ἐξάγειν ἑαυτόν) is the word for taking one's own life, which I.9 forbids (E4); the Phaedo (62b-c) keeps us at our post.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ τὸ ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν
But if, having loved the fineness in actions, he chooses the actions, deceived by the traces of the fine, he has been bewitched, pursuing the fine that is below: for in general all busying about what is like the true, and all drawing towards it, belongs to one deceived by those things that draw towards them. This is what nature's magic does: for to pursue what is not good as good, drawn by its appearance with unreasoning impulses, belongs to one led where he did not want to go, without knowing it. And what else would one call this but magic? Only he, then, is unbewitched who, drawn by the other parts of himself, says that none of the things they call good is good, but only what he knows himself, not deceived and not pursuing, but having it. So he would not be drawn anywhere.
!flag cheated by the mere track and trace of the Authentic Good | The Greek says "deceived by the traces of the fine" (τοῖς ἴχνεσι τοῦ καλοῦ), the beautiful; the Good comes after, where the not-good is pursued as good.
!note "Led where he did not want to go": no one does wrong willingly, but by ignorance of the good (Plato, Protagoras 358c-d; Gorgias 468c-d).

@ch IV.4.45 | Each goes where it belongs, by a soundless path
Each thing in the All acts and is affected according to its nature, as each part of an animal serves the whole and gives and receives, in a kind of co-awareness of all with all. We too bring into the All not only bodily acting but our other nature, joined by what is akin in us to what is akin outside, up to the daemonic place and beyond: we cannot hide what we are. The bad man is pushed by nature's drawings to his place, the good man drawn otherwise, as by cords; all goes by a soundless path, by a justice none can escape, and the good man knows where he goes and hopes to be with gods. Souls change places like the stars, and punishments are cures of sick parts, for the health of the whole.

@p
From all that has been said, then, this is clear: that as each of the things in the All is in its nature and disposition, so it contributes to the All, and is affected, and acts; just as in each living being each of its parts, as it is in nature and make, so contributes to the whole and serves it, and has been given its rank and its use. It gives what is its own, and receives what comes from the others, as much of it as its nature can receive; and there is as it were a co-awareness of all with all; and if each of the parts were a living being too, it would also have the works of a living being, which are other than those of the part.
!flag in the orders in which each of the parts is also animate | The Greek is a supposition: "if each of the parts were a living being too" (εἰ ... ζῷον ἦν), it would have a living being's works besides a part's.
!note Co-awareness (συναίσθησις) is the self-awareness of the All, as in IV.4.24-25; the body whose parts serve the whole is Plato's (Timaeus 30c-31a).

@p
@greek καὶ δὴ κἀκεῖνο ἀναφαίνεται
And this too comes to light, how it is with us: that we too do something in the All, not only what body does to body, and suffers in turn of the same kind, but we bring in our other nature as well, joined by the kindred things we have to the kindred things outside; and indeed, becoming joined, or rather being joined, by our souls and dispositions to what comes next in the daemonic place, and to what is beyond them, there is no way we can escape notice as to what kind of men we are. We do not all, then, give the same things, nor receive the same: for how could we share with another what we do not have, such as good? Nor again shall we bring anything good to what cannot receive good.
!flag thence onwards with those above the Celestials | The Greek says "to what comes next in the daemonic place, and what is beyond them" (τὰ ἐπέκεινα αὐτῶν): beyond the daemons, the gods; nothing of the Celestials.

@p
@greek τὴν οὖν αὑτοῦ τις κακίαν
Someone, then, who has joined his own wickedness to the whole is known for who he is, and, according to his own nature, is pushed into what he has, and from here, when he is set free, into another place of the same kind, by nature's drawings. But for the good man the takings and the givings and the changes of place are different, as if he were moved by certain drawings of nature, as by cords. So wonderful in power and order is this All, all things coming about by a soundless path, according to a justice that no one can escape; of which the bad man understands nothing, but is led, not knowing, to where he must be carried in the All; but the good man both knows, and goes away where he must, and knows before he goes away where he must live when he has come there, and is of good hope that he will be with gods.
!flag transpose the cords | The Greek says the good man's changes are "as if moved by certain drawings of nature, as by cords" (ὥσπερ ἐκ μηρίνθων ὁλκαῖς τισι φύσεως): other cords, not the same ones transposed.
!flag a wonder of power and wisdom | The Greek says the All is wonderful "in power and order" (δυνάμεως καὶ τάξεως); "wisdom" is MacKenna's.
!note "By a soundless path, according to justice": Hecuba's prayer to Zeus in Euripides' Trojan Women (887-888), "treading a soundless path you lead all mortal things by justice". The cords are the puppet's of Plato's Laws (I 644d-645a); good hope to be with gods is the Phaedo's (63b-c, 69c).

@p
@greek ἐν μὲν γὰρ ὀλίγῳ ζῴῳ
For in a small living being the changes of its parts are small, and their co-awarenesses, and its parts cannot be living beings, except perhaps for a short while in some; but in one where the distances are so great, and each thing in it has room to move, and there are many living beings, the movements and the changes of place must be greater. We see the sun and the moon and the other stars changing place and moving in order. It is not unreasonable, then, that souls too should change place, not keeping always the same character, but ranked in proportion to what they have suffered and what they do, some taking the place as of the head, others as of the feet, in concord with the All: for the All too has differences towards the better and the worse. But a soul that neither chooses the better here, nor has a share in the worse, has exchanged this place for another, a pure one, taking the one it chose.
!flag taking this sphere in free election | MacKenna has the soul leave a purer place for this one; the Greek says it "took in exchange for this place another, a pure one" (ἄλλον τόπον καὶ καθαρὸν ἠλλάξατο τοῦτον), which it chose: it goes up from here.
!note The souls' changes of place are the Phaedo's (113d-114c) and the myth of Er's (Republic X 617d-620d), where each chooses its next life.

@p
@greek αἱ δὲ κολάσεις ὥσπερ
The punishments are like those of sick parts: for some, astringent drugs; for others, removals, or changes; so that the All may be healthy, each being put where it should be. And the health of the All comes by one thing being changed, and another being taken away from here, as being sick here, and set where it will not be sick.
!note Punishment as the soul's medicine is Plato's (Gorgias 478d-480b; Laws X 904a-905c), and so is the part cut away for the health of the whole (Laws V 735d-736a).

# Milestone E18: IV.5 On difficulties about the soul, third part, or on sight, and IV.6 On perception and memory, beside
# MacKenna's vol. III (1924, the Fourth Ennead; pp. 102-121). MacKenna's chapters are the Greek's in both treatises. His
# headings were caught by the OCR in two places within his chapters ("PROBLEMS OF THE SOUL"), which the flags avoid. In
# IV.5.8 he marks a passage as a tentative rendering of an obscure and corrupt place, in square brackets.

@treatise IV.5 | On difficulties about the soul, third part, or on sight
The third of the books On difficulties about the soul, also called On sight. Does seeing need a body between the eye and what is seen, air or some other transparent body? Plotinus argues that it does not. The air between is not stamped like wax and does not pass the form along: at night we see fires and stars across the dark, and every bit of the air holds the whole face that is seen, which no stamp could do. Seeing comes from the sympathy of the All, one living being whose parts feel one another, and so does hearing. Light is not an affection of the air but the activity of a shining body, going out from it as an image of the life within it; it is bodiless, does not perish or run back, and is wherever its source is active and nothing hinders, like an image in a mirror, or the life that a soul gives a body. Last, a puzzle put off from the third chapter: could sight from here see a body outside the heaven, which is not part of the one living being? The hypothesis contradicts itself and must be let go.

@ch IV.5.1 | Does seeing need something between?
Perceiving needs a body, for without a body the soul is in the intelligible; it comes about through organs made like the things perceived. But does sight need a body between the eye and the colour? Thick bodies hinder seeing, and thinner ones hinder it less; what lies between need not be affected, as the rod between the torpedo fish and the hand is not. If seeing comes by sympathy, the unlike thing between will not be affected, and what is made to be affected will be affected all the more with nothing between.

@p
Since we put off the question whether one can see when there is nothing between, such as air or another of the bodies called transparent, we must look into it now. That seeing, and perceiving in general, must come about through some body, has been said: for without a body the soul would be wholly in the intelligible. And since perceiving is the grasping not of intelligibles but of sensibles only, the soul must somehow be brought into contact with the sensibles, through things made like them, and make some sharing with them, of knowledge or of affection. That is why the knowledge comes through bodily organs: through these, which are as it were grown together with it or continuous with it, it goes as it were into one with the sensibles themselves, and so a kind of like affection with them comes about.
!flag by means of whatever may bridge the gap | The Greek says "through things made like them" (διὰ τῶν προσομοίων): the organs are made like the sensibles, and it is this likeness, not a bridge, that joins the soul to them; the likeness comes back in IV.5.8.
!flag a certain degree of identity (which is the basis of knowledge) | The Greek says "a kind of like affection" (ὁμοπαθείας τινός): the organ is affected as the thing is, which is likeness of affection, not identity; the bracket is MacKenna's.
!note "Has been said": in IV.4.23, where the soul, to perceive sensibles, must use a body as its instrument, being likened to them through it. "The bodies called transparent" (διαφανῆ) are Aristotle's: for him sight needs a medium, the transparent made actual by light, and in a void nothing would be seen, as Democritus wrongly thought (On the soul II.7, 418b4-419a21).

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν δεῖ συναφήν
If, then, there must be some contact with the things known, why would one inquire about the things known by some kind of touch? But about sight (and whether about hearing too, later): about seeing, then, whether there must be some body between the sight and the colour. Or the body between might perhaps touch on it by accident, but contributes nothing to seeing for those who see. But if dense bodies, like earthy ones, hinder seeing, and the thinner what lies between, the better we see, one would count what lies between as a hindrance to seeing; or, if not a hindrance, one would not call it a help either.
!flag such an intervening material may be a favouring circumstance | The Greek νύττοι is "might prod" or "touch on" (the text is uncertain), but nothing in it says the body between favours seeing: the same sentence says it contributes nothing.
!flag such as clay | The Greek says "earthy ones" (τὰ γεηρά), bodies of earth, the densest of the elements.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τὸ πάθος
But suppose the medium receives the affection first and is as it were stamped. A sign of it, they say, is that if someone is in front of us, looking towards the colour, he sees it too: if no affection came to be in what is between, it would not reach us either. Or the medium need not be affected, if what is made to be affected is affected; or, if it is affected, it is affected with something else: for the rod between the torpedo fish and the hand is not affected with what the hand is affected with. And yet there too, if the rod and the line were not between, the hand would not be affected. Or this too might be disputed: for if the fish comes inside a net, the fisherman, they say, is numbed.
!flag anyone facing to the object from the side opposite to ourselves sees it equally | The Greek says "if someone is in front of us (ἔμπροσθέν τις ἡμῶν), looking towards the colour": a man standing between us and the colour, in the very space the affection must cross, sees it too; not one on the far side. The bracket before it is MacKenna's.
!note The torpedo (νάρκη), the numbing ray, is Meno's image for Socrates (Meno 80a-c); Aristotle tells how it numbs the fish it hunts (History of Animals IX.37, 620b19-24). The line (ἡ θρίξ) is the horsehair line of the rod.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ γὰρ κινδυνεύει
But the argument is in danger of going to the so-called sympathies. If this thing is made to be affected sympathetically by that one because it has some likeness to it, what is between, being unlike, would not be affected; or it would not be affected in the same way. And if so, the thing made to be affected would be affected much more if nothing is between, even if what is between is such as to be affected somewhat itself.
!note Sympathy (συμπάθεια), the feeling-together of the parts of the All as of one living being, was the subject of IV.4.32-45; that "like is affected by like" goes back to the early philosophers (Aristotle, On generation and corruption I.7, 323b1-15).

@ch IV.5.2 | No theory of sight needs a medium
Whatever theory of sight one holds, nothing need lie between: not for those who send light out of the eye, nor for the atomists' images, which want the void; and for those who explain sight by sympathy, what is between can only dim it, though in a living being nature may want it so. Air is not affected by what passes through it, but only parted, as by a falling stone or rising fire. If we perceived through the air being affected first, we would perceive the air next to us, as with warmth; but sight is not by contact, and the air must be lit only because it is dark.

@p
If, then, seeing is such that the light of the eye joins up with the light as far as the sensible thing, this light must be between, and this hypothesis requires this between. But if the coloured body lying there works a change, what prevents the change from going straight to the eye, with nothing between? Even if, now, when there is something there, what lies in front of the eyes is of necessity changed somehow. And those who pour the sight out would not be bound to say that something must in any case be between, unless they feared the ray might fall; but it is a ray of light, and light goes straight. Those who make resistance the cause would in any case need what is between. The champions of the images, who say they pass through the void, look for room so that they may not be hindered; so, if having nothing between hinders them still less, they will not dispute the hypothesis.
!flag this all the more, since as things are | The Greek says "even if" (εἰ καὶ): granted that the air in front of the eyes is in fact changed now, when there is air there, that does not make it needed. The bracket that follows is MacKenna's.
!note Three theories of sight: the ray poured out from the eye (Plato's Timaeus 45b-46a, and the mathematicians' optics); the Stoics', for whom the air, stretched by the breath from the eye, is pressed on like a staff (Diogenes Laertius VII.157); and the atomists', for whom thin images (εἴδωλα) flow from things through the void into the eye (Epicurus, Letter to Herodotus 46-50).

@p
@greek ὅσοι δὲ συμπαθείᾳ
Those who say seeing comes by sympathy will say that we see less if something is between, insofar as it hinders, impedes and dims the sympathy; or rather, it follows for them to say that even what is akin always dims it, insofar as it too is affected. For if a body continuous in depth were burned by fire falling on it, still its depth would be less affected than the front, on which the fire falls. But if they were sympathetic parts of one living being, would it be affected less because something is between? Or it would be affected less, but the affection would be in measure, as much as nature wanted, what is between keeping off the excess; unless perhaps what is given were such that what is between is not affected at all.
!flag there will scarcely be less sensation because of the intervening substance | The Greek asks whether it would be affected less, and answers that it would (ἧττον μὲν ἂν πάθοι), but in measure, "as much as nature wanted" (ὅσον ἐβούλετο ἡ φύσις), the between keeping off the excess.
!flag where the element introduced is of a kind to overleap the bridge | The Greek says "unless what is given were such that what is between is not affected at all" (ὥστε ὅλως τὸ μεταξὺ μὴ πάσχειν); nothing overleaps.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ συμπαθὲς τῷ ἓν ζῷον
But if we are affected because the All is sympathetic by being one living being, since we are in one and of one, must there not be continuity when there is perception of what is far? Or continuity, and the between, are there because the living being must be continuous, but the affection belongs to the continuous by accident; or else we shall say that everything is affected by everything. But if this thing is affected by that, and another by another, not the same, one would not need the between everywhere.
!note "In one and of one": we are parts within the one living being, the All, and belong to it, as in IV.4.32 and IV.4.45. That the All is one living being with a soul is the Timaeus' (30b-d).

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν ἐπὶ ὄψεως
If, then, someone were to say that sight needs it, he must say why: for it does not appear that what goes through air always affects the air; it only parts it. If a stone falls from above, what else happens than that the air does not stand its ground? For it is not reasonable either that it falls by the pushing round, since its movement is natural; for then fire too would go up by the pushing round. But that is absurd: fire outruns the pushing round of the air by its own movement, which is swift. And if someone says the pushing round is quickened by the swiftness, that would happen by accident, not to carry it up: for the rush upward comes from the logs too, though they do not push. And we too, when we move, cut the air, and the pushing round does not push us; the air only follows and fills what is emptied by us.
!flag in trees the upthrust from the root depends on no such external propulsion | The Greek ξύλα are the logs of a fire: the flame rushes up from the wood, though the wood does not push it (οὐκ ὠθούντων); nothing of trees or roots.
!note "The pushing round" (ἀντιπερίστασις) is the replacement by which air, pushed aside, closes in behind a moving body and drives it on: Plato's Timaeus 79e-80c, and Aristotle, who uses it for thrown things (Physics IV.8, 215a14-17; VIII.10, 266b27-267a20). Plotinus denies that it moves natural motions, which go of themselves.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν τοῖς σώμασι
If, then, the air stands apart for such bodies without being affected, what prevents it from letting the forms that come to sight pass even without standing apart? And if the forms do not even come by as in a stream, what need is there for the air to be affected, and for the affection to come to us through it by its being affected first? For if our perceiving came from the air being affected first, we would not see the seen thing by looking at it, but would get the perception from what lies next to us, as with being warmed. There it is not the fire far off but the air next to us, warmed, that seems to warm us: for this is by touch; but in seeing it is not by touch. That is why the sensible thing, put on the eye, does not make us see; but what is between must be lit, because the air is dark. If it were not dark, perhaps there would have been no need of light at all: for the dark, being a hindrance to seeing, must be mastered by light. And perhaps a thing brought up to the sight is not seen because it brings the air's shadow and its own.
!flag If it were not for this dark substance there would probably be no reason for the existence of light | The Greek says that if the air were not dark, perhaps "there would have been no need of light" (οὐδ’ ἂν ἐδέησε φωτός) for seeing; not that light would have no reason to exist.
!note That a coloured thing laid on the eye is not seen is Aristotle's (On the soul II.7, 419a12-13); for him this shows the medium is needed, for Plotinus that sight is not by contact.

@ch IV.5.3 | Fires at night, and the whole face in every part of the air
The strongest witness: at night, in the dark, we see fires, the stars and their shapes, and the beacons and the signal towers for ships, though their light does not light the dark between; if the air passed the form on, we should see a dim copy, not the bright thing. If seeing with nothing between failed, it would be because sympathy was gone. Nor is the air stamped like wax: each bit of it would hold a bit of the thing, yet everyone around sees the whole, so that each bit holds the whole face; this comes from greater necessities, of soul and of one living being.

@p
The greatest evidence that we do not see the form of the sensible thing through the air being affected, as by passing it on, is that at night, in the dark, fire and the stars are seen, and their shapes. No one will say that the forms came to be in the dark and so joined on to the eye; or else there would be no dark, the fire having shone its form into it. For even when the dark is very deep, and the stars too are hidden, and the light from the fires does not shine out into it, the fire is seen from the beacon towers, and from the towers that give signals to ships. And if someone, going against what perception shows, says that in these cases too the fire passes through the air, the sight should have grasped the dim thing in the air, not the fire itself, as bright as it is.
!note The Greek of the third sentence has "and the fire" in Volkmann's brackets, as a doubtful word. Beacon fires (φρυκτωρίαι) carried news from height to height, as in Aeschylus' Agamemnon (281-316), and lighthouses, such as the Pharos of Alexandria, signalled to ships.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ μεταξὺ σκότου
But if what is beyond is seen with darkness between, much more would it be seen with nothing between. But one might pause at this: that with nothing between it will not be possible to see, not because nothing is between, but because the sympathy of the living being with the things, and of its parts with one another by being one, is taken away. For perceiving, in whatever way, seems to be for this reason: that this All is a living being in sympathy with itself. If it were not, how would one thing share in the power of another, and above all of one far off?
!flag We may hold one thing certain | The Greek says "one might pause at this" (ἐπιστήσειεν): a doubt raised, not something held certain: perhaps with nothing between we could not see, not because nothing is between, but because sympathy would be taken away.

@p
@greek τοῦτο δὴ ἐπισκεπτέον
This, then, must be looked into: if there were another cosmos, another living being, not contributing to this one, and there were sight on the back of the heaven, would it see that other from a measured distance, or would this have no relation to that? But this later.
!flag would our sphere see that other as from a mutually present distance | The Greek asks whether the sight "on the back of the heaven" would see that other "from a measured distance" (ἐκ διαστήματος συμμέτρου), one suited to seeing; not "our sphere", nor a distance "mutually present".
!note "The back of the heaven" (τὰ νῶτα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) is where the souls stand in the Phaedrus and see what is beyond the heaven (247b-c). The question is taken up in IV.5.8.

@p
@greek νῦν δὲ κἀκεῖνο
For now one might bring in this witness too, that seeing does not come about by the medium being affected. If the air were affected, it would surely have to be affected bodily: that is, as an impression comes to be in wax. Then a part of the seen thing would have to be stamped on each bit of the air, so that the bit touching the sight would be just as large as the bit of the seen thing that the pupil could receive in its own size. But in fact the whole is seen, and all who are in the air, straight opposite and from the sides, see it over a long way, near and behind, if they are not blocked: so that each bit of the air holds the whole of the face that is seen, as it were; and this not by a body's affection, but by greater necessities, of soul, and of one living being in sympathy.
!flag the greater laws, the spiritual, of a living being one and self-sensitive | The Greek says "greater necessities" (μείζους ἀνάγκας), "of soul" (ψυχικάς), and of one living being "in sympathy" (συμπαθοῦς): necessities, not laws, and sympathy, not self-sensitiveness.
!note The impression in wax is Plato's (Theaetetus 191c-d) and Aristotle's, for whom sense takes the form without the matter, as wax takes the seal's sign without its iron or gold (On the soul II.12, 424a17-21). IV.6 turns the same argument against imprints in the soul.

@ch IV.5.4 | The light that joins the eye to the thing
If the light that joins sight to its object is ensouled, the soul in it, seeing is like touch and needs nothing between to be affected; light from outside is needed for seeing far. The seen thing is not idle: touch reports differences, and would feel what is far if nothing blocked it; we feel a fire as soon as the air between does. At dawn we see the light far off before it reaches the air round us. If the soul used light like a staff, the perceiving would be by pushing, and it would need to have been near the thing before.

@p
But how is it with the light that joins the sight to what is around the sight, as far as the sensible thing? First, it does not need the air between, unless perhaps light could not be spoken of without air (in that way the air is between by accident); but the light itself would be between without being affected: there is no need of affection here at all, but all the same of what is between; and if light is not a body, not of a body. And the sight would need the light from outside and between not for seeing simply, but for seeing far. Whether light could come to be without air, later; now we must look at this.
!note "Later": in IV.5.6. "The light of the sight" is the fire within the eye of Plato's Timaeus (45b-d), which joins with the daylight like with like and forms one body stretching to the thing seen.

@p
@greek εἰ μὲν γὰρ τὸ φῶς
If this joining light becomes ensouled, and the soul is carried through it and comes to be in it, as with the light within too, then in grasping, which is seeing, it would not need the light as something between: seeing will be like touch, the power of sight grasping in the light, with nothing between affected; but the sight goes out there.
!flag as it does in its more inward acts such as understanding — which is what vision really is | The Greek compares the light inside the eye: the soul is in the joining light "as with the light within too" (ὥσπερ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἔνδον), in the grasping "which is seeing" (ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁρᾶν); nothing is said of understanding.

@p
@greek οὗ δὴ ζητητέον
Here we must ask whether the sight has to travel there because there is some distance, or because there is some body in the distance. If because there is a body in the distance, it will see if this separating thing is taken away; but if simply because there is distance, one must suppose the nature of the visible to be idle, doing nothing at all. But that cannot be: for touch does not only say that something is near and touch it, but, being affected, reports the differences of what is touched; and if nothing separated them, it would perceive what is far too. For we perceive fire at the same time as the air between does, not waiting for that to be warmed. Indeed, the solid body is warmed more than the air: so it is warmed through the air, rather, but not because of it. If, then, the one has the power to act, and the other to be acted upon, in any way at all, why does it need some other medium for what it is able to act on? That is to need a hindrance.
!flag if the intervenient is the sole attractive agent | The Greek says "if simply because there is distance" (εἰ δ’ ὅτι διάστημα ἁπλῶς): the sight travels because of the bare interval, not drawn by anything in it.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ ὅταν τὸ φῶς
For when the sun's light comes on, it is not that the air must perceive first and then we, but at the same time; and often before it comes near the sight, while it is still elsewhere, so that we see without the air being affected, with what is unaffected between, and the light, to which the sight must join, not yet come. And seeing the stars, or any fire, at night is hard to square with this hypothesis.
!note The sun's coming light is dawn: we see the sunlit hills far off before the light is round us. The light "to which the sight must join" is the Timaeus' daylight again (45c).

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ μένει
But if the soul stays by itself and needs light like a staff to reach the thing, the grasping would have to be forceful, the light pressing back and stretched, and the sensible thing, as colour, would have to push back itself: for that is how touches through a medium are. And then it must first have come near, with nothing between at that time: for in that way touching through a medium later makes knowledge, as by memory, and still more by reasoning; but in fact it is not so. And if the light next to the sensible thing must be affected and then pass it on as far as the sight, the hypothesis becomes the same as the one by which the sensible thing first changes what is between, against which difficulties have already been raised elsewhere.
!flag the percipient mind or soul remains within itself | The Greek says only "the soul" (ἡ ψυχή); "mind" is MacKenna's, as often in these chapters. The bracket before it is his too.
!flag but this process of memory and comparison is excluded by the theory of first knowledge through the agency of a medium | The Greek says "but in fact it is not so" (νῦν δὲ οὐχ οὕτως): we do not in fact first come near what we see, and know it later by memory or reasoning; it is a fact, not a theory, that rules this out.
!note The staff (βακτηρία) and the light "pressing back" (ἀντερείδοντος) are the Stoics': the air between the eye and the thing, stretched by the breath, is like a staff, by which what is seen is reported as a blind man feels by his stick (Diogenes Laertius VII.157). Plotinus answers that a staff tells us only of what we have touched before; "reasoning" (συλλογισμός) is inference from a sign to a thing known already.

@ch IV.5.5 | Hearing is the same question
In hearing the air struck first, between two bodies that clash, seems needed; but what is between, from there on, may be there only by accident. If the air were master of the sound, why would bronze on bronze sound different from bronze on something else? The air sounds when it is struck as a solid before it scatters, so the clash itself is the sound, as the sounds inside animals show, of bones rubbing and grinding, with no air between. The question is the same as for sight: a kind of co-perception within one living being.

@p
About hearing, then: must we grant here that the air next to what makes the noise suffers the first movement from it, and that the noise comes to perception because the air as far as the hearing suffers the same? Or is what is between there by accident, because it is present in the middle, and, if it were taken away, once the noise had come about, as when two bodies clash, would the perception meet us at once? Or the first air, the air that is struck, is needed, but from there on what is between is another matter. For here the air seems to be master of the noise: two bodies clashing together would not make even the beginning of a noise unless the air, struck in their swift meeting and pushed out, struck the next and passed it on as far as the ears and hearing.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ ὁ ἀὴρ κύριος
But if the air is master of the noise, and the stroke comes from its being moved, what would the differences of voices and noises come from? Bronze sounds one way against bronze, another against something else, and one thing another way against another; but the air is one, and so is the stroke in it: for the differences are not only by loud and soft. And if a stroke made a noise because it came against air, it must be said that it did not do so as air: for air sounds when it takes the stand of a solid body, staying like something solid before it is poured away; so that the things that clash, and their collision, are enough, and this stroke, come to perception, is the noise. The sounds inside animals bear witness too, which are not in air, but come when one part clashes with and strikes another: as the bendings of bones rubbing on each other, with no air between, and grindings. But let this be left in doubt, the question having become the same here too as was said for sight, the affection in hearing too being a kind of co-perception, as in a living being.
!flag until (by its distinctive character) it is sent pulsing outwards | The Greek says air sounds when it stands like a solid "before it is poured away" (πρὶν χυθῆναι), before it scatters; the bracket, and the pulsing, are MacKenna's.
!flag we are brought to the same conclusion as in the case of sight | The Greek says "let this be left in doubt" (ἠπορήσθω), the question here having become the same as for sight: a question left open, not a conclusion.
!note Aristotle: sound comes from a stroke of one solid on another, in air, and the air must be struck quickly and firmly, before it scatters; bronze and smooth hard things sound best (On the soul II.8, 419b4-25). "Co-perception" (συναίσθησις) is the shared awareness of the parts of one living being, as in IV.4.45.

@ch IV.5.6 | Light is not the air's affection
Would there be light without air? If light were the air's affection, without air there would be none; but light belongs first to fiery and shining bodies, and to some stones. If it is a quality it needs a body; if it is an activity from something, it would cross a void too and go beyond. It does not fall, is not drawn along by the air, and goes when its source goes; it is the activity of the sun's body, from a subject but not into one, as life is the activity of soul whether a body is there or not. The dark air does not make light but dims it, and air that is lit stays as it was.

@p
But would light come to be if there were no air, the sun shining on the surfaces of bodies, with a void between, which now too is lit by accident, because it is there? But if the other things are affected because the air is affected, light too would have its existence through the air, being its affection; so the affection would not be, if what is to be affected were not. Or, first, light is not the air's first, nor its as air: for it belongs also to each fiery and shining body itself; and indeed the colour of such stones is bright.
!flag The fact is that primarily light is no appanage of air | The Greek says light is not the air's "first, nor its as air" (οὐκ αὐτοῦ πρώτως οὐδ’ ᾗ αὐτός): air may be lit, but light belongs to it neither first nor by its own nature.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ τὸ εἰς ἄλλο
But would what goes into another, from what has such a colour, be there if that other were not? If it is only a quality, and the quality of something, then, since every quality is in a subject, we must look for the body that light will be in. But if it is an activity from another, why should it not be, and fall on what lies beyond too, if there is no body next to it but, as it were, a void between, if that is possible? For being taut, why will it not cross, riding on nothing? And if it were such as to fall, it would be carried down: for neither the air nor anything at all that is lit will be what draws it from the source of light and forces it to go forward. Since it is not an accident either, so as to be always on another, nor another's affection, so as to need something to be affected; or else it would have had to stay when it had come; but in fact it goes away: so it could come as well.
!flag it is powerful, and may very well pass over unhelped | The Greek says it is "taut" (ἀτενές), stretched straight, and asks why it should not cross "riding on nothing" (οὐκ ἐποχούμενον).
!flag it would vanish when the object or substance disappeared ; but it does not | The Greek argues the other way: if light were the air's affection, it "would have had to stay" once it had come (ἔδει μένειν), as an affection stays in what has it; "but in fact it goes away" (νῦν δὲ ἄπεισιν), with its source; so it is no affection of the air.
!note Against Aristotle, for whom light is not a body but the activity of the transparent as transparent, and colour moves the transparent which is actual (On the soul II.7, 418b4-20): Plotinus makes light the activity of the shining body, not of the medium.

@p
@greek ποῦ οὖν;
Where, then? Or there need only be place. Or in that way the body of the sun will lose the activity that goes out of it; and this was the light. And if so, the light will not be anything's either. But the activity is from a subject, not into a subject; though the subject would be affected somewhat, if it were there.
!flag Perhaps ; and (from this untenable consequence) we may gather that the light never was an appanage of anything | The Greek does not agree: that "the light will not be anything's" (οὐδὲ τὸ φῶς τινος ἔσται) is a further absurdity of the objection, which Plotinus answers: the activity is "from a subject" (ἔκ τινος ὑποκειμένου), the sun's, though not into one.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ζωὴ
But just as life, being the activity of soul, is the activity of something that would be affected, the body for example, if it were there, and is so also when it is not, what would prevent it being so with light too, if indeed it is some activity of what is luminous? For even now it is not the darkness of the air that begets light; rather, being mixed with earth, it makes the light dark and not truly pure: so that it is like saying that something is sweet if it is mixed with something bitter. And if someone says light is a change of the air, we must say that the air itself would have had to be changed by the change, and its darkness, altered, to have become not dark. But in fact the air stays as it is, as if it had suffered nothing. And the affection must be of that whose affection it is: so neither is light the air's colour, but it is on its own, and the air is there. Let this, then, be looked at in this way.
!note The life of the soul goes out whether or not a body is there to take it, as in IV.4.18-20, where the body has a trace of soul as air has light. That light is from a subject but not into one is Plotinus' "double activity": the activity of a thing, which is the thing, and the activity from it, as heat from fire (V.4.2, V.1.6).

@ch IV.5.7 | Light, the outward activity of a shining body
Light does not perish or run back: it is an activity that does not flow, so it is there while its source is, and where nothing hinders. Every being has an activity that is its likeness, an image of the life within, reaching far or near; so in eyes that shine, and in creatures that glow in the dark when they swell and not when they shrink. Light from bodies is the outward activity of a luminous body; in such bodies it is their being; mixed with matter it gives colour. It is bodiless, and does not properly come or go, like the image in a mirror. So too a soul that is the activity of a soul before it stays while that stays; and the body's life, when the body perishes, is simply no longer there.

@p
Does it perish, then, or run back? Perhaps from this too we might gain something for what came before. If it were inside, so that what had received it had it as its own already, perhaps one would have said that it perishes. But if it is an activity that does not flow (for then it would flow round, and be poured inside, more than what was being cast on it from the active thing), it would not perish while the source of light stays in being. And when that is moved, it is in another place, not as if an ebb or a change of flow had come about, but because the activity is that thing's, and comes to be present as far as nothing hinders. For even if the sun's distance from us were many times what it is now, there would be light as far as there, with nothing hindering or standing in the way between.
!flag but in circuit, with more of it | The Greek's bracketed clause tells what would happen if light did flow (περιέρρει γὰρ ἄν): it would flow round and pour inside, more than was being sent from the source; MacKenna makes it a description of light as it is.

@p
@greek ἔστι δὲ ἡ μὲν ἐν αὐτῷ
The activity in the luminous body itself is like the life of the body, and greater, and like the beginning and spring of its activity; the one beyond the limit of the body, an image of the one within, is a second activity, which does not stand apart from the first. For each of the things that are has an activity which is its likeness, so that while it is, that is too, and while it stays, that reaches far, further in one thing, less far in another; some activities are weak and dim, some even unnoticed, but in some things they are greater and reach far; and when they reach far, one must think the activity is there where the active and powerful thing is, and also where it reaches. One can see it too in the eyes of animals whose eyes shine, where light comes to be outside their eyes as well; and indeed in animals that have fire gathered inside, which shines out into the outside in the dark when they swell, and when they contract there is no light outside; nor has it perished, but it either is or is not outside.
!flag the other lies next to the surface, the outer image of the inner content | The Greek says the second activity is "after the limit of the body" (μετὰ τὸ πέρας τοῦ σώματος): outside it, going out from it, not lying on its surface.
!note Every being has an activity that is its likeness: Plotinus' double activity again (V.4.2), by which each thing gives out an image of itself, as the One gives intellect and intellect soul (V.1.6-7). Animals whose eyes shine in the dark, and things seen in darkness, are in Aristotle (On the soul II.7, 419a2-6); those with fire inside are glow-worms and fireflies.

@p
@greek τί οὖν; εἰσελήλυθεν;
What then? Has it gone in? Or it is not outside because the fire is not turned to the outside either, but has sunk inward. Has the light, then, sunk in too? Or no, only the fire; and when that has sunk in, the rest of the body is in front of it, so that it is not active towards the outside. So the light from bodies is the activity of a luminous body towards the outside; but the light in such bodies themselves, those that are such primarily, is wholly their being, the being according to the form of the primarily luminous body. When such a body is mixed with matter, it gives colour; but the activity alone does not give colour, but as it were colours over the surface, since it belongs to another and hangs from that, as it were, and what stands away from that stands away from its activity too.
!flag it gives merely an incipient on which colour might be formed | The Greek says the activity alone "as it were colours over" (οἷον ἐπιχρώννυσιν), a tint on the surface, not a base on which colour might be formed; and the "other" whose activity it is, is the luminous body, not MacKenna's "(primal light)".

@p
@greek ἀσώματον δὲ πάντως
One must set it down as wholly bodiless, even if it is a body's. That is why "it has gone away" and "it is present" are not said of it properly, but in another way, and its existence is as an activity. For the image in the mirror too must be called the activity of the thing seen in it, acting on what can be affected, without flowing; but if the thing is present, the image too appears there, and is there in this way, as an image of colour shaped thus; and if the thing goes away, the transparent no longer has what it had before, when the seen thing was there to act upon it.
!note The mirror image is the soul's figure in I.4.10 and in IV.3.12, where the souls see their images in the mirror of Dionysus; matter as a mirror is in III.6.7-13.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴς ψυχῆς
So too with the soul: insofar as it is the activity of another soul before it, while the earlier stays, the activity that comes next stays too. But what if something is not an activity, but from an activity, such as we said the body's own life is, like the light that is already mixed with bodies? Or here it is because what makes the colour is mixed in as well. But what of the body's life? It has it from another soul lying beside it. When, then, the body perishes (for nothing can be without a share of soul): when the body perishes, and neither the soul that gave it life is enough for it nor any that may lie beside it, how could life still stay? What then? Has this life perished? No, not this either: for this too is an image of the shining; it is simply no longer there.
!flag it is clear that the life-principle can no longer remain | The Greek asks it: "how could life still stay?" (πῶς ἂν ἔτι ζωὴ μένοι;), and goes on to answer that it has not perished either.
!note "As we said": the body's own life, a trace of soul, which makes it a living body of such a kind, is in IV.4.18-20 and 28-29. Soul as the activity of a soul before it is the soul of the All and nature, its image (IV.4.13-14, III.8.4-5).

@ch IV.5.8 | Could we see a body outside the heaven?
Could sight from here see a body outside the heaven, with nothing in the way? If seeing comes by sympathy within one living being, it could not, unless that body were a part of it, even if it were coloured like the things here. One might call it absurd that sight should not see a colour present to it; but it seems absurd because here we act and are acted on within one and as of one. If perception is by likeness, it is the soul of this living being that makes things like, and what is there would be nothing to it. The hypothesis says soul and not soul, akin and not akin, all and not all, and must be let go.

@p
But if there were a body outside the heaven, and some sight from here, with nothing hindering it from seeing, would it see what is not in sympathy with it, if sympathy now comes by the nature of one living being? Or, if sympathy comes because the things that perceive and the things perceived are of one living being, the perceptions too would not be so, unless this body outside were a part of this living being: if it were, perhaps they would. But if it were not a part, but a coloured body, having the other qualities too, of the same kind as the organ here?
